description: NTC's American Idioms Dictionary — 21 866 idiomatic phrases with definitions and examples. Compacted from zaghloul404/englishidioms (CC0/research). Filtered to single-sense common phrases ≤ 5 words.
_note: HOT subset: NTC entries also in MWE index (tokenizer-frequent)

by all accounts.monolingual: from all the reports [that are available]; according to what everyone is saying. _ According to all accounts, the police were on the scene immediately. _ By all accounts, it was a very poor performance.
examples: According to all accounts, the police were on the scene immediately.

ace in the hole.monolingual: Fig. something important held in reserve. _The twenty-dollar bill I keep in my shoe is my ace in the hole.
examples: The twenty-dollar bill I keep in my shoe is my ace in the hole.

add fuel to the fire.monolingual: Fig. to make a problem worse; to say or do something that makes a bad situation worse; to make an angry person get even angrier. (Alludes to causing a flame to grow larger when fuel is added.) _Shouting at a crying child just adds fuel to the fire.
examples: Shouting at a crying child just adds fuel to the fire.

alive and kicking.monolingual: Fig. well and healthy. _ Jane: How is Bill since his illness last month? Mary: Oh; he’s alive and kicking. _The last time I saw Tom, he was alive and well.
examples: Jane: How is Bill since his illness last month? Mary: Oh; he’s alive and kicking.

all over the world.monolingual: Fig. everywhere. _Gravity acts the same all over the earth. _Human nature is the same all over the world.
examples: Gravity acts the same all over the earth.

all the same.monolingual: nevertheless; anyhow. _ They were told not to bring presents, but they brought them all the same. _ His parents told him to stay home, but John went out just the same.
examples: They were told not to bring presents, but they brought them all the same.

just the same.monolingual: nevertheless; anyhow. _ They were told not to bring presents, but they brought them all the same. _ His parents told him to stay home, but John went out just the same.
examples: They were told not to bring presents, but they brought them all the same.

all things to all people.monolingual: Fig. [for someone or something] liked or used by all people; [for someone or something] everything that is wanted by all people. _ You simply can’t be all things to all people. _The candidate set out to be all things to all men and came off looking v
examples: You simply can’t be all things to all people.

and so forth.monolingual: with additional related or similar things mentioned (but not specified). _ She told me everything about her kids and so forth. _ I heard about problems at work and so forth. _ He told me about all his health problems, including his arthritis and so o
examples: She told me everything about her kids and so forth.

and so on.monolingual: with additional related or similar things mentioned (but not specified). _ She told me everything about her kids and so forth. _ I heard about problems at work and so forth. _ He told me about all his health problems, including his arthritis and so o
examples: She told me everything about her kids and so forth.

at first blush.monolingual: when first examined; at an early stage. _ At first glance, the problem appeared quite simple. Later we learned just how complex it really was. _He appeared quite healthy at first glance. _At first blush, she appeared to be quite old.
examples: At first glance, the problem appeared quite simple.

at full tilt.monolingual: as fast as possible. _ The motor was running at full speed. _ John finished his running at full tilt. _ When the horse reached the back stretch he was at full throttle.
examples: The motor was running at full speed.

backhanded compliment.monolingual: an unintended or ambiguous compliment. _Backhanded compliments are the only kind he ever gives! _And I think his left-handed compliments are all given by accident, too!

left-handed compliment.monolingual: an unintended or ambiguous compliment. _Backhanded compliments are the only kind he ever gives! _And I think his left-handed compliments are all given by accident, too!

ball of fire.monolingual: an energetic and ambitious person; a go-getter. _ That guy is a real ball of fire when it comes to sales. _ I don’t want to hire some young fireball. I need wisdom and thoughtfulness.
examples: That guy is a real ball of fire when it comes to sales.

beat around the bush.monolingual: Fig. to avoid answering a question; to stall; to waste time. _ Stop beating around the bush and answer my question. _ Let’s stop beating about the bush and discuss this matter.
examples: Stop beating around the bush and answer my question.

beside the point.monolingual: irrelevant; of no importance. _That’s very interesting, but beside the point. _ That’s beside the point. You’re evading the issue.
examples: That’s very interesting, but beside the point.

born and bred.monolingual: born and nurtured through childhood, usually in a specific place. _ She was born and raised in a small town in western Montana. _ Freddy was born and bred on a farm and had no love for city life.
examples: She was born and raised in a small town in western Montana.

buckle up.monolingual: to buckle one’s seat belt, as in a car or plane. _ Please buckle up so our f light can begin. _ I wish you would obey the law and belt up.
examples: Please buckle up so our f light can begin.

belt up.monolingual: to buckle one’s seat belt, as in a car or plane. _ Please buckle up so our f light can begin. _ I wish you would obey the law and belt up.
examples: Please buckle up so our f light can begin.

build castles in the air.monolingual: Fig. to daydream; to make plans that can never come true. _Ann spends most of her time building castles in Spain. _ I really like to sit on the porch in the evening, just building castles in the air.
examples: Ann spends most of her time building castles in Spain.

build on.monolingual: to add to something by constructing an extension. _Do you plan to build onto this house? _ Yes, we are going to build on.
examples: Yes, we are going to build on.

built like a brick outhouse.monolingual: Fig. well-built—either strong or full-sized. (Built more strongly than is typical. The second form is potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _Look at that guy’s muscles—he’s built like a brick shithouse. _This garage is built like a brick
examples: Look at that guy’s muscles—he’s built like a brick shithouse.

built like a brick shithouse.monolingual: Fig. well-built—either strong or full-sized. (Built more strongly than is typical. The second form is potentially offensive. Use only with discretion.) _Look at that guy’s muscles—he’s built like a brick shithouse. _This garage is built like a brick
examples: Look at that guy’s muscles—he’s built like a brick shithouse.

bundle of joy.monolingual: Fig. a baby. _ We are expecting a bundle of joy next September. _ When your little bundle from heaven arrives, things will be a little hectic for a while.
examples: We are expecting a bundle of joy next September.

burst into tears.monolingual: Fig. to begin to cry suddenly. _ After the last notes of her song, the audience burst into tears, such was its beauty and tenderness. _ The children burst into tears on hearing of the death of their dog.
examples: After the last notes of her song, the audience burst into tears, such was its beauty and tenderness.

buy the farm.monolingual: Sl. to die; to get killed. (The farm is a burial plot.) _ I’ll pass through this illness; I’m too young to buy the farm. _ He lived for a few hours after his collapse, but then he bought it.
examples: I’ll pass through this illness; I’m too young to buy the farm.

buy it.monolingual: Sl. to die; to get killed. (The farm is a burial plot.) _ I’ll pass through this illness; I’m too young to buy the farm. _ He lived for a few hours after his collapse, but then he bought it.
examples: I’ll pass through this illness; I’m too young to buy the farm.

by the way.monolingual: 1. a phrase indicating that the speaker is adding information. (By the by is not as frequent.) _ Tom: Is this one any good? Clerk: This is the largest and, by the way, the most expensive one we have in stock. _ Bill: I’m a realtor. Is your house for
examples: Tom: Is this one any good? Clerk: This is the largest and, by the way, the most expensive one we have in stock.

win the day.monolingual: to be successful; to win a competition, argument, etc. (Originally meaning to win a battle.) _ Our team didn’t play well at first, but we won the day in the end. _ Preparation won the day and James passed his exams.
examples: Our team didn’t play well at first, but we won the day in the end.

carved in stone.monolingual: Fig. permanent or not subject to change. (Often in the negative.) _Now, this isn’t carved in stone yet, but this looks like the way it’s going to be. _ Is this policy carved in stone, or can it still be modified?
examples: Now, this isn’t carved in stone yet, but this looks like the way it’s going to be.

cash on the barrelhead.monolingual: Rur. cash at the time of purchase. _ Jonson’s store doesn’t give credit. Everything is cash on the barrelhead. _They offered me fifty thousand dollars cash on the line for Aunt Nancy’s old house.
examples: Jonson’s store doesn’t give credit.

catch some rays.monolingual: Fig. to get some sunshine; to tan in the sun. _ We wanted to catch some rays, but the sun never came out the whole time we were there. _ I went to Hawaii to bag some rays.
examples: We wanted to catch some rays, but the sun never came out the whole time we were there.

catch someone napping.monolingual: to come upon someone who is unprepared; to surprise someone. _ The enemy soldiers caught our army napping. _ The thieves caught the security guard napping. _ I didn’t expect you so soon. You caught me off balance. _ The teacher asked a trick question
examples: The enemy soldiers caught our army napping.

champ at the bit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a horse] to bite at its bit, eager to move along. _Dobbin was champing at the bit, eager to go.
examples: Dobbin was champing at the bit, eager to go.

chomp at the bit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a horse] to bite at its bit, eager to move along. _Dobbin was champing at the bit, eager to go.
examples: Dobbin was champing at the bit, eager to go.

change horses in midstream.monolingual: Fig. to make major changes in an activity that has already begun; to choose someone or something else after it is too late. (Alludes to someone trying to move from one horse to another while crossing a stream.) _ I’m already baking a cherry pie. I ca
examples: I’m already baking a cherry pie.

chill out.monolingual: Sl. to calm down. _ Before we can debate this matter, you’re all gonna have to chill out. So sit down and stop bickering. _ Everybody cooled out after the emergency, and everything was fine.
examples: Before we can debate this matter, you’re all gonna have to chill out.

cool out.monolingual: Sl. to calm down. _ Before we can debate this matter, you’re all gonna have to chill out. So sit down and stop bickering. _ Everybody cooled out after the emergency, and everything was fine.
examples: Before we can debate this matter, you’re all gonna have to chill out.

close down.monolingual: [for someone] to close a business, office, shop, etc., permanently or temporarily. _ This shop will have to close down if they raise taxes. _ The fire department closed down all the stores on the block because of the gas leak.
examples: This shop will have to close down if they raise taxes.

shut down.monolingual: [for someone] to close a business, office, shop, etc., permanently or temporarily. _ This shop will have to close down if they raise taxes. _ The fire department closed down all the stores on the block because of the gas leak.
examples: This shop will have to close down if they raise taxes.

close enough for government work.monolingual: sufficiently close; done just well enough. (Alludes to the notion that work for the government is not done with care or pride.) _ I didn’t do the best job of mending your shirt, but it’s close enough for government work.
examples: I didn’t do the best job of mending your shirt, but it’s close enough for government work.

good enough for government work.monolingual: sufficiently close; done just well enough. (Alludes to the notion that work for the government is not done with care or pride.) _ I didn’t do the best job of mending your shirt, but it’s close enough for government work.
examples: I didn’t do the best job of mending your shirt, but it’s close enough for government work.

come on strong.monolingual: to seem aggressive; to impress people initially as very aggressive and assertive. _She has a tendency to come on strong, but she’s really a softie. _The new president comes on strong at first.
examples: She has a tendency to come on strong, but she’s really a softie.

come through.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to do what one is expected to do, especially under difficult conditions. _ You can depend on Jane. She’ll always come through. _Tom came through at the last minute with everything we needed.
examples: You can depend on Jane.

come to a close.monolingual: to end; to progress to an ending. _ The celebration came to an end about midnight.
examples: The celebration came to an end about midnight.

come to an end.monolingual: to end; to progress to an ending. _ The celebration came to an end about midnight.
examples: The celebration came to an end about midnight.

come to nothing.monolingual: to amount to nothing; to be worthless. _ So all my hard work comes to nothing. _ Yes, the whole project comes to naught.
examples: So all my hard work comes to nothing.

get to the point.monolingual: to get to the important part (of something). _ He has been talking a long time. I wish he would come to the point. _We are talking about money, Bob! Come on, get to the point.
examples: He has been talking a long time.

come with the territory.monolingual: Fig. to be expected under circumstances like this. (Alludes to the details and difficulties attendant to something like the assignment of a specific sales territory to a salesperson. When one accepts the assignment, one accepts the problems.) _ There
examples: There is a lot of paperwork in this job.

conk off.monolingual: 1. Sl. (from years ago.) to fall asleep. _I conked off about midnight. _I was so tired that I nearly conked off. _ I was afraid I would conk out while I was driving.
examples: I conked off about midnight.

conk out.monolingual: 1. Sl. (from years ago.) to fall asleep. _I conked off about midnight. _I was so tired that I nearly conked off. _ I was afraid I would conk out while I was driving.
examples: I conked off about midnight.

hold the purse strings.monolingual: Fig. to be in charge of the money in a business or a household. _ I control the purse strings at our house. _ Mr. Williams is the treasurer. He controls the purse strings.
examples: I control the purse strings at our house.

cook the books.monolingual: to cheat in bookkeeping; to make the accounts appear to balance when they do not. _ Jane was charged with cooking the accounts of her mother’s store. _ It’s hard to tell whether she really cooked the accounts or just didn’t know what she was doing.
examples: Jane was charged with cooking the accounts of her mother’s store.

cool off.monolingual: 1. Lit. to lose or reduce heat. _ I wish my soup would cool off. I’m hungry. _It’ll cool down this evening, after dusk.
examples: I wish my soup would cool off.

cool down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to lose or reduce heat. _ I wish my soup would cool off. I’m hungry. _It’ll cool down this evening, after dusk.
examples: I wish my soup would cool off.

cost the earth.monolingual: Fig. to be expensive; to cost a lot of money. _ Mary’s dress is real silk. It must have cost a pretty penny. _ Taking care of a fancy car like that can cost a pretty penny, let me tell you. _ It cost an arm and a leg, so I didn’t buy it. _ A house th
examples: Mary’s dress is real silk.

count noses.monolingual: Fig. to count people. _ I’ll tell you how many people are here after I count heads. _ Let’s count noses so we can be sure everyone is back on the bus.
examples: I’ll tell you how many people are here after I count heads.

crowd in.monolingual: to push or squeeze into some place. _Please don’t try to crowd into this place. _ Too many people are trying to crowd in.
examples: Please don’t try to crowd into this place.

cut a wide swath.monolingual: to seem important; to attract a lot of attention. _In social matters, Mrs. Smith cuts a wide swath. _ Bob cuts a big swath whenever he appears in his military uniform.
examples: In social matters, Mrs.

cut from the same cloth.monolingual: Fig. sharing a lot of similarities; seeming to have been created, reared, or fashioned in the same way. _She and her brother are cut from the same cloth. They both tell lies all the time. _ Father and son are made from the same mold and even sound al
examples: She and her brother are cut from the same cloth.

cut someone some slack.monolingual: Sl. to give someone a break; to allow someone a reprieve from the consequences of an action. _Come on, cut me a break! I’m a good guy! _ I was only a few minutes late! Cut me a break! Don’t dock my pay! _ Cut me some slack and I’ll be sure to pay you
examples: Cut me some slack and I’ll be sure to pay you all I owe in a month.

cut the cheese.monolingual: Sl. to release intestinal gas. (Crude. Use caution with the topic.) _Who cut the cheese? _People who cut the mustard in the car have to get out and walk.
examples: People who cut the mustard in the car have to get out and walk.

cut the mustard.monolingual: Sl. to release intestinal gas. (Crude. Use caution with the topic.) _Who cut the cheese? _People who cut the mustard in the car have to get out and walk.
examples: People who cut the mustard in the car have to get out and walk.

dash off.monolingual: to run away; to leave in a hurry. _I must dash away. See you tomorrow. _Juan had to dash away to an appointment. _ Ken dashed off and left me behind to deal with the angry customer.
examples: I must dash away.

day in, day out.monolingual: on every day; for each day. _She watches soap operas day in and day out. _ They eat nothing but vegetables, day in, day out.
examples: She watches soap operas day in and day out.

diarrhea of the mouth.monolingual: Fig. constant talking; a “disorder” involving constant talking. _ Wow, does he ever have diarrhea of the mouth! _ You’re getting diarrhea of the jawbone again.
examples: You’re getting diarrhea of the jawbone again.

dig down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to excavate deeply. _They are really having to dig deep to reach bedrock. _ We are not to the buried cable yet. We will have to dig down some more.
examples: They are really having to dig deep to reach bedrock.

dig deep.monolingual: 1. Lit. to excavate deeply. _They are really having to dig deep to reach bedrock. _ We are not to the buried cable yet. We will have to dig down some more.
examples: They are really having to dig deep to reach bedrock.

do drugs.monolingual: to take illegal drugs; to use illegal drugs habitually. _ Sam doesn’t do drugs, and he doesn’t drink. _ Richard started doing dope when he was very young.
examples: Sam doesn’t do drugs, and he doesn’t drink.

drag on.monolingual: to go on slowly for a very long time; to last a very long time. _ The lecture dragged on and on. _ Why do these things have to drag on so? _ How much longer do you think his speech will drag out?
examples: The lecture dragged on and on.

drag out.monolingual: to go on slowly for a very long time; to last a very long time. _ The lecture dragged on and on. _ Why do these things have to drag on so? _ How much longer do you think his speech will drag out?
examples: The lecture dragged on and on.

dressed to kill.monolingual: Fig. dressed in fancy or stylish clothes. fit to kill.) _ Wow, look at Sally! She’s really dressed to kill. _ A person doesn’t go on vacation dressed to kill. _ When Joe came to pick Mary up for the movie, he was dressed up fit to kill and carrying a
examples: Wow, look at Sally! She’s really dressed to kill.

dressed to the nines.monolingual: Fig. dressed very stylishly with nothing overlooked. _ She showed up for the picnic dressed to the nines. _Clare is usually dressed to the teeth in order to impress people.
examples: She showed up for the picnic dressed to the nines.

drive someone crazy.monolingual: 1. Lit. to force someone into a state of insanity or mental instability. _ The sound of the wind howling drove me crazy. _The dog’s constant barking drove me insane.
examples: The sound of the wind howling drove me crazy.

drop a brick.monolingual: Fig. to announce shocking or startling news. _ They really dropped a bombshell when they announced that the mayor would resign. _ Friday is a good day to drop a bomb like that. It gives the business world the weekend to recover. _They must choose the
examples: They really dropped a bombshell when they announced that the mayor would resign.

fall by the wayside.monolingual: 1. Lit. to leave a march or procession in exhaustion to recover beside the pathway. _ A few of the marchers dropped by the wayside in the intense heat.
examples: A few of the marchers dropped by the wayside in the intense heat.

drop someone a line.monolingual: to write a letter or a note to someone. (The line refers to lines of writing.) _I dropped Aunt Jane a line last Thanksgiving. _She usually drops me a few lines around the first of the year. _ Drop me a note when you get a chance.
examples: I dropped Aunt Jane a line last Thanksgiving.

dine out.monolingual: to eat a meal at a restaurant. _ I like to eat a meal out every now and then. _ Yes, it’s good to eat out and try different kinds of food. _It costs a lot of money to dine out often.
examples: I like to eat a meal out every now and then.

everybody and his brother.monolingual: Fig. everybody; lots of people. _The state fair was packed. Everybody and his brother was there. _ Everybody and his uncle was asking me where you was today.
examples: The state fair was packed.

fade out.monolingual: to diminish and go away altogether. _ The light in the distance faded out as the sun began to set. _ The light faded out as the candles burned themselves out, one by one. _ As it got farther into the distance, the car faded away.
examples: The light in the distance faded out as the sun began to set.

fade away.monolingual: to diminish and go away altogether. _ The light in the distance faded out as the sun began to set. _ The light faded out as the candles burned themselves out, one by one. _ As it got farther into the distance, the car faded away.
examples: The light in the distance faded out as the sun began to set.

come apart at the seams.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to break apart where its parts are joined. _ The dress fell apart at the seams. _ I wouldn’t have thought that a coat that cost that much money would just come apart at the seams.
examples: The dress fell apart at the seams.

feel the pinch.monolingual: Fig. experiencing hardship because of having too little money. _The Smiths used to go abroad every year, but now that he’s retired, they’re really feeling pinched. _You’re bound to feel the pinch a little when you’re a student.
examples: The Smiths used to go abroad every year, but now that he’s retired, they’re really feeling pinched.

fit the bill.monolingual: to be acceptable. _Jane: I need some string. Tom: Here’s some twine. Will it fill the bill? _ I need cloth to make a shirt. This muslin ought to fit the bill.
examples: Jane: I need some string.

fit for a king.monolingual: Fig. very nice; luxurious. _What a delicious meal. It was fit for a king. _Our room at the hotel was fit for a king.
examples: What a delicious meal.

flake out.monolingual: Sl. to collapse with exhaustion; to lie down because of exhaustion. _All the hikers f lacked out when they reached the campsite. _ After a few hours, the hikers all f laked out.
examples: All the hikers f lacked out when they reached the campsite.

flog a dead horse.monolingual: Fig. to insist on talking about something that no one is interested in, or that has already been thoroughly discussed. _The history teacher lectured us every day about the importance of studying history, until we begged him to stop f logging a dead h
examples: The history teacher lectured us every day about the importance of studying history, until we begged him to stop f logging a dead horse.

beat a dead horse.monolingual: Fig. to insist on talking about something that no one is interested in, or that has already been thoroughly discussed. _The history teacher lectured us every day about the importance of studying history, until we begged him to stop f logging a dead h
examples: The history teacher lectured us every day about the importance of studying history, until we begged him to stop f logging a dead horse.

on a lark.monolingual: for a joke; as something done for fun. _ For a lark, I wore a clown’s wig to school. _ On a lark, I skipped school and drove to the beach.
examples: For a lark, I wore a clown’s wig to school.

for the hell of it.monolingual: because it is slightly evil; for no good reason. (Use caution with hell.) _ The kids broke the window just for the devil of it. _ We just drove over for the heck of it.
examples: The kids broke the window just for the devil of it.

for the time being.monolingual: for the present; for now; temporarily. _This quick fix will have to do for the moment. _ This is all right for the time being. It’ll have to be improved next week, however. _ This good feeling will last only for the time being.
examples: This quick fix will have to do for the moment.

forever and a day.monolingual: forever. _ I will love you forever and ever. _ This car won’t keep running forever and ever. We’ll have to get a new one sometime upcoming. _ We have enough money to last forever and a day.
examples: I will love you forever and ever.

scared to death.monolingual: 1. Lit. frightened to the point of dying. _ This poor animal has been frightened to death by the attacking dogs.
examples: This poor animal has been frightened to death by the attacking dogs.

full of hot air.monolingual: Fig. full of nonsense; talking nonsense. _ Oh, shut up, Mary. You’re full of hot air. _ Don’t pay any attention to Bill. He’s full of beans. _ My English professor is full of bull. _ You’re full of it.
examples: Oh, shut up, Mary.

full of beans.monolingual: Fig. full of nonsense; talking nonsense. _ Oh, shut up, Mary. You’re full of hot air. _ Don’t pay any attention to Bill. He’s full of beans. _ My English professor is full of bull. _ You’re full of it.
examples: Oh, shut up, Mary.

full of it.monolingual: Fig. full of nonsense; talking nonsense. _ Oh, shut up, Mary. You’re full of hot air. _ Don’t pay any attention to Bill. He’s full of beans. _ My English professor is full of bull. _ You’re full of it.
examples: Oh, shut up, Mary.

funny bone.monolingual: a spot near the elbow bone that is very sensitive to the touch. _ Ouch, I hit my funny bone. _ Effie bumped her crazy bone and made a horrendous face.
examples: Ouch, I hit my funny bone.

fuss around.monolingual: to go about complaining; to move about in a busy manner. _ Don’t fuss about so much. Things will take care of themselves. _Now, stop fussing around and sit down.
examples: Don’t fuss about so much.

get a move on.monolingual: to start to hurry. _ We are going to leave in five minutes, Jane. Get a hurry on! _ Mary! Get a move on! We can’t wait all day.
examples: We are going to leave in five minutes, Jane.

get about.monolingual: to manage to move around. _ I broke my hip last year, but I can still get about. _ Dad can’t get around too much anymore, so I go over to help him.
examples: I broke my hip last year, but I can still get about.

get around.monolingual: to manage to move around. _ I broke my hip last year, but I can still get about. _ Dad can’t get around too much anymore, so I go over to help him.
examples: I broke my hip last year, but I can still get about.

get down to business.monolingual: to begin to get serious; to begin to negotiate or conduct business. _ All right, everyone. Let’s get down to business. There has been enough chitchat. _When the president and vice president arrive, we can get down to business.
examples: All right, everyone.

get the ball rolling.monolingual: Fig. to get a process started. _ If I could just get the ball rolling, then other people would help. _ Who else would start the ball rolling? _ I had the ball rolling, but no one helped me with the project.
examples: If I could just get the ball rolling, then other people would help.

get the lead out.monolingual: Inf. to hurry; to move faster. (This originally refers to getting lead weights (used in exercise) off so you can move faster.) _ Come on, you guys. Get the lead out! _ If you’re going to sell cars, you’re going to have to shake the lead out.
examples: Come on, you guys.

give someone a ring.monolingual: Fig. to call someone on the telephone. _ Nice talking to you. Give me a ring sometime. _ Give me a buzz when you’re in town.
examples: Nice talking to you.

give something a try.monolingual: to make a try at something. _ Why don’t you give it a go and see if you like it?

give something a go.monolingual: to make a try at something. _ Why don’t you give it a go and see if you like it?

give something a whirl.monolingual: to make a try at something. _ Why don’t you give it a go and see if you like it?

give the devil his due.monolingual: Fig. to give your foe proper credit (for something). (This usually refers to a person who has been evil—like the devil.) _ She’s very messy in the kitchen, but I have to give the devil her due. She bakes a terrific cherry pie. _ John is a bit too nos
examples: She’s very messy in the kitchen, but I have to give the devil her due.

go about.monolingual: 1. [for a rumor] to go from person to person. _ What is this story about you that I hear going about? _There was a nasty rumor about Gerald going around.
examples: There was a nasty rumor about Gerald going around.

go around.monolingual: 1. [for a rumor] to go from person to person. _ What is this story about you that I hear going about? _There was a nasty rumor about Gerald going around.
examples: There was a nasty rumor about Gerald going around.

go ballistic.monolingual: Fig. to become irrationally enraged. (Ballistic refers to a missile launching; postal refers to an enraged post office employee attacking those at his place of work. See also go into orbit.) _ The boss went ballistic when he saw my expense report. _
examples: The boss went ballistic when he saw my expense report.

go down the drain.monolingual: Sl. to fail; to be thrown away or wasted. _Everything we have accomplished has gone down the chute. _ The whole project went down the drain.
examples: Everything we have accomplished has gone down the chute.

do someone one better.monolingual: to do something superior to what someone else has done; to top someone. _That was a great joke, but I can go you one better. _Your last song was beautifully sung, but Mary can do you one better.
examples: That was a great joke, but I can go you one better.

go south.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make an escape; to disappear. (Not necessarily in a southerly direction.) _ Lefty went South the minute he got out of the pen. _ The mugger headed South just after the crime.
examples: Lefty went South the minute he got out of the pen.

head south.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make an escape; to disappear. (Not necessarily in a southerly direction.) _ Lefty went South the minute he got out of the pen. _ The mugger headed South just after the crime.
examples: Lefty went South the minute he got out of the pen.

go to the dogs.monolingual: Fig. to go to ruin; to deteriorate. _My whole life seems to be going to pot. _My lawn is going to pot. I had better weed it.
examples: My whole life seems to be going to pot.

go up in flames.monolingual: 1. Lit. to burn up completely. _ The entire forest went up in f lames! _ The expensive house went up in smoke.
examples: The expensive house went up in smoke.

go up in smoke.monolingual: 1. Lit. to burn up completely. _ The entire forest went up in f lames! _ The expensive house went up in smoke.
examples: The expensive house went up in smoke.

go with the flow.monolingual: Inf. to cope with adversity; to accept one’s lot. _ No, just relax and go with the f low. _ Go with it. Don’t fight it.
examples: No, just relax and go with the f low.

go without.monolingual: to manage while not having any of something that is needed; to not have any of something. _ We were a poor family and usually went without. _ I didn’t have enough money to buy a new coat so I did without.
examples: We were a poor family and usually went without.

do without.monolingual: to manage while not having any of something that is needed; to not have any of something. _ We were a poor family and usually went without. _ I didn’t have enough money to buy a new coat so I did without.
examples: We were a poor family and usually went without.

grist for the mill.monolingual: Fig. something useful or needed. _ Bob bases the novels he writes on his own experience, so everything that happens to him is grist for the mill. _ Ever since I started making patchwork quilts, every scrap of cloth I find is grist for the mill.
examples: Bob bases the novels he writes on his own experience, so everything that happens to him is grist for the mill.

grist to the mill.monolingual: Fig. something useful or needed. _ Bob bases the novels he writes on his own experience, so everything that happens to him is grist for the mill. _ Ever since I started making patchwork quilts, every scrap of cloth I find is grist for the mill.
examples: Bob bases the novels he writes on his own experience, so everything that happens to him is grist for the mill.

gut feeling.monolingual: a personal, intuitive feeling or response. _ I have a gut feeling that something bad is going to happen. _ My gut reaction is that we should hire Susan for the job.
examples: I have a gut feeling that something bad is going to happen.

gut reaction.monolingual: a personal, intuitive feeling or response. _ I have a gut feeling that something bad is going to happen. _ My gut reaction is that we should hire Susan for the job.
examples: I have a gut feeling that something bad is going to happen.

tough sledding.monolingual: Fig. a very difficult time. _ They had some hard sledding when they were first married. _ It was tough sledding for sure when our crops failed that year.
examples: They had some hard sledding when they were first married.

hard to swallow.monolingual: not easily believed; hardly believable. _ Her story was hard to swallow, and it finally was proven to be a lie.
examples: Her story was hard to swallow, and it finally was proven to be a lie.

have a fit.monolingual: to be very angry; to show great anger. _ The teacher had a fit when the dog ran through the classroom. _ John threw a fit when he found his car had been damaged.
examples: The teacher had a fit when the dog ran through the classroom.

throw a fit.monolingual: to be very angry; to show great anger. _ The teacher had a fit when the dog ran through the classroom. _ John threw a fit when he found his car had been damaged.
examples: The teacher had a fit when the dog ran through the classroom.

have another think coming.monolingual: to have to rethink something because one was wrong the first time. (Think is a noun here.) _She’s quite wrong. She has another think coming if she wants to walk in here like that. _ You have another guess coming if you think you can treat me like tha
examples: She’s quite wrong.

have other fish to fry.monolingual: Fig. to have other things to do; to have more important things to do. _ I can’t take time for your problem. I have other fish to fry. _ I won’t waste time on your question. I have bigger fish to fry.
examples: I can’t take time for your problem.

have it made.monolingual: to have succeeded; to be set for life. _ I have a good job and a nice little family. I have it made. _ He’s really got it made since he won the lottery.
examples: I have a good job and a nice little family.

head for the hills.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flee to higher ground. _ The river’s rising. Head for the hills! _ Head for the hills! Here comes the f lood!
examples: The river’s rising.

take to the hills.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flee to higher ground. _ The river’s rising. Head for the hills! _ Head for the hills! Here comes the f lood!
examples: The river’s rising.

run for the hills.monolingual: 1. Lit. to flee to higher ground. _ The river’s rising. Head for the hills! _ Head for the hills! Here comes the f lood!
examples: The river’s rising.

hit home.monolingual: Fig. to really make sense; [for a comment] to make a very good point. _ Mary’s criticism of my clothes hit home, so I changed. _ The teacher’s comment struck home and the student vowed to work harder.
examples: Mary’s criticism of my clothes hit home, so I changed.

hit the bottle.monolingual: Fig. Inf. to go on a drinking bout; to get drunk. _ Jed’s hitting the bottle again. _ He’s been hitting the booze for a week now.
examples: Jed’s hitting the bottle again.

hit the bricks.monolingual: 1. Fig. Inf. to start walking; to go into the streets. _ I have a long way to go. I’d better hit the bricks. _ Go on! Hit the pavement! Get going!
examples: I have a long way to go.

hit the pavement.monolingual: 1. Fig. Inf. to start walking; to go into the streets. _ I have a long way to go. I’d better hit the bricks. _ Go on! Hit the pavement! Get going!
examples: I have a long way to go.

hit the roof.monolingual: Fig. to get very angry. _ She really hit the ceiling when she found out what happened. _ My dad’ll hit the roof when he finds out that I wrecked his car.
examples: She really hit the ceiling when she found out what happened.

press the panic button.monolingual: Fig. to panic suddenly. _ She hit the panic button and just went to pieces. _ Don’t press the panic button. Relax and keep your eyes open.
examples: She hit the panic button and just went to pieces.

say uncle.monolingual: Fig. to admit defeat. _ Joe kept pounding on Jim, trying to get him to holler uncle. _ He twisted my arm until I cried uncle.
examples: Joe kept pounding on Jim, trying to get him to holler uncle.

hurry up.monolingual: to move faster. _Hurry up! You’re going to be late. _ Please hurry on. We have a lot to do today.
examples: Hurry up! You’re going to be late.

in a fog.monolingual: Fig. dazed; not paying attention to what is going on around one; not alert. _ Jane always seems to be in a fog. _ When I get up, I’m in a fog for an hour. _ After surgery, I was in a haze until the anesthetic wore off.
examples: Jane always seems to be in a fog.

in any case.monolingual: no matter what happens. _ I intend to be home by supper time, but in any case by eight o’clock. _ In any event, I’ll see you this evening.
examples: I intend to be home by supper time, but in any case by eight o’clock.

in any event.monolingual: no matter what happens. _ I intend to be home by supper time, but in any case by eight o’clock. _ In any event, I’ll see you this evening.
examples: I intend to be home by supper time, but in any case by eight o’clock.

in bad shape.monolingual: 1. Lit. injured or debilitated in any manner. _Fred had a little accident, and he’s in bad shape. _ Tom needs exercise. He’s in bad shape.
examples: Fred had a little accident, and he’s in bad shape.

in bad taste.monolingual: rude; vulgar; obscene. _ Mrs. Franklin felt that your joke was in bad taste. _ We found the play to be in poor taste, so we walked out in the middle of the second act.
examples: Mrs. Franklin felt that your joke was in bad taste.

in line.monolingual: standing and waiting in a line of people. (On line is used especially in the New York City area.) _ I’ve been in line for an hour. _ Get in line if you want to buy a ticket. _ We waited on line to see the movie.
examples: I’ve been in line for an hour.

in nothing flat.monolingual: Fig. very quickly; in much less time than expected. _ Of course I can get there in a hurry. I’ll be there in nothing f lat. _ We covered the distance between New York and Philadelphia in nothing f lat. _ The waiter brought our food in no time flat.
examples: Of course I can get there in a hurry.

in the final analysis.monolingual: in truth; when all the facts are known; when the truth becomes known. (Usually used when someone is speculating about what the final outcome will be.) _ In the final analysis, it is usually the children who suffer most in a situation like this. _ In
examples: In the final analysis, it is usually the children who suffer most in a situation like this.

in the first place.monolingual: initially; to begin with. _ In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one. In the second place, you don’t need one. _ In the first instance, I don’t have the time. In the second place, I’m not interested.
examples: In the first place, you don’t have enough money to buy one.

jack around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time. _ Stop jacking around and get some work done! _ The kids spend most of the day jerking around.
examples: The kids spend most of the day jerking around.

jerk around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time. _ Stop jacking around and get some work done! _ The kids spend most of the day jerking around.
examples: The kids spend most of the day jerking around.

jump through hoops.monolingual: Fig. to do everything possible to obey or please someone; to bend over backwards (to do something). (Trained circus animals jump through hoops.) _ She expects us to jump through hoops for her. _ What do you want me to do— jump through a hoop?
examples: She expects us to jump through hoops for her.

jump to conclusions.monolingual: Fig. to judge or decide something without having all the facts; to reach unwarranted conclusions. _Now don’t jump to conclusions. Wait until you hear what I have to say. _Please find out all the facts so you won’t leap to conclusions.
examples: Now don’t jump to conclusions.

kick the habit.monolingual: to break a habit. _It’s hard to kick a habit, but it can be done. I stopped biting my nails. _ I used to drink coffee every morning, but I kicked the habit.
examples: It’s hard to kick a habit, but it can be done.

kick ass.monolingual: Sl. to actively motivate people to do something. _ It looks like I’m going to have to kick ass to get people moving around here.
examples: It looks like I’m going to have to kick ass to get people moving around here.

kick butt.monolingual: Sl. to actively motivate people to do something. _ It looks like I’m going to have to kick ass to get people moving around here.
examples: It looks like I’m going to have to kick ass to get people moving around here.

examples: The customer kicked up such a fuss about the food that the manager came to apologize.

know the score.monolingual: Fig. to know the facts; to know the facts about life and its difficulties. _Bob is so naive. He sure doesn’t know the score. _I know what you’re trying to do. Oh, yes, I know what’s what.
examples: Bob is so naive.

lay about.monolingual: to lie around. (Common errors for lie about, lie around.) _ Don’t just lay around all day! _ I need to lay around for a few days.
examples: I need to lay around for a few days.

lay it on thick.monolingual: Fig. to exaggerate or overstate praise, excuses, or blame. _ Sally was laying it on thick when she said that Tom was the best singer she had ever heard. _ After Bob finished making his excuses, Sally said that he was pouring it on thick. _ Bob always
examples: Sally was laying it on thick when she said that Tom was the best singer she had ever heard.

jump for joy.monolingual: Fig. to jump up because one is happy; to be very happy. _ Tommy leapt for joy because he had won the race. _ We all leapt for joy when we heard the news.
examples: Tommy leapt for joy because he had won the race.

leave someone holding the baby.monolingual: Fig. to allow someone to take all the blame; to leave someone appearing to be guilty. _ They all ran off and left me holding the bag. It wasn’t even my fault. _It was all the mayor’s fault, but he wasn’t left holding the bag.
examples: They all ran off and left me holding the bag.

lie low.monolingual: Fig. to keep quiet and not be noticed; to avoid being conspicuous. (Lay is a common error for lie.) _ I suggest you lie low for a few days. _ The robber said that he would lay low for a short time after the robbery.
examples: I suggest you lie low for a few days.

log off.monolingual: to record one’s exit from a computer system. (This action may be recorded, or logged, automatically in the computer’s memory.) _ I closed my files and logged off. _ What time did you log out?
examples: I closed my files and logged off.

log out.monolingual: to record one’s exit from a computer system. (This action may be recorded, or logged, automatically in the computer’s memory.) _ I closed my files and logged off. _ What time did you log out?
examples: I closed my files and logged off.

look out for number one.monolingual: to take care of oneself first. _ You gotta look after number one, right? _ It’s a good idea to look out for number one. Who else will?
examples: It’s a good idea to look out for number one.

make a point.monolingual: 1. Lit. to score a point in a game. _ Bob made a point in the last match. _ Karen made twenty points in the second half.
examples: Bob made a point in the last match.

make a scene.monolingual: Fig. to make a public display or disturbance. _ When John found a f ly in his drink, he started to create a scene. _ Oh, John, please don’t make a scene. Just forget about it.
examples: When John found a f ly in his drink, he started to create a scene.

mess around.monolingual: 1. to waste time; to do something ineffectually. _ Stop messing around and get busy. _I wish you wouldn’t mess about so much. You waste a lot of time that way.
examples: Stop messing around and get busy.

mess about.monolingual: 1. to waste time; to do something ineffectually. _ Stop messing around and get busy. _I wish you wouldn’t mess about so much. You waste a lot of time that way.
examples: Stop messing around and get busy.

mill about.monolingual: to wander or move around aimlessly within a small area. _ Everyone was milling around, looking for something to do. _The students milled about between classes.

monkey business.monolingual: silliness; dishonest tricks. _That’s enough monkey business. Now, settle down. _ Stop the funny business. This is serious!
examples: That’s enough monkey business.

move around.monolingual: to move here and there a bit; to stir; to walk around a bit. _ Stay where you are. Don’t move around at all! _ I wish you would stop moving about.
examples: Stay where you are.

move about.monolingual: to move here and there a bit; to stir; to walk around a bit. _ Stay where you are. Don’t move around at all! _ I wish you would stop moving about.
examples: Stay where you are.

move up in the world.monolingual: Fig. to advance (oneself ) and become successful. _The harder I work, the more I move up in the world. _ Keep your eye on John. He’s really coming up in the world.
examples: The harder I work, the more I move up in the world.

no biggie.monolingual: Inf. [of something] not difficult or troublesome. _Don’t worry. It’s no big deal to wash the car. _ No problem. It’s no biggie.
examples: Don’t worry. It’s no big deal to wash the car.

no hard feelings.monolingual: Fig. no anger or resentment. _I hope you don’t have any hard feelings. _ No, I have no hard feelings.

not in the least.monolingual: certainly not; absolutely not. _No, it doesn’t bother me—not at all. _I’m not complaining. Not me. Not in the least.
examples: No, it doesn’t bother me—not at all.

not worth a dime.monolingual: worthless. _ This land is all swampy. It’s not worth a dime. _ This pen I bought isn’t worth a dime. It has no ink.

not worth beans.monolingual: Fig. worthless. _ Your advice isn’t worth a hill of beans. _ This old cow isn’t worth a plugged nickel.
examples: Your advice isn’t worth a hill of beans.

on and off.monolingual: occasionally; erratically; now and again. _ I feel better off and on, but I’m not well yet. _ He only came to class on and off.
examples: I feel better off and on, but I’m not well yet.

in the world.monolingual: Fig. really; indeed; in fact. (Used as an intensifier after who, what, when, where, how.) _What on earth do you mean? _How in creation do you expect me to do that? _Who in the world do you think you are?

on average.monolingual: generally; usually. _ On the average, you can expect about a 10 percent failure rate. _ This report looks OK, on average.
examples: On the average, you can expect about a 10 percent failure rate.

in the hot seat.monolingual: Fig. in a difficult position; subject to much attention or criticism. _ I was really in the hot seat for a while. _ Now that John is on the hot seat, no one is paying any attention to what I do.
examples: I was really in the hot seat for a while.

on the money.monolingual: exactly right; in exactly the right place; in exactly the right amount (of money). _ That’s a good answer, Bob. You’re right on the money. _ This project is going to be finished right on the nose.
examples: That’s a good answer, Bob.

on the nose.monolingual: exactly right; in exactly the right place; in exactly the right amount (of money). _ That’s a good answer, Bob. You’re right on the money. _ This project is going to be finished right on the nose.
examples: That’s a good answer, Bob.

one at a time.monolingual: the first one, then the next one, then the next one, etc.; each in turn. _I have to deal with problems one by one. I can’t handle them all at once. _ Okay, just take things one at a time. _ The children came into the room one by one.
examples: I have to deal with problems one by one.

out cold.monolingual: 1. Fig. unconscious. _ I fell and hit my head. I was out cold for about a minute. _ Tom fainted! He’s out like a light!

out of shape.monolingual: not in good physical condition. _I get out of breath when I run because I’m out of shape. _ Keep exercising regularly, or you’ll get out of condition.
examples: I get out of breath when I run because I’m out of shape.

in the long run.monolingual: Fig. long term; over a long period of time. _ Over the long haul, this model will prove best. _ This will last in the long haul.
examples: Over the long haul, this model will prove best.

in the short run.monolingual: Fig. for the immediate future. _Over the short haul, you’d be better off to put your money in the bank. _ Over the short haul, you may wish you had done something different. But things will work out all right.
examples: Over the short haul, you’d be better off to put your money in the bank.

pale in comparison.monolingual: Fig. to appear to be deficient in comparison to something else. _ My work pales by comparison with yours. You are a real pro.
examples: My work pales by comparison with yours.

pass away.monolingual: Euph. to die. _ My aunt passed away last month. _ When I pass on, I won’t care about the funeral.

pass on.monolingual: Euph. to die. _ My aunt passed away last month. _ When I pass on, I won’t care about the funeral.

examples: Whenever we go out, my father picks up the tab.

play dumb.monolingual: to pretend to be ignorant [of something]. _ I played ignorant even though I knew about the surprise party. _John played dumb when I asked him if he knew who had been on the telephone.
examples: I played ignorant even though I knew about the surprise party.

play the ponies.monolingual: to wager on horse races. _I used to play the ponies every afteroon during the summer. Then I ran out of money.
examples: I used to play the ponies every afteroon during the summer.

play to the gallery.monolingual: to perform in a manner that will get the strong approval of the audience; to perform in a manner that will get the approval of the lower elements in the audience. _John is a competent actor, but he has a tendency to play to the crowd. _ When he made
examples: John is a competent actor, but he has a tendency to play to the crowd.

examples: There is no need to convince us of the value of hard work.

precious little.monolingual: very few; very little. (Few for people or things that can be counted, and little for amounts.) _ We get precious few tourists here in the winter. _There’s precious little food in the house and there is no money.
examples: We get precious few tourists here in the winter.

push off.monolingual: to leave. (As if one were pushing a boat away from a dock.) _ Well, it looks like it’s time to push off. _ It’s time to go. Let’s shove off.
examples: Well, it looks like it’s time to push off.

shove off.monolingual: to leave. (As if one were pushing a boat away from a dock.) _ Well, it looks like it’s time to push off. _ It’s time to go. Let’s shove off.

examples: Do you need one? I have quite a few.

haul someone over the coals.monolingual: Fig. to give someone a severe scolding. _ My mother hauled me over the coals for coming in late last night. _The manager raked me over the coals for being late again.
examples: My mother hauled me over the coals for coming in late last night.

examples: Okay, I think we are reading from the same page now.

right away.monolingual: immediately. _John: Take this over to Sue. Bill: Right away. _John: How soon can you do this? Sue: Right away.

rolling in it.monolingual: Fig. having large amounts of something, usually money. _ That family is rolling in money. _ Bob doesn’t need to earn money. He’s rolling in it.
examples: That family is rolling in money.

run a temperature.monolingual: to have a body temperature higher than normal; to have a fever. _ I ran a fever when I had the f lu. _ The baby is running a temperature and is grouchy.
examples: I ran a fever when I had the f lu.

run amok.monolingual: to go awry; to go bad; to turn bad; to go into a frenzy. (From a Malay word meaning to run wild in a violent frenzy.) _Our plan ran amok. _He ran amuck early in the school year and never quite got back on the track.
examples: Our plan ran amok.

run riot.monolingual: Fig. to get out of control. _ The dandelions have run riot in our lawn. _ The children ran wild at the birthday party and had to be taken home.
examples: The dandelions have run riot in our lawn.

run wild.monolingual: Fig. to get out of control. _ The dandelions have run riot in our lawn. _ The children ran wild at the birthday party and had to be taken home.
examples: The dandelions have run riot in our lawn.

scream bloody murder.monolingual: Fig. to complain bitterly; to complain unduly. _When we put him in an office without a window, he screamed bloody murder. _ There is something wrong next door. Everyone is yelling bloody murder.
examples: When we put him in an office without a window, he screamed bloody murder.

bet the farm.monolingual: Fig. to liquidate all one’s assets in order to raise money to invest in something. _ It’s a risky proposition. I wouldn’t bet the farm on it.
examples: It’s a risky proposition.

send someone to the showers.monolingual: Fig. to order a player from the playing field, thus ending the player’s participation for the day. _ The coach had sent four players to the showers before the end of the game. _ He was angry enough to send them all to the locker room.
examples: The coach had sent four players to the showers before the end of the game.

fend for oneself.monolingual: to get along by oneself; to support oneself. _ I’m sorry, I can’t pay your rent anymore. You’ll just have to shift for yourself. _ When I became twenty years old, I left home and began to fend for myself.
examples: I’m sorry, I can’t pay your rent anymore.

shoot the bull.monolingual: Inf. to chat and gossip. (The same as throw the bull. Use caution with crap, shit.) _Let’s get together sometime and shoot the bull. _You spend too much time shooting the crap.
examples: Let’s get together sometime and shoot the bull.

sing a different tune.monolingual: Fig. to change one’s manner, usually from bad to good. (Almost the same as dance to another tune.) _When she learned that I was a bank director, she began to sing a different tune. _ You will sing another tune as soon as you find out how right I am!
examples: When she learned that I was a bank director, she began to sing a different tune.

small print.monolingual: an important part of a document that is not easily noticed because of the smallness of the printing. _ You should have read the small print before signing the contract. _ You should always read the fine print of an insurance policy.
examples: You should have read the small print before signing the contract.

fine print.monolingual: an important part of a document that is not easily noticed because of the smallness of the printing. _ You should have read the small print before signing the contract. _ You should always read the fine print of an insurance policy.
examples: You should have read the small print before signing the contract.

easy money.monolingual: money obtained without much effort. _ Don’t become dependent on soft money. _ In college he got spoiled by soft money—a check from his parents every week.
examples: Don’t become dependent on soft money.

some pumpkins.monolingual: someone or something great or special. (Old.) _ That chick is some punkins! _ Isn’t this little gadget really some pumpkins?

spill the beans.monolingual: Fig. to give away a secret or a surprise. _ There is a surprise party for Heidi on Wednesday. Please don’t spill the beans. _ Paul spilled the works about Heidi’s party.
examples: There is a surprise party for Heidi on Wednesday.

splash about.monolingual: 1. to move about in a volume of a liquid, splashing. _ The children splashed about in the pool. _ They splashed around for an hour.
examples: The children splashed about in the pool.

splash around.monolingual: 1. to move about in a volume of a liquid, splashing. _ The children splashed about in the pool. _ They splashed around for an hour.
examples: The children splashed about in the pool.

steal the show.monolingual: Fig. to give the best performance in a show, play, or some other event; to get attention for oneself. _ The lead in the play was very good, but the butler stole the show. _ Ann always tries to steal the spotlight when she and I make a presentation.
examples: The lead in the play was very good, but the butler stole the show.

step on it.monolingual: to hurry up; to make a vehicle go faster. (As if stepping on an automobile’s accelerator. _ Step on the gas. We are going to be late! _ Step on it! Let’s go!
examples: Step on the gas.

stretch the truth.monolingual: Fig. to exaggerate. _ When he claimed to have a Ph.D., he was stretching the truth. _ Sally tends to stretch the point when telling tales about her wild teenage years.
examples: When he claimed to have a Ph.

sweat bullets.monolingual: Fig. to be very anxious and tense. _ What a terrible test! I was really sweating blood at the last. _ Bob is such a bad driver. I sweat bullets every time I ride with him.
examples: What a terrible test! I was really sweating blood at the last.

sweetheart deal.monolingual: a private agreement reached between a public agency or government official and a private company that includes illicit payments or special favors. _ They found that the mayor was involved in a number of sweetheart agreements. _Most of the building co
examples: They found that the mayor was involved in a number of sweetheart agreements.

take a chance.monolingual: to try something where failure or bad fortune is likely. _ Come on, take a chance. You may lose, but it’s worth trying. _ I’m not reckless, but I don’t mind taking a risk now and then.
examples: Come on, take a chance.

take a risk.monolingual: to try something where failure or bad fortune is likely. _ Come on, take a chance. You may lose, but it’s worth trying. _ I’m not reckless, but I don’t mind taking a risk now and then.
examples: Come on, take a chance.

take a dive.monolingual: to fake being knocked out in a boxing match. _ Wilbur wouldn’t take a fall. He doesn’t have it in him. _The boxer took a dive in the second round and made everyone suspicious.
examples: Wilbur wouldn’t take a fall.

hazard a guess.monolingual: to guess. _ Even if you don’t know, please take a guess. _ If you don’t know the answer, hazard a guess.
examples: Even if you don’t know, please take a guess.

take a hike.monolingual: 1. Fig. to go on a hike; to do hiking. _ It’s a beautiful day. Let’s take a hike in the woods. _ We took a hike through the forest to visit John’s cabin.
examples: It’s a beautiful day.

take a walk.monolingual: 1. Fig. to go on a hike; to do hiking. _ It’s a beautiful day. Let’s take a hike in the woods. _ We took a hike through the forest to visit John’s cabin.
examples: It’s a beautiful day.

take a bath.monolingual: to bathe. _ I take a shower every morning. _ John takes a hot bath to relax.
examples: I take a shower every morning.

take ill.monolingual: to become ill. _ I took sick with a bad cold last week. _ I hope I don’t take ill before final exams.
examples: I took sick with a bad cold last week.

tell its own story.monolingual: Fig. [for the state of something] to indicate clearly what has happened. _ The upturned boat told its own tale. The fisherman had drowned. _ The girl’s tear-stained face told its own story.
examples: The upturned boat told its own tale.

tell its own tale.monolingual: Fig. [for the state of something] to indicate clearly what has happened. _ The upturned boat told its own tale. The fisherman had drowned. _ The girl’s tear-stained face told its own story.
examples: The upturned boat told its own tale.

throw in the towel.monolingual: Fig. (From boxing, where this is done by a boxer’s trainer to stop the fight.) to signal that one is going to quit; to quit. _ When John could stand no more of Mary’s bad temper, he threw in the towel and left. _ Don’t give up now! It’s too soon to t
examples: When John could stand no more of Mary’s bad temper, he threw in the towel and left.

throw the bull.monolingual: Sl. Fig. to chat; to boast. (Use caution with crap.) _ Tom could really throw the bull and sound right as rain. _You’re just throwing the crap. Can it!
examples: Tom could really throw the bull and sound right as rain.

thumb a ride.monolingual: to get a ride from a passing motorist; to make a sign with one’s thumb that indicates to passing drivers that one is asking for a ride. _My car broke down on the highway, and I had to thumb a ride to get back to town. _ Sometimes it’s dangerous to hi
examples: My car broke down on the highway, and I had to thumb a ride to get back to town.

tie one on.monolingual: Sl. to get drunk. _The boys went out to tie one on. _They laid one on, but good.
examples: The boys went out to tie one on.

hang one on.monolingual: Sl. to get drunk. _The boys went out to tie one on. _They laid one on, but good.
examples: The boys went out to tie one on.

time after time.monolingual: repeatedly; over and over (again). _ You’ve made the same error time after time! Please try to be more careful! _ I’ve told you time and again not to do that. _ You keep saying the same thing over and over, time and time again. Stop it!
examples: I’ve told you time and again not to do that.

to no avail.monolingual: Cliché with no effect; unsuccessful. _ All of my efforts were to no avail. _ Everything I did to help was of no avail. Nothing worked.
examples: All of my efforts were to no avail.

toddle off.monolingual: to walk away. _ Not even noticing what had happened, the old lady got up and toddled away. _ Sam toddled away, leaving us behind to explain things to the boss. _ Wally toddled off, leaving his dinner untouched. _ Don’t just toddle off when I’m talkin
examples: Not even noticing what had happened, the old lady got up and toddled away.

toe the line.monolingual: Fig. to do what one is expected to do; to follow the rules. _ You’ll get ahead, Sally. Don’t worry. Just toe the mark, and everything will be okay. _ John finally got fired. He just couldn’t learn to toe the line.
examples: You’ll get ahead, Sally.

tough luck.monolingual: That is too bad. (Said as a reply to someone relating an unfortunate situation.) _ Tough luck, but that’s the way the cookie crumbles. _That’s too bad, tough cookies.
examples: Tough luck, but that’s the way the cookie crumbles.

tough cookies.monolingual: That is too bad. (Said as a reply to someone relating an unfortunate situation.) _ Tough luck, but that’s the way the cookie crumbles. _That’s too bad, tough cookies.
examples: Tough luck, but that’s the way the cookie crumbles.

trail off.monolingual: to fade away, as with speech, words, singing, etc. _ Her voice trailed off as she saw who was waiting at the door. _ Ken’s words trailed away as he passed out.
examples: Her voice trailed off as she saw who was waiting at the door.

trail away.monolingual: to fade away, as with speech, words, singing, etc. _ Her voice trailed off as she saw who was waiting at the door. _ Ken’s words trailed away as he passed out.
examples: Her voice trailed off as she saw who was waiting at the door.

turn around.monolingual: to reverse direction; to face the opposite direction or turn completely. _ The bus turned around and went the other way. _ Please turn around so I can see who you are.
examples: The bus turned around and went the other way.

turn about.monolingual: to reverse direction; to face the opposite direction or turn completely. _ The bus turned around and went the other way. _ Please turn around so I can see who you are.
examples: The bus turned around and went the other way.

turn back the clock.monolingual: 1. Lit. to set a clock to an earlier time. _I have to turn the clocks back each fall. _ Please turn back the clock.
examples: I have to turn the clocks back each fall.

under no circumstances.monolingual: Fig. absolutely never. _Andy: Under no circumstances will I ever go back there again! Rachel: Why? What happened? _Sue: Can I talk you into serving as a referee again? Mary: Heavens, no! Not under any circumstances!

on in years.monolingual: Fig. old; elderly. _ My uncle is up in years and can’t hear too well. _ Many people lose their hearing somewhat when they are along in years.
examples: My uncle is up in years and can’t hear too well.

up the ante.monolingual: 1. Fig. to raise the opening stakes in a betting game. _Pete upped the ante on that the poker game to $100 per hand. _ Don’t up the ante any more. You’re betting far too much money already.
examples: Pete upped the ante on that the poker game to $100 per hand.

up to scratch.monolingual: Fig. as good as is required; meeting the minimum requirements. _ Sorry, Tom. Your performance isn’t up to snuff. You’ll have to improve or find another job. _My paper wasn’t up to scratch, so I got an F.
examples: Sorry, Tom. Your performance isn’t up to snuff.

look out for someone.monolingual: Fig. to watch over and care for someone. _ When I was a kid, my older brother always watched out for me. _ I really needed someone to look out for me then.
examples: When I was a kid, my older brother always watched out for me.

water over the dam.monolingual: Fig. past and unchangeable events. _ Your quarrel with Lena is water over the dam; now you ought to concentrate on getting along with her. _ George and I were friends once, but that’s all water under the bridge now.
examples: Your quarrel with Lena is water over the dam; now you ought to concentrate on getting along with her.

water under the bridge.monolingual: Fig. past and unchangeable events. _ Your quarrel with Lena is water over the dam; now you ought to concentrate on getting along with her. _ George and I were friends once, but that’s all water under the bridge now.
examples: Your quarrel with Lena is water over the dam; now you ought to concentrate on getting along with her.

wear two hats.monolingual: Fig. to have more than one set of responsibilities; to hold more than one office. _ The mayor is also the police chief. She wears more than one hat. _ I have too much to do to wear more than one hat. _He wears two hats; he’s both CEO and chairman of
examples: The mayor is also the police chief.

wet behind the ears.monolingual: Fig. young and inexperienced. _John’s too young to take on a job like this! He’s still wet behind the ears! _ He may be wet behind the ears, but he’s well-trained and totally competent. _Tom is going into business by himself ? Why, he’s hardly dry be
examples: He may be wet behind the ears, but he’s well-trained and totally competent.

when push comes to shove.monolingual: Fig. when things get a little pressed; when the situation gets more active or intense. _When push comes to shove, you know I’ll be on your side. _ If push comes to shove at the meeting, the front office can back you up with some statistics.
examples: When push comes to shove, you know I’ll be on your side.

wipe the slate clean.monolingual: Fig. to get rid of or erase someone’s (bad) record. (As if erasing information recorded on a slate.) _I’d like to wipe my slate clean and start all over again. _ Bob did badly in high school, but he wiped his slate clean and did a good job in college
examples: I’d like to wipe my slate clean and start all over again.

wither on the vine.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for fruit] to shrivel on the vine or stem, unharvested. _If we don’t get out there into the field, the grapes will wither on the vine. _The apples will die on the vine if not picked soon.
examples: If we don’t get out there into the field, the grapes will wither on the vine.

die on the vine.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for fruit] to shrivel on the vine or stem, unharvested. _If we don’t get out there into the field, the grapes will wither on the vine. _The apples will die on the vine if not picked soon.
examples: If we don’t get out there into the field, the grapes will wither on the vine.

work like a horse.monolingual: Fig. to work very hard. _ She has an important deadline coming up, so she’s been working like a beaver. _You need a vacation. You work like a slave in that kitchen. _ I’m too old to work like a horse. I’d prefer to relax more.
examples: She has an important deadline coming up, so she’s been working like a beaver.

hang by a thread.monolingual: 1. Lit. to hang by something very thin, such as a thread or a hair. _ The tiniest part of the mobile hung by a thread, the rest are on plastic cords.
examples: The tiniest part of the mobile hung by a thread, the rest are on plastic cords.

above par.monolingual: better than average or normal. _ His work is above par, so he should get paid better.
examples: His work is above par, so he should get paid better.

above the law.monolingual: not subject to the law; immune to the law. _ None of us is above the law. We have to obey all of them.
examples: None of us is above the law.

ace out.monolingual: to be fortunate or lucky. _ Freddy aced out at the dentist’s office with only one cavity.
examples: Freddy aced out at the dentist’s office with only one cavity.

across the board.monolingual: Fig. [distributed] equally for everyone or everything. _ The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.
examples: The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.

act out.monolingual: to behave badly. (Usually used to describe young people.) _ Your son has been acting out in the classroom, and his teacher feels that professional intervention is desirable.
examples: Your son has been acting out in the classroom, and his teacher feels that professional intervention is desirable.

act up.monolingual: [for a thing or a person] to behave badly. _This car is acting up again.
examples: This car is acting up again.

add insult to injury.monolingual: Fig. Cliché to make a bad situation worse; to hurt the feelings of a person who has already been hurt. _First, the basement f looded, and then, to add insult to injury, a pipe burst in the kitchen. _My car barely started this morning, and to add insu
examples: First, the basement f looded, and then, to add insult to injury, a pipe burst in the kitchen.

after all.monolingual: 1. anyway; in spite of what had been decided. (Often refers to a change in plans or a reversal of plans.) _ It looks like Tom will go to law school after all.
examples: It looks like Tom will go to law school after all.

after the fact.monolingual: after something has happened; after something, such as a crime, has taken place. (Originally a legal phrase.) _ John is always making excuses after the fact.
examples: John is always making excuses after the fact.

against all odds.monolingual: despite very low probability; in a most unlikely way. _ Against all odds, she managed to win the trophy.
examples: Against all odds, she managed to win the trophy.

against the clock.monolingual: Fig. in a race with time; in a great hurry to get something done before a particular time. _In a race against the clock, they rushed the accident victim to the hospital.
examples: In a race against the clock, they rushed the accident victim to the hospital.

agree to disagree.monolingual: Cliché [for two or more parties] to calmly agree not to come to an agreement in a dispute. _ We have accomplished nothing except that we agree to disagree.
examples: We have accomplished nothing except that we agree to disagree.

air out.monolingual: [for something] to remain in the fresh air and become fresher. _ The pillows are airing out on the balcony.
examples: The pillows are airing out on the balcony.

all and sundry.monolingual: Cliché everyone; one and all. _Cold drinks were served to all and sundry.
examples: Cold drinks were served to all and sundry.

all at once.monolingual: 1. Lit. all at the same time. _The entire group spoke all at once.
examples: The entire group spoke all at once.

all ears.monolingual: Fig. listening eagerly and carefully. _ Well, hurry up and tell me. I’m all ears.
examples: Well, hurry up and tell me.

all eyes and ears.monolingual: Fig. listening and watching eagerly and carefully. _ Be careful what you say. The children are all eyes and ears. _ Tell us quick. We are all eyes and ears!
examples: Be careful what you say.

all the rage.monolingual: Fig. in current fashion; being a current fad. _ A new dance called the “f loppy disc” is all the rage. _ Wearing a rope instead of a belt was all the rage in those days.
examples: A new dance called the “f loppy disc” is all the rage.

all there.monolingual: Fig. alert, aware, and mentally sound. (Usually negative.) _ After talking with Larry today, I get the feeling that he’s not quite all there. _You do such foolish things sometimes! I wonder if you’re all there.
examples: After talking with Larry today, I get the feeling that he’s not quite all there.

all thumbs.monolingual: Fig. very awkward and clumsy, especially with one’s hands. _Poor Bob can’t play the piano at all. He’s all thumbs. _Mary is all thumbs when it comes to gardening.
examples: Poor Bob can’t play the piano at all.

all told.monolingual: Fig. totaled up; including all parts. _ All told, he earned about $700 last week. _ All told, he has many fine characteristics.
examples: All told, he earned about $700 last week.

all wet.monolingual: 1. Lit. completely wet. _ I fell in and got all wet.
examples: I fell in and got all wet.

ancient history.monolingual: Fig. someone or something from so long ago as to be completely forgotten or no longer important, as a former relationship. _ Bob? I never think about Bob anymore. He’s ancient history. _ His interest in joining the army is now ancient history.
examples: Bob? I never think about Bob anymore.

and change.monolingual: plus a few cents; plus a few hundredths. (Used in citing a price or other decimal figure to indicate an additional fraction of a full unit.) _This one only costs ten bucks and change. _The New York Stock Exchange was up seven points and change for th
examples: This one only costs ten bucks and change.

and the like.monolingual: and other similar things. _ Whenever we go on a picnic, we take potato chips, hot dogs, soda pop, and the like. _I’m very tired of being yelled at, pushed around, and the like.
examples: Whenever we go on a picnic, we take potato chips, hot dogs, soda pop, and the like.

and then some.monolingual: and even more; and more than has been mentioned. _ John is going to have to run like a deer and then some to win this race. _ The cook put the amount of salt called for into the soup and then some.
examples: John is going to have to run like a deer and then some to win this race.

any old thing.monolingual: Fig. just anything, not necessarily old. _ Just give me one. I don’t care which. Just give me any old thing.
examples: Just give me one.

any port in a storm.monolingual: Fig. when one is having serious trouble, one must accept any solution, whether one likes the solution or not. _I don’t want to live with my parents, but it’s a case of any port in a storm. I can’t find an apartment I can afford. _ He hates his job, b
examples: I don’t want to live with my parents, but it’s a case of any port in a storm.

apples and oranges.monolingual: Fig. two entities that are not similar. (Used especially in reference to comparisons of unlike things.) _ You can’t talk about Fred and Ted in the same breath! They’re like apples and oranges. _Talking about her current book and her previous bestsell
examples: You can’t talk about Fred and Ted in the same breath! They’re like apples and oranges.

as a rule.monolingual: in general; usually. _As a rule, men should wear tuxedos at formal dinners. _ As a rule, the bus picks me up at 7:30 every morning.
examples: As a rule, men should wear tuxedos at formal dinners.

as luck would have it.monolingual: by good or bad luck; as it turned out; by chance. _ As luck would have it, we had a f lat tire. _ As luck would have it, the check came in the mail today.
examples: As luck would have it, we had a f lat tire.

as well.monolingual: also; in addition. _ Could I have a second helping of potatoes as well? _ I’m feeling tired, and dizzy as well.
examples: I’m feeling tired, and dizzy as well.

ask for the moon.monolingual: Fig. to make outlandish requests or demands for something, such as a lot of money or special privileges. _ She’s asking for the moon, and she’s not going to get it. _ Don’t ask for the moon. Be reasonable!
examples: She’s asking for the moon, and she’s not going to get it.

assault and battery.monolingual: a violent attack [upon someone] followed by a beating. (A technical legal charge.) _ Richard was charged with two counts of assault and battery. _ Dave does not go out at night because he does not want to be a victim of assault and battery.
examples: Richard was charged with two counts of assault and battery.

at cross-purposes.monolingual: with opposing viewpoints; with goals that interfere with each other. _ We are arguing at crosspurposes. We aren’t even discussing the same thing. _ Bill and Tom are working at cross-purposes. They’ll never get the job done right.
examples: We are arguing at crosspurposes.

at first.monolingual: initially; at the very beginning. _ He was shy at first. Then he became more friendly. _At first we chose the red one. Later we switched to the blue one.
examples: He was shy at first.
