at home.monolingual: at or in one’s dwelling. _ Is Mary at home, or is she still at work? _ What time will she be at home?

at large.monolingual: 1. free; uncaptured. (Usually said of criminals not in custody.) _At noon, the day after the robbery, the thieves were still at large. _There is a murderer at large in the city!
examples: At noon, the day after the robbery, the thieves were still at large.

at last.monolingual: finally; after a long wait. _ The train has come at last. _ At last, we have gotten something to eat.
examples: The train has come at last.

at peace.monolingual: 1. relaxed and happy. _ I am always at peace when I sit in my rocking chair. _ When the warm breeze is blowing, I am at peace.
examples: I am always at peace when I sit in my rocking chair.

at rest.monolingual: 1. not moving; not active. _ After the hectic day, the office was finally at rest at 8:00 p.m. _ When the car is at rest, you can get into the backseat.
examples: After the hectic day, the office was finally at rest at 8:00 p.

at sea.monolingual: 1. Lit. on the sea; away on a voyage on the ocean. _The ship is at sea now, and you can’t disembark. _I spent many happy days at sea on my cruise.
examples: The ship is at sea now, and you can’t disembark.

at sixes and sevens.monolingual: lost in bewilderment; at loose ends. _ Mrs. Smith is at sixes and sevens since the death of her husband. _Bill is always at sixes and sevens when he’s home by himself.
examples: Mrs. Smith is at sixes and sevens since the death of her husband.

at stake.monolingual: Fig. ready to be won or lost; at risk; hanging in the balance. _ That’s a very risky investment. How much money is at stake? _I have everything at stake on this wager.
examples: That’s a very risky investment.

at the last minute.monolingual: Fig. at the last possible chance; in the last few minutes, hours, or days. (Often an exaggeration.) _Please don’t make reservations at the last minute. _Why do you ask all your questions at the last minute?
examples: Please don’t make reservations at the last minute.

at the wheel.monolingual: 1. operating the wheel that turns a ship’s rudder; at the helm. _The cabin boy was at the wheel with the captain close by.
examples: The cabin boy was at the wheel with the captain close by.

at will.monolingual: whenever one wants; freely. _ You’re free to come and go at will. _ The soldiers were told to fire their guns at will. _ You can eat anything you want at will.
examples: You’re free to come and go at will.

back to square one.monolingual: Fig. back to the beginning. (As with a board game.) _ Negotiations have broken down, and it’s back to square one. _We lost our appeal of the lower court decision, so back to square one.
examples: Negotiations have broken down, and it’s back to square one.

back to the drawing board.monolingual: Fig. time to start from the start; it is time to plan something over again. (Plans or schematics are drawn on a drawing board. Note the variations shown in the examples.) _ It didn’t work. Back to the drawing board. _I flunked English this semester.
examples: It didn’t work.

back up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for objects] to obstruct and accumulate in a pathway or channel. _ Something clogged the sewer and it backed up.
examples: Something clogged the sewer and it backed up.

bag of bones.monolingual: an extremely skinny person or animal with bones showing. (The skin is the figurative bag.) _I’ve lost so much weight that I’m just turning into a bag of bones. _ Get that old bag of bones off the racetrack!
examples: I’ve lost so much weight that I’m just turning into a bag of bones.

bag of tricks.monolingual: Fig. a collection of special techniques or methods. _ What have you got in your bag of tricks that could help me with this problem? _Here comes Mother with her bag of tricks. I’m sure she can help us.
examples: Here comes Mother with her bag of tricks.

balance out.monolingual: to equal out; to become even or fair. _These things all balance out in the end. _Don’t worry. Things will balance out.
examples: These things all balance out in the end.

bang for the buck.monolingual: value for the money spent; excitement for the money spent; a favorable cost-to-benefit ratio. (Expressed as an amount of bang for the buck.) _I didn’t get anywhere near the bang for the buck I expected. _How much bang for the buck did you really thin
examples: I didn’t get anywhere near the bang for the buck I expected.

bar none.monolingual: with no exceptions. (Follows an assertion.) _ This is the best of all, bar none.
examples: This is the best of all, bar none.

barf out.monolingual: Sl. to become deranged, to a greater or lesser degree. _ Terry barfed out when he heard about the damage Nick had done to his car. _ Yuck! I thought I was going to barf out.
examples: Terry barfed out when he heard about the damage Nick had done to his car.

bark up the wrong tree.monolingual: Fig. to make the wrong choice; to ask the wrong person; to follow the wrong course. (Alludes to a dog in pursuit of an animal, where the animal is in one tree and the dog is barking at another tree.) _ If you think I’m the guilty person, you’re barki
examples: If you think I’m the guilty person, you’re barking up the wrong tree.

batten down the hatches.monolingual: Fig. to prepare for difficult times. (From a nautical expression meaning, literally, to seal the hatches against the arrival of a storm. The word order is fixed.) _ Here comes that contentious Mrs. Jones. Batten down the hatches! _Batten down the hat
examples: Here comes that contentious Mrs.

be that as it may.monolingual: Cliché even if what you say is true. _ I am sorry to hear about your troubles, but, be that as it may, you still must carry out your responsibilities. _ Be that as it may, I still cannot help you.
examples: I am sorry to hear about your troubles, but, be that as it may, you still must carry out your responsibilities.

beam up.monolingual: Sl. to die. (Alluding to the television program Star Trek.) _ Pete Dead? I didn’t think he was old enough to beam up. _I was so exhausted after climbing four f lights that I was afraid I would beam up.
examples: Pete Dead? I didn’t think he was old enough to beam up.

bear fruit.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant or tree] to yield fruit. _ Our apple tree didn’t bear fruit this year.
examples: Our apple tree didn’t bear fruit this year.

beat the clock.monolingual: Fig. to do something before a deadline; to finish before the time is up. (Alludes to accomplishing something before a clock reaches a specific time.) _ Sam beat the clock, arriving a few minutes before the doors were locked. _ They were afraid they w
examples: Sam beat the clock, arriving a few minutes before the doors were locked.

beer up.monolingual: Sl. to drink a lot of beer. _Those guys are out there beering up like mad. _ Stop beering up and go home!
examples: Those guys are out there beering up like mad.

behind closed doors.monolingual: in secret; away from observers, reporters, or intruders, usually in a closed room. _ They held the meeting behind closed doors, as the law allowed. _ Every important issue was decided behind closed doors.
examples: They held the meeting behind closed doors, as the law allowed.

behind the scenes.monolingual: without receiving credit or fame; out of public view. (Referring originally to those who worked on a theatrical piece but do not appear on the stage.) _ The people who worked behind the scenes are the real heroes of this project. _ I worked behind th
examples: The people who worked behind the scenes are the real heroes of this project.

behind the times.monolingual: old-fashioned. _ Sarah is a bit behind the times. Her clothes are quite old-fashioned. _ Our 90- year-old state senator is a bit behind the times.
examples: Sarah is a bit behind the times.

believe it or not.monolingual: (you may) choose to accept something as true or not; it may seem amazing but it’s true. _ It’s late, but believe it or not, I just got home from work. _ I’m over fifty years old, believe it or not.
examples: It’s late, but believe it or not, I just got home from work.

bells and whistles.monolingual: Fig. extra, fancy add-ons or gadgets. _ I like cars that are loaded with all the bells and whistles. _ All those bells and whistles add to the cost.
examples: I like cars that are loaded with all the bells and whistles.

belly out.monolingual: [for a sheet of fabric, such as a ship’s sail] to fill out in the wind. _ The sails bellied out as the ship turned to catch the wind. _ When the sails bellied out, we began to move forward.
examples: The sails bellied out as the ship turned to catch the wind.

belly up.monolingual: 1. intoxicated by alcohol. _ Fred was boiled— belly up—glassy-eyed. _After four beers, I was belly up, for sure.
examples: Fred was boiled— belly up—glassy-eyed.

below par.monolingual: not as good as average or normal. _I feel a little below par today. I think I am getting a cold. _ His work is below par, and he is paid too much money.
examples: I feel a little below par today.

bend down.monolingual: to curve downward; [for someone] to lean down. _ Please bend down and pick up the little bits of paper you just dropped. _ The snow-laden bushes bent down.
examples: Please bend down and pick up the little bits of paper you just dropped.

bend over.monolingual: [for someone] to bend down at the waist. _ I bent over and picked up the coin. _ When he bent over, something ripped.
examples: I bent over and picked up the coin.

betwixt and between.monolingual: 1. Lit. between (people or things). _I liked the soup and the dessert and all that came betwixt and between. _ I sat betwixt and between all the actors who weren’t on stage.
examples: I liked the soup and the dessert and all that came betwixt and between.

beyond the pale.monolingual: Fig. unacceptable; outlawed. (A pale is a barrier made of wooden stakes.) _Your behavior is simply beyond the pale. _Because of Tom’s rudeness, he’s considered beyond the pale and is never asked to parties anymore.
examples: Your behavior is simply beyond the pale.

big bucks.monolingual: a very large amount of money. _ He earns big bucks for doing almost nothing.
examples: He earns big bucks for doing almost nothing.

bite the big one.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ I was so tired that I thought I was going to bite the big one. _ I hope I am old and gray when I bite the big one.
examples: I was so tired that I thought I was going to bite the big one.

bite the bullet.monolingual: Sl. to accept something difficult and try to live with it. _ You are just going to have to bite the bullet and make the best of it. _Jim bit the bullet and accepted what he knew had to be.
examples: You are just going to have to bite the bullet and make the best of it.

bite the dust.monolingual: 1. Sl. to die. _A shot rang out, and another cowboy bit the dust. _The soldier was too young to bite the dust.
examples: A shot rang out, and another cowboy bit the dust.

black out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for lights] to go out. _ Suddenly the lights blacked out. _ The power went dead and everything blacked out from the heat.
examples: Suddenly the lights blacked out.

blaze a trail.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make and mark a trail. _The scout blazed a trail through the forest.
examples: The scout blazed a trail through the forest.

blaze up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for flames] to expand upward suddenly. _ The fire blazed up and warmed all of us. _ As the fire blazed up, we moved away from the fireplace.
examples: The fire blazed up and warmed all of us.

blessed event.monolingual: Fig. the birth of a child. _ My sister is expecting a blessed event sometime in May. _ The young couple anxiously awaited the blessed event.
examples: My sister is expecting a blessed event sometime in May.

blimp out.monolingual: to overeat; to eat too much and gain weight. _ I blimp out almost every weekend. _ If I could stop blimping out, I could lose some weight.
examples: I blimp out almost every weekend.

bliss out.monolingual: Sl. to be overcome with happiness. _She blissed out at the concert, because she loves that kind of music.
examples: She blissed out at the concert, because she loves that kind of music.

blood and guts.monolingual: 1. Fig. strife; acrimony. _ There is a lot of blood and guts around here, but we get our work done anyway. _ Cut out the blood and guts and grow up.
examples: There is a lot of blood and guts around here, but we get our work done anyway.

blossom forth.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant] to burst into flower. _ All the trees blossomed forth at the same time. _ Each spring my tulips blossom forth in all their glory.
examples: All the trees blossomed forth at the same time.

blossom out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant or tree] to become covered with flowers. _ The apple tree blossomed out for the last time.
examples: The apple tree blossomed out for the last time.

blow away.monolingual: [for something light] to be carried away by the wind. _ The leaves blew away on the autumn winds. _ My papers blew away!
examples: The leaves blew away on the autumn winds.

blow hot and cold.monolingual: Fig. to be changeable or uncertain (about something). _ He keeps blowing hot and cold on the question of moving to the country. _ He blows hot and cold about this. I wish he’d make up his mind.
examples: He keeps blowing hot and cold on the question of moving to the country.

blow in.monolingual: [for something] to cave in to the pressure of moving air. _ The door blew in during the storm. _ The window blew in from the wind.
examples: The door blew in during the storm.

blow over.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to diminish; to subside. (As with a storm or a temper tantrum.) _ Her display of temper finally blew over. _ The storm will blow over soon, I hope.
examples: Her display of temper finally blew over.

blow up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to explode. _ The bomb might have blown up if the children had tried to move it. _ The firecracker blew up.
examples: The bomb might have blown up if the children had tried to move it.

bog down.monolingual: to become encumbered and slow. (As if one were walking through a bog and getting stuck in the mud. Often preceded by a form of get.) _ The process bogged down and almost stopped. _The truck got bogged down in the mud soon after it started.
examples: The process bogged down and almost stopped.

boil over.monolingual: [for a liquid] to overflow while being boiled. _ The sauce boiled over and dripped onto the stove. _ Don’t let the stew boil over!
examples: The sauce boiled over and dripped onto the stove.

bone of contention.monolingual: Fig. the subject or point of an argument; an unsettled point of disagreement. _We’ve fought for so long that we’ve forgotten what the bone of contention is. _The question of a fence between the houses has become quite a bone of contention.
examples: We’ve fought for so long that we’ve forgotten what the bone of contention is.

booby prize.monolingual: a mock prize given to the worst player or performer. _Bob should get the booby prize for the worst showing in the race.
examples: Bob should get the booby prize for the worst showing in the race.

boot up.monolingual: [of a computer] to begin operating; to start up one’s computer. _He turned on the computer and it booted up. _ Try to boot up again and see what happens.
examples: He turned on the computer and it booted up.

booze up.monolingual: Sl. to drink heavily. _ Those guys are always boozing up. _ Stop boozing up and go home.
examples: Those guys are always boozing up.

borrow trouble.monolingual: Fig. to worry needlessly; to make trouble for oneself. _ Worrying too much about death is just borrowing trouble. _ Do not get involved with politics. That’s borrowing trouble.
examples: Worrying too much about death is just borrowing trouble.

bottom out.monolingual: Fig. to reach the lowest or worst point of something. _ All my problems seem to be bottoming out. They can’t get much worse. _ Interest rates bottomed out last February.
examples: All my problems seem to be bottoming out.

bow and scrape.monolingual: Fig. to be very humble and subservient. _Please don’t bow and scrape. We are all equal here. _The salesclerk came in, bowing and scraping, and asked if he could help us.
examples: Please don’t bow and scrape.

bowl up.monolingual: to fill a pipe bowl with smokable material. _The detective bowled up and struck a match. _ Roger bowled up, but forgot to light his pipe.
examples: The detective bowled up and struck a match.

brace up.monolingual: to take heart; to be brave. _ Brace up! Things could be worse. _ I told John to brace up because things would probably get worse before they got better.
examples: Brace up! Things could be worse.

break down.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall apart; [for something] to stop operating. _ The air-conditioning broke down, and we got very warm. _ The car broke down on the long trip.
examples: The air-conditioning broke down, and we got very warm.

break even.monolingual: for income to equal expenses. (This implies that money was not made or lost.) _ Unfortunately, my business just managed to break even last year. _ I made a bad investment, but I broke even.
examples: Unfortunately, my business just managed to break even last year.

break out.monolingual: 1. to burst forth suddenly, as with a fire, a riot, giggling, shouting, etc. _ A fire broke out in the belfry. _ A round of giggling broke out when the teacher tripped.
examples: A fire broke out in the belfry.

break the bank.monolingual: Fig. to use up all one’s money. (Alludes to casino gambling, in the rare event when a gambler wins more money than the house has on hand.) _It will hardly break the bank if we go out to dinner just once. _ Buying a new dress at a discount price won’t
examples: It will hardly break the bank if we go out to dinner just once.

break the ice.monolingual: 1. Fig. to attempt to become friends with someone. _ He tried to break the ice, but she was a little cold. _ A nice smile does a lot to break the ice.
examples: He tried to break the ice, but she was a little cold.

break up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to fall apart; to be broken to pieces. (Typically said of a ship breaking up on rocks.) _In the greatest storm of the century, the ship broke up on the reef. _ It broke up and sank.
examples: In the greatest storm of the century, the ship broke up on the reef.

break wind.monolingual: Euph. to expel gas from the anus. _Someone in the bus broke wind. It smelled terrible. _ He broke wind with an embarrassing noise.
examples: Someone in the bus broke wind.

breathe a sigh of relief.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sigh in a way that signals one’s relief that something has come to an end. _ At the end of the contest, we all breathed a sigh of relief.
examples: At the end of the contest, we all breathed a sigh of relief.

breathe easy.monolingual: to assume a relaxed state after a stressful period. _After this crisis is over, I’ll be able to breathe easy again. _ He won’t be able to breathe easy until he pays off his debts.
examples: After this crisis is over, I’ll be able to breathe easy again.

breathe in.monolingual: to inhale; to take air into the lungs. _ Now, relax and breathe in. Breathe out. _Breathe in deeply; enjoy the summer air.
examples: Now, relax and breathe in.

breathe out.monolingual: to exhale. _ Now, breathe out, then breathe in. _ The doctor told me to breathe out slowly.
examples: Now, breathe out, then breathe in.

breeze off.monolingual: to leave quickly or abruptly. _Don’t just breeze off! Stay and talk. _ Lily breezed off in a huffy manner.
examples: Don’t just breeze off! Stay and talk.

brew up.monolingual: Fig. to build up; [for something] to begin to build and grow. (Typically said of a storm.) _ A bad storm is brewing up in the west. _ Something serious is brewing up in the western sky.
examples: A bad storm is brewing up in the west.

bridge the gap.monolingual: 1. Lit. to make a bridge that reaches across a space. _ The engineers decided to bridge the gap with a wooden structure.
examples: The engineers decided to bridge the gap with a wooden structure.

bright and early.monolingual: very early in the morning or the workday. _Yes, I’ll be there bright and early. _I want to see you here on time tomorrow, bright and early, or you’re fired!
examples: Yes, I’ll be there bright and early.

brighten up.monolingual: to become brighter; to lighten, especially with sunshine. _The sky is brightening up a little. _When the morning sky brightens up just a little, the birds begin to sing.
examples: The sky is brightening up a little.

bright-eyed and bushy-tailed.monolingual: Fig. awake and alert. (Often used ironically, as in the first example. The idea is that one is like a frisky animal, such as a squirrel.) _ Jill: Hi, Jane! How are you on this beautiful morning? Jane: Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, just as you might e
examples: Jill: Hi, Jane! How are you on this beautiful morning? Jane: Bright-eyed and bushy-tailed, just as you might expect, since I’ve only had three hours of sleep.

bring home the bacon.monolingual: Fig. to earn a salary; to bring home money earned at a job. _ I’ve got to get to work if I’m going to bring home the bacon. _ Go out and get a job so you can bring home the bacon.
examples: I’ve got to get to work if I’m going to bring home the bacon.

bring up the rear.monolingual: to move along behind everyone else; to be at the end of the line. (Originally referred to marching soldiers. Fixed order.) _Here comes John, bringing up the rear. _ Hurry up, Tom! Why are you always bringing up the rear?
examples: Here comes John, bringing up the rear.

broad in the beam.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of a ship] wide at amidships. _ This old tub is broad in the beam and sits like a ball in the water, but I love her.
examples: This old tub is broad in the beam and sits like a ball in the water, but I love her.

brown out.monolingual: [for the electricity] to diminish in power and dim the lights, causing a brownout. (Something less than a blackout, when there is no power.) _ The power kept browning out. _ The lights started to brown out, and I thought maybe there was a power short
examples: The power kept browning out.

bubble over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for boiling or effervescent liquid] to spill or splatter over the edge of its container. _ The pot bubbled over and put out the f lame on the stove. _The stew bubbled over.
examples: The pot bubbled over and put out the f lame on the stove.

buck up.monolingual: to cheer up; to perk up. _Come on, now, buck up. Things can’t be all that bad. _ She began to buck up when I showed her the results of the tests.
examples: Come on, now, buck up.

buckle under.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to collapse. _With heavy trucks on it, the bridge buckled under. _ The table buckled under.
examples: With heavy trucks on it, the bridge buckled under.

bud out.monolingual: [for a flowering plant or tree] to develop buds. _ How early in the spring do the trees bud out around here? _ The trees bud out in early spring.
examples: The trees bud out in early spring.

bug off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to cease bothering [someone]. _ Hey, bug off! Your comments are annoying. _ I wish you would bug off!
examples: Hey, bug off! Your comments are annoying.

bug out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to pack up and leave or retreat. _Orders are to bug out by oh-nine-hundred. _ Okay, everybody, move it! We’re bugging out.
examples: Orders are to bug out by oh-nine-hundred.

build a better mousetrap.monolingual: to develop or invent something superior to a device that is widely used. (From the old saying, “If you build a better mousetrap, the world will beat a path to your door.”) _Harry thought he could build a better mousetrap, but everything he “invented”
examples: Harry thought he could build a better mousetrap, but everything he “invented” had already been thought of.

build down.monolingual: [for traffic] to reduce in volume or diminish. _ At about six, the going-home traffic begins to build down. _ When traffic builds down, I leave for home.
examples: At about six, the going-home traffic begins to build down.

build up.monolingual: to increase; to develop. _ The storm clouds are building up. Better close the windows.
examples: The storm clouds are building up.

bum out.monolingual: Sl. to have a bad experience. (Originally referred to a bad experience with drugs.) _ Are you going to bum out again tonight? _ Man, is he bummed out!

bunch up.monolingual: to pack together or cluster. _ Spread out. Don’t bunch up!

bundle off.monolingual: to leave in a hurry; to take all one’s parcels or baggage and leave in a hurry. _ She got ready and bundled off after her bus. _ Her arms full, Lily bundled off in a rush.
examples: She got ready and bundled off after her bus.

burn away.monolingual: 1. [for something] to burn until there is no more of it. _ All the oil burned away. _ The logs burned away and the fireplace was cooling down.
examples: All the oil burned away.

burn down.monolingual: 1. [for a building] to be destroyed by fire. _ The barn burned down. _There was a fire, and the old factory was burned down.
examples: The barn burned down.

burn off.monolingual: [for some excess volatile or flammable substance] to burn away or burn up. _ A film of oil on the surface of the water was burning off, making dense black smoke. _ The alcohol burned off and left a delicious f lavor in the cherries jubilee.
examples: A film of oil on the surface of the water was burning off, making dense black smoke.

burn the midnight oil.monolingual: Fig. to stay up working, especially studying, late at night. (Alludes to working by the light of an oil lamp late in the night.) _ I have a big exam tomorrow so I’ll be burning the midnight oil tonight. _ If you burn the midnight oil night after nigh
examples: I have a big exam tomorrow so I’ll be burning the midnight oil tonight.

burn up.monolingual: to become destroyed or consumed by fire. _The wood burned up and left only ashes. _The deed burned up in the fire.
examples: The wood burned up and left only ashes.

burst forth.monolingual: to come forth explosively. _ The words burst forth and frightened everyone. _ The blossoms burst forth in the first warm days of the year.
examples: The words burst forth and frightened everyone.

burst out.monolingual: to explode outward; to break open under force. _ The door burst out and released the trapped people. _ When the glass burst out, Gerald was cut by some splinters.
examples: The door burst out and released the trapped people.

burst out laughing.monolingual: to begin to laugh suddenly. _ The entire audience burst out laughing when the clown took a fall. _Every time I think of you sitting there with a lap full of spaghetti, I burst out laughing.
examples: The entire audience burst out laughing when the clown took a fall.

bury the hatchet.monolingual: Fig. to make peace. _ Let’s stop arguing and bury the hatchet. _ Tom and I buried the hatchet and we are good friends now.
examples: Let’s stop arguing and bury the hatchet.

bush out.monolingual: [for a plant, bush, beard, head of hair] to develop many small branches or hairs. _His beard bushed out and really needed trimming. _I hope the hedge bushes out nicely this year.
examples: His beard bushed out and really needed trimming.

business as usual.monolingual: having things go along as usual. _ Even right after the f lood, it was business as usual in all the stores. _ Please, everyone, business as usual. Let’s get back to work.
examples: Even right after the f lood, it was business as usual in all the stores.

bust a move.monolingual: Sl. to leave (a place.) _Let’s go. Time to bust a move. _ Let’s bust a move. Lots to do tomorrow.
examples: Let’s go. Time to bust a move.

bust up.monolingual: 1. Sl. [for lovers] to separate or break up. (Bust is a nonstandard form of burst meaning ‘break’ here.) _ Tom and Alice busted up for good. _ They busted up last week.
examples: Tom and Alice busted up for good.

but good.monolingual: severely; thoroughly. _She told him off but good. _ Joe beat up Bill but good.
examples: She told him off but good.

butt out.monolingual: to exit [as abruptly as one has intruded]. (Compare this with butt in (on someone or something). Usually a command.) _ Butt out! Leave me alone! _ Please butt out of my life!

button up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fasten one’s buttons. _ Your jacket’s open. You’d better button up. It’s cold. _ I’ll button up in the car.
examples: Your jacket’s open.

buy time.monolingual: to postpone an event hoping that the situation will improve. _You are just stalling to buy time. _Maybe I can buy some time by asking the judge for a continuance.
examples: You are just stalling to buy time.

buzz off.monolingual: Fig. to leave quickly. _I’ve got to buzz off. Bye. _ It’s time for me to buzz off.
examples: I’ve got to buzz off.

by and large.monolingual: generally; usually. (Originally a nautical expression.) _ I find that, by and large, people tend to do what they are told to do. _ By and large, rosebushes need lots of care.
examples: I find that, by and large, people tend to do what they are told to do.

by any means.monolingual: by any way possible. _ I need to get there soon by any means. _I must win this contest by any means, fair or unfair.
examples: I need to get there soon by any means.

by hand.monolingual: made by human hands and handheld tools as opposed to a machine. _ This fine wooden cabinet was made by hand. _ I carved this figurine by hand.
examples: This fine wooden cabinet was made by hand.

by mistake.monolingual: in error; accidentally. _I’m sorry. I came into the wrong room by mistake. _ I chose the wrong road by mistake. Now we are lost.
examples: I’m sorry. I came into the wrong room by mistake.

by no means.monolingual: absolutely not; certainly not. _ I’m by no means angry with you. _ Bob: Did you put this box here? Tom: By no means. I didn’t do it, I’m sure.
examples: I’m by no means angry with you.

by the same token.monolingual: Cliché a phrase indicating that the speaker is introducing parallel or closely contrasting information. _Tom: I really got cheated! Bob: You think they’ve cheated you, but, by the same token, they believe that you’ve cheated them. _ Some say he is a
examples: Tom: I really got cheated! Bob: You think they’ve cheated you, but, by the same token, they believe that you’ve cheated them.

call a spade a spade.monolingual: Fig. to call something by its right name; to speak frankly about something, even if it is unpleasant. (Considered offensive by some. Use only with discretion.) _Well, I believe it’s time to call a spade a spade. We are just avoiding the issue. _ Let’
examples: Well, I believe it’s time to call a spade a spade.

call back.monolingual: 1. to call [someone] again on the telephone at a later time. _Call back later, please. _I will call back when you are not so busy.
examples: Call back later, please.

call it a day.monolingual: to quit work and go home; to say that a day’s work has been completed. _ I’m tired. Let’s call it a day. _ The boss was mad because Tom called it a day at noon and went home.
examples: I’m tired. Let’s call it a day.

call it a night.monolingual: to end what one is doing at night and go [home] to bed. _At midnight, I called it a night and went to bed. _ Guest after guest called it a night, and at last we were alone.
examples: At midnight, I called it a night and went to bed.

calm down.monolingual: to relax; to become less busy or active. _Now, now, calm down. You look so nervous. _Please calm down. Nothing bad is going to happen.
examples: Now, now, calm down.

camp it up.monolingual: [for performers] to overact or behave in an affected manner. _The cast began to camp it up in the second act, and the critics walked out. (Fixed order.) _ There is no need to camp it up. Play it the way it was written.
examples: The cast began to camp it up in the second act, and the critics walked out.

camp out.monolingual: to live out of doors temporarily in a tent or camping vehicle, as on a vacation or special camping trip. _ I love to camp out in the winter.
examples: I love to camp out in the winter.

carry on.monolingual: to behave badly or mischievously. _The children always carry on when the teacher’s out of the room. _Stop carrying on and go to sleep!
examples: The children always carry on when the teacher’s out of the room.

carry over.monolingual: to extend into another time period or location. _ I don’t like for bills to carry over into the next month. _ Please do not let the paragraph carry over.
examples: I don’t like for bills to carry over into the next month.

carry the ball.monolingual: 1. Lit. to be the player who is relied on to gain yardage, especially in football. _ It was the fullback carrying the ball. _Yes, Tom always carries the ball.
examples: It was the fullback carrying the ball.

case the joint.monolingual: 1. Sl. to look over some place to figure out how to break in, what to steal, etc. (Underworld.) _ First of all you gotta case the joint to see where things are. _You could see he was casing the joint the way he hung around.
examples: First of all you gotta case the joint to see where things are.

catch it.monolingual: to get into trouble and receive punishment. _ I know I’m going to catch it for denting mom’s car when I get home. _ Bob hit Billy in the face. He really caught it from the teacher for that.
examples: I know I’m going to catch it for denting mom’s car when I get home.

caught short.monolingual: 1. left without any money temporarily. _ I’m caught a little short. Can I borrow a few bucks?
examples: I’m caught a little short.

cave in.monolingual: [for a roof or ceiling] to collapse. _The roof of the mine caved in when no one was there. _ The tunnel caved in on the train.
examples: The roof of the mine caved in when no one was there.

chances are.monolingual: the likelihood is (followed by a clause stating what is likely). _Chances are that she would have been late even if she had left on time.
examples: Chances are that she would have been late even if she had left on time.

change hands.monolingual: [for something] to be sold or passed from owner to owner. (From the “point of view” of the object that is passed on.) _How many times has this lot changed hands in the last ten years? _ We built this house in 1970, and it has never changed hands.
examples: We built this house in 1970, and it has never changed hands.

change the channel.monolingual: Sl. to switch to some other topic of conversation. _ Just a minute. I think you changed the channel. Let’s go back to the part about you owing me money. _ Let’s change the channel here before there is a fight.
examples: Just a minute. I think you changed the channel.

character assassination.monolingual: Fig. seriously harming someone’s reputation. _ The review was more than a negative appraisal of his performance. It was total character assassination.
examples: The review was more than a negative appraisal of his performance.

charge off.monolingual: to move quickly or run away. _ He got angry and charged off. _ Juan charged off to talk to the boss.
examples: He got angry and charged off.

check out.monolingual: [for someone or something] to prove to be correctly represented. _ Everything you told me checks out with what other witnesses said.
examples: Everything you told me checks out with what other witnesses said.

cheek by jowl.monolingual: Fig. side by side; close together. _ The pedestrians had to walk cheek by jowl along the narrow streets. _The two families lived cheek by jowl in one house.
examples: The pedestrians had to walk cheek by jowl along the narrow streets.

cheer up.monolingual: [for a sad person] to become happy. _ After a while, she began to cheer up and smile more. _ Cheer up! Things could be worse.
examples: After a while, she began to cheer up and smile more.

chicken feed.monolingual: Fig. a small amount of anything, especially of money. _ Of course I can afford $800. That’s just chicken feed. _ It may be chicken feed to you, but that’s a month’s rent to me.
examples: Of course I can afford $800.

chip away.monolingual: [for something] to break off or break away in small chips. _ The edges of the marble step chipped away over the years. _Some of the stone figures had chipped away so badly that we couldn’t see what they were.
examples: The edges of the marble step chipped away over the years.

choke up.monolingual: 1. to feel like crying. _I choked up when I heard the news. _He was beginning to choke up as he talked.
examples: I choked up when I heard the news.

chuck it in.monolingual: Inf. to quit; to give up. (Fixed order.) _ I was so depressed, I almost chucked it in. _ If I didn’t have to keep the job to pay my bills, I’d have chucked it in long ago.
examples: I was so depressed, I almost chucked it in.

clam up.monolingual: to say nothing. (Closing one’s mouth in the way that a clam closes up.) _ The minute they got him in for questioning, he clammed up. _ You’ll clam up if you know what’s good for you.
examples: The minute they got him in for questioning, he clammed up.

clear the air.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get rid of stale or bad air. _ Open some windows and clear the air. It’s stuffy in here.
examples: Open some windows and clear the air.

clear the table.monolingual: to remove the dishes and other eating utensils from the table after a meal. (Compare this with set the table.) _ Will you please help clear the table? _ After you clear the table, we’ll play cards.
examples: After you clear the table, we’ll play cards.

clear up.monolingual: 1. [for the sky] to become more clear or sunny. _Suddenly, the sky cleared up. _When the sky cleared up, the breeze began to blow.
examples: Suddenly, the sky cleared up.

clock in.monolingual: to record one’s time of arrival, usually by punching a time clock. _ What time did she clock in? _ She forgot to clock in today.
examples: She forgot to clock in today.

clock out.monolingual: to record one’s time of departure, usually by punching a time clock. _ I will clock out just before I go home. _ Jim clocked out early Tuesday to go to the doctor.
examples: I will clock out just before I go home.

clog up.monolingual: [for a channel or conduit] to become blocked. _ The canal clogged up with leaves and mud.
examples: The canal clogged up with leaves and mud.

close to home.monolingual: Fig. affecting one personally and intimately. _ Her remarks were a bit too close to home. I took her review as a personal insult.
examples: Her remarks were a bit too close to home.

close up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an opening] to close completely. _ The door closed up and would not open again. _The wound will close up completely in a day or so.
examples: The door closed up and would not open again.

cloud over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for the sky] to fill with clouds; [for the sun] to be obscured by clouds. _ It was beginning to cloud over, so we went inside. _ The sky clouded over and it began to get chilly.
examples: It was beginning to cloud over, so we went inside.

cloud up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for the sky] to get cloudy, as if it were going to rain. _All of a sudden it clouded up and began to rain. _ It usually clouds up at the top of the mountain.
examples: All of a sudden it clouded up and began to rain.

cock of the walk.monolingual: someone who acts more important than others in a group. _ The deputy manager was cock of the walk until the new manager arrived. _He loved acting cock of the walk and ordering everyone about.
examples: The deputy manager was cock of the walk until the new manager arrived.

cock-and-bull story.monolingual: a hard-to-believe, made-up story; a story that is a lie. _ Don’t give me that cock-and-bull story. _ I asked for an explanation, and all I got was your ridiculous cock-and-bull story!
examples: Don’t give me that cock-and-bull story.

cold comfort.monolingual: no comfort or consolation at all. _ She knows there are others worse off than her, but that’s cold comfort. _It was cold comfort to the student that others had failed as he had done.
examples: She knows there are others worse off than her, but that’s cold comfort.

cold turkey.monolingual: Sl. immediately; without tapering off or cutting down gradually. _ Tom stopped smoking cold turkey. _ She gave up her drinking habit cold turkey and had no ill effects.
examples: Tom stopped smoking cold turkey.

come a cropper.monolingual: Fig. to have a misfortune; to fail. (Meaning ‘fall off one’s horse.’) _ Bob invested all his money in the stock market just before it fell. Boy, did he come a cropper. _ Jane was out all night before she took her final. She really came a cropper.
examples: Bob invested all his money in the stock market just before it fell.

come about.monolingual: 1. to happen. _ How did this damage come about? _ This came about due to the windstorm.
examples: This came about due to the windstorm.

come across.monolingual: 1. to be compliant. _Oh, she’ll come across, just you wait; she’ll do what we want.
examples: Oh, she’ll come across, just you wait; she’ll do what we want.

come apart.monolingual: to break apart; to break up. _ The missile came apart in midair. _ I was afraid our car would come apart on that rough road.
examples: The missile came apart in midair.

come back.monolingual: to return; to return to an advantageous or favorable state or condition. _Walter practiced every day, hoping to come back from his injury. _When will the good old days come back?
examples: Walter practiced every day, hoping to come back from his injury.

come down.monolingual: 1. Sl. to happen. _ Hey, man! What’s coming down? _ When something like this comes down, I have to stop and think things over.
examples: When something like this comes down, I have to stop and think things over.

come down to earth.monolingual: 1. Lit. to arrive on earth from above. _ An angel came down to earth and made an announcement.
examples: An angel came down to earth and made an announcement.

come forth.monolingual: to come out; to move forward and appear. _ Please come forth and meet your cousins. _ All the stage crew came forth and received some applause.
examples: Please come forth and meet your cousins.

come forward.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move oneself forward. _ Come forward and stand before the whole class.
examples: Come forward and stand before the whole class.

come from behind.monolingual: to advance from a losing position. (Alludes to being behind in a score or in a race.) _ Our team came from behind to win the game. _ The horse I bet on came from behind and almost placed second.
examples: Our team came from behind to win the game.

come full circle.monolingual: Fig. to return to the original position or state of affairs. _The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now.
examples: The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now.

come hell or high water.monolingual: Fig. no matter what happens. (Use hell with caution.) _I’ll be there tomorrow, come hell or high water. _ Come hell or high water, I intend to own my own home.
examples: I’ll be there tomorrow, come hell or high water.

come in handy.monolingual: [for something] to be useful. _ I think that this gadget will come in handy in the kitchen.
examples: I think that this gadget will come in handy in the kitchen.

come into being.monolingual: to begin existence. _ This idea came into being during the last decade. _ When did this organization come into being?
examples: This idea came into being during the last decade.

come into the world.monolingual: Fig. to be born. _ I came into this world nearly seventy years ago. _ Little Timmy came into the world on a cold and snowy night.
examples: I came into this world nearly seventy years ago.

come off.monolingual: Inf. to happen; to take place. _ What time does this party come off ? _ How did your speech come off ? _ It came off very well.
examples: It came off very well.

come out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to exit; to leave the inside of a place. _ Please come out. We have to leave. _ When do you think they will all come out?
examples: Please come out.

come out in the wash.monolingual: Fig. to work out all right. (Alludes to a clothing stain that can be removed by washing.) _ Don’t worry about that problem. It’ll all come out in the wash. _This trouble will go away. It’ll come out in the wash.
examples: Don’t worry about that problem.

come over.monolingual: 1. to join this party or side; to change sides or affiliation. _Tom was formerly an enemy spy, but last year he came over. _I thought that Bill was a Republican. When did he come over?
examples: Tom was formerly an enemy spy, but last year he came over.

come to a head.monolingual: Fig. [for a problem] to reach a critical or crucial stage. _At the end of the week, everything came to a head and Sam was fired.
examples: At the end of the week, everything came to a head and Sam was fired.

come to grief.monolingual: Fig. to experience something unpleasant or damaging. _ In the end, he came to grief because he did not follow instructions.
examples: In the end, he came to grief because he did not follow instructions.

come to life.monolingual: 1. Lit. to act as if alive after a period of seeming not to be alive. _As the anesthetic wore off, the patient came to life. _ After CPR, the child came to life.
examples: As the anesthetic wore off, the patient came to life.

come to light.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to become known or to be discovered. _Many surprises have come to light since then. _ Nothing new has come to light since we talked last.
examples: Many surprises have come to light since then.

come to mind.monolingual: Fig. [for a thought or idea] to enter into one’s consciousness or be remembered. _ Do I know a good barber? No one comes to mind right now. _ Another idea comes to mind. Why not check in the phone book?
examples: Do I know a good barber? No one comes to mind right now.

come to pass.monolingual: to happen; to take place. _ And when do you think all these good things will come to pass? _ Do you think it will really come to pass?

come to think of it.monolingual: I just remembered. _ Come to think of it, I know someone who can help. _ I have a screwdriver in the trunk of my car, come to think of it.
examples: Come to think of it, I know someone who can help.

come together.monolingual: 1. to touch together; to meet. _The ends of the boards just came together. They were almost too short. _We came together in the park, just as we had agreed.
examples: The ends of the boards just came together.

come true.monolingual: to materialize as expected or hoped. _ Jane’s wishes had come true. _ Dave wondered if his dreams would ever come true.
examples: Jane’s wishes had come true.

come up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to come from a lower place to a higher one. _ You can come up now. They are gone. _ Come up and enjoy the view from the tallest rooftop in the county.
examples: You can come up now.

come what may.monolingual: Cliché no matter what might happen. _ I’ll be home for the holidays, come what may. _ Come what may, the mail will get delivered.
examples: I’ll be home for the holidays, come what may.

cooking with gas.monolingual: doing [something] exactly right. _ That’s great! Now you’re cooking with gas! _I knew she was finally cooking with gas when she answered all the questions correctly.
examples: I knew she was finally cooking with gas when she answered all the questions correctly.

cooler heads prevail.monolingual: Fig. the ideas or influence of less emotional people prevail. (Used of a tense situation.) _ One hopes that cooler heads will prevail and soon everything will calm down.
examples: One hopes that cooler heads will prevail and soon everything will calm down.

count down.monolingual: to count backwards to an event that will start when zero is reached. _ The project manager was counting down—getting ready for the launch of the rocket. _ I can still hear the captain counting down: “Five, four, three, two, one, zero, blast off!”
examples: The project manager was counting down—getting ready for the launch of the rocket.

count off.monolingual: [for a series of people, one by one] to say aloud the next number in a fixed sequence. _ The soldiers counted off by threes. _The sergeant told them to count off.
examples: The soldiers counted off by threes.

crack a smile.monolingual: to grin; to smile. _I was tellin’ my best jokes, but Jim never cracked a smile. _ She looked surprised, and then cracked a big, beautiful smile.
examples: I was tellin’ my best jokes, but Jim never cracked a smile.

crack up.monolingual: 1. to have a wreck. _ The plane cracked up and killed two of the passengers. _Whose car cracked up on the expressway?
examples: The plane cracked up and killed two of the passengers.

crap out.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ Max almost crapped out from the beating he took. _The old dog just crapped out. What shall we do?
examples: Max almost crapped out from the beating he took.

creep up.monolingual: [for darkness] to move gradually and slowly [toward someone or something]. _ Dusk crept up and swallowed us in darkness.
examples: Dusk crept up and swallowed us in darkness.

crop out.monolingual: to appear on the surface; [for something] to reveal itself in the open; to begin to show above the surface. _A layer of rock cropped out at the edges of the desert.
examples: A layer of rock cropped out at the edges of the desert.

crop up.monolingual: to appear without warning; to happen suddenly; [for something] to begin to reveal itself in the open. _ Some new problems cropped up at the last minute.
examples: Some new problems cropped up at the last minute.

cross over.monolingual: 1. to cross something such as a river or a street. _This is a very wide river. Where do we cross over? _Let’s cross over here where it’s shallow.
examples: This is a very wide river.

crowd together.monolingual: to pack tightly together. _ The tenants crowded together in the lobby. _ All the kittens crowded together to keep warm.
examples: The tenants crowded together in the lobby.

crumble up.monolingual: to break up into little pieces. _ The cake, which was very dry, crumbled up when I tried to cut it. _ The paper of the old book crumbled up when I turned the pages.
examples: The cake, which was very dry, crumbled up when I tried to cut it.

crumple up.monolingual: to fold up; to collapse. _ She was so frightened that she just crumpled up. _ Fran crumpled up in a dead faint.
examples: She was so frightened that she just crumpled up.

cry oneself to sleep.monolingual: to weep until sleep overtakes one. _ The baby finally cried herself to sleep.
examples: The baby finally cried herself to sleep.

cry wolf.monolingual: Fig. to cry or complain about something when nothing is really wrong. (From the story wherein a child sounds the alarm frequently about a wolf when there is no wolf, only to be ignored when there actually is a wolf.) _ Pay no attention. She’s just cr
examples: Pay no attention.

cut a deal.monolingual: to arrange a deal; to negotiate an agreement. _ Maybe we can cut a deal. Let’s talk. _ The two lawyers cut a deal that left me with my car, although she got the house.
examples: Maybe we can cut a deal.

cut and dried.monolingual: fixed; determined beforehand; usual and uninteresting. (Can be hyphenated before nominals.) _ I find your writing quite boring. It’s too cut and dried. _ The lecture was, as usual, cut and dried.
examples: I find your writing quite boring.

cut back.monolingual: to turn back; to reverse direction. _ Suddenly, the bull cut back in our direction and began chasing us. _ The road cuts back about a mile ahead, and it goes west again.
examples: Suddenly, the bull cut back in our direction and began chasing us.

cut both ways.monolingual: to affect both sides of an issue equally. _ Remember that your suggestion that costs should be shared cuts both ways. Your division will have to reduce its budget as well. _ If our side cannot take along supporters to the game, then yours cannot eith
examples: Remember that your suggestion that costs should be shared cuts both ways.

cut corners.monolingual: Fig. to take shortcuts; to save money or effort by finding cheaper or easier ways to do something. _ They’re always finding ways to cut corners. _ I won’t cut corners just to save money. I put quality first.
examples: They’re always finding ways to cut corners.

cut off.monolingual: 1. to stop by itself or oneself. _ The machine got hot and cut off. _Bob cut off in midsentence.
examples: The machine got hot and cut off.

cut out.monolingual: to depart; to leave in a hurry. _ Good-bye. I have to cut out now. _It’s time I was cutting out. I’m late already.
examples: Good-bye. I have to cut out now.

cut to the chase.monolingual: Sl. to focus on what is important; to abandon the preliminaries and deal with the major points. _ All right, let’s stop the idle chatter and cut to the chase. _ After a few introductory comments, we cut to the chase and began negotiating.
examples: All right, let’s stop the idle chatter and cut to the chase.

cut up.monolingual: to act wildly; to show off and be troublesome; to act like a clown. _ Tom, Billy! Stop cutting up, or I’ll send you to the principal’s office. _ If you spent more time studying than cutting up, you’d get better grades.
examples: Tom, Billy! Stop cutting up, or I’ll send you to the principal’s office.

damp off.monolingual: [for seedlings] to die from too much water. _ All the new plants damped off, and we had to buy some from the nursery. _ The little seedlings damped off and withered away.
examples: All the new plants damped off, and we had to buy some from the nursery.

dark horse.monolingual: Fig. someone or something whose abilities, plans, or feelings are little known to others. (From a race horse about which little or nothing is known.) _ It’s difficult to predict who will win the prize—there are two or three dark horses in the tournam
examples: It’s difficult to predict who will win the prize—there are two or three dark horses in the tournament.

dart about.monolingual: to move about quickly. _ The little fish were darting about everywhere. _ People were darting about, to and fro, during the noon rush hour.
examples: The little fish were darting about everywhere.

day after day.monolingual: every day; daily; all the time. _ He wears the same clothes day after day. _ She visits her husband in the hospital day after day.
examples: He wears the same clothes day after day.

daylight robbery.monolingual: Fig. the practice of blatantly or grossly overcharging. _It’s daylight robbery to charge that amount of money for a hotel room! _ The cost of renting a car at that place is daylight robbery.
examples: The cost of renting a car at that place is daylight robbery.

dead and buried.monolingual: 1. Lit. dead and interred, and soon to be forgotten. _ Now that Uncle Bill is dead and buried, we can read his will.
examples: Now that Uncle Bill is dead and buried, we can read his will.

dead center.monolingual: at the exact center of something. _ The arrow hit the target dead center. _ When you put the f lowers on the table, put them dead center.
examples: The arrow hit the target dead center.

dead meat.monolingual: Fig. dead; as good as dead. (Usually an exaggeration.) _ If you don’t do exactly as I say, you are dead meat!

dead on.monolingual: exactly right; on target. _ That’s a good observation, Tiffany. You are dead on. _ Your criticism is dead on!
examples: That’s a good observation, Tiffany.

dead to the world.monolingual: 1. sound asleep. _After all that exercise, he’s dead to the world. _ He’s dead to the world, and I can’t rouse him.
examples: After all that exercise, he’s dead to the world.

die away.monolingual: Fig. to fade away. _ The sound of the waterfall finally died away. _When the applause died away, the tenor sang an encore.
examples: The sound of the waterfall finally died away.

die back.monolingual: [for vegetation] to die back to the stems or roots. _ The hedge died back in the winter but regenerated leaves in the spring. _ This kind of grass dies back every year.
examples: The hedge died back in the winter but regenerated leaves in the spring.

die down.monolingual: to fade to almost nothing; to decrease gradually. _The fire died down and went out. _As the applause died down, a child came on stage with an armload of roses for the singer.
examples: The fire died down and went out.

die off.monolingual: [for a living thing] to perish one by one until there are no more. _Most of the larger lizards died off eons ago. _ It would be really bad if all the owls died off. _ The cucumber blossoms all died off.
examples: Most of the larger lizards died off eons ago.

die out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a species or family] to perish totally because of the failure to produce offspring. _I am the last one in the family, so I guess our line will die out with me. _ The owls might die out if you ruin their nesting area.
examples: I am the last one in the family, so I guess our line will die out with me.

dim out.monolingual: [for a light] to grow dim and go out altogether. _ The lights dimmed out twice during the storm. _ I was afraid that the lights would dim out completely.
examples: The lights dimmed out twice during the storm.

a dime a dozen.monolingual: Fig. abundant; cheap and common. _ People who can write good books are not a dime a dozen. _ Romantic movies are a dime a dozen.
examples: People who can write good books are not a dime a dozen.

dine in.monolingual: to eat at home rather than at a restaurant. _I think we will dine in tonight. _ I am tired of dining in. Let’s go out.
examples: I think we will dine in tonight.

dirty work.monolingual: 1. Fig. unpleasant or uninteresting work. _ My boss does all the traveling. I get all the dirty work to do. _She’s tired of doing all the dirty work at the office.
examples: My boss does all the traveling.

dish the dirt.monolingual: Sl. to spread gossip; to gossip. _ Let’s sit down, have a drink, and dish the dirt. _ David goes down to the tavern to dish the dirt.
examples: Let’s sit down, have a drink, and dish the dirt.

divide and conquer.monolingual: to cause the enemy to divide and separate into two or more factions, and then move in to conquer all of them. _Mary thought she could divide and conquer the board of directors, but they had survived such tactics many times, and her efforts failed. _
examples: Mary thought she could divide and conquer the board of directors, but they had survived such tactics many times, and her efforts failed.

do a slow burn.monolingual: Fig. to be quietly angry. _ I did a slow burn while I was waiting in line for a refund.
examples: I did a slow burn while I was waiting in line for a refund.

do or die.monolingual: Fig. trying as hard as one can. _ I was determined to get there—do or die. _ (Used as an attributive) He has the obsessive do-or-die attitude.
examples: I was determined to get there—do or die.

do someone proud.monolingual: to make someone proud. _ Bill’s kids sure did him proud at the boat race. _ Mary resolved she would do her friends proud.
examples: Bill’s kids sure did him proud at the boat race.

do the honors.monolingual: to act as host or hostess and serve one’s guests by pouring drinks, slicing meat, making (drinking) toasts, etc. _ All the guests were seated, and a huge juicy turkey sat on the table. Jane turned to her husband and said, “Bob, will you do the honors
examples: All the guests were seated, and a huge juicy turkey sat on the table.

do the trick.monolingual: to do exactly what is needed. _ This new paint scraper really does the trick. _ Is this envelope large enough to do the trick?
examples: This new paint scraper really does the trick.

dog and pony show.monolingual: Fig. a display, demonstration, or exhibition of something—such as something one is selling. (As in a circus act where trained dogs leap onto and off of trained ponies.) _ Gary went into his standard dog and pony show, trying to sell us on an upgrade
examples: Gary went into his standard dog and pony show, trying to sell us on an upgrade to our software.

dog in the manger.monolingual: one who unreasonably prevents other people from doing or having what one does not wish them to do or have. (From one of Aesop’s fables in which a dog—which cannot eat hay—lay in the hayrack [manger] and prevented the other animals from eating the hay
examples: Jane is a real dog in the manger.

double over.monolingual: [for a person] to bend at the waist. _ Suddenly, he doubled over and collapsed. _ The people in the audience doubled over with laughter.
examples: Suddenly, he doubled over and collapsed.

down in the mouth.monolingual: Fig. sad-faced; depressed and unsmiling. _ Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth. _ Bob has been down in the mouth since he was laid off from his job.
examples: Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth.

down the drain.monolingual: Fig. gone; wasted. _ Well, there’s 400 bucks down the drain. _ A lot of money went down the drain in that Wilson deal.
examples: Well, there’s 400 bucks down the drain.

down the road.monolingual: 1. Lit. farther along on this same road. _ Just continue down the road until you come to a little church. Turn left there.
examples: Just continue down the road until you come to a little church.

down under.monolingual: Australia and New Zealand. _ I’ve always wanted to visit down under. _ We spent Christmas down under.
examples: I’ve always wanted to visit down under.

drain away.monolingual: [for something] to flow away. _All the water drained away and exposed the mud and rocks on the bottom of the pond. _When the water drained away, we found three snapping turtles in the bottom of the pond.
examples: All the water drained away and exposed the mud and rocks on the bottom of the pond.

drain out.monolingual: to flow out or empty. _All the milk drained out of the container onto the bottom of the refrigerator. _ All the oil drained out of the crankcase.
examples: All the milk drained out of the container onto the bottom of the refrigerator.

draw a blank.monolingual: 1. Fig. to get no response; to find nothing. _ I asked him about Tom’s financial problems, and I just drew a blank. _ We looked in the files for an hour, but we drew a blank.
examples: I asked him about Tom’s financial problems, and I just drew a blank.

draw up.monolingual: to pull up more tightly; to shrink up. _ When they got wet, his trunks drew up and became very tight. _ This cheap underwear has a tendency to draw up.
examples: When they got wet, his trunks drew up and became very tight.

drift along.monolingual: to float along; to be carried along on no particular course. _The boat just drifted along lazily with the current. _ The project drifted along until we received the leadership we needed.
examples: The boat just drifted along lazily with the current.

drift off.monolingual: to move slowly away. _ The boat slowly drifted off and was gone. _The clouds drifted off and the sun came out.
examples: The boat slowly drifted off and was gone.

drive a hard bargain.monolingual: to work hard to negotiate prices or agreements in one’s own favor. _All right, sir, you drive a hard bargain. I’ll sell you this car for $12,450. _You drive a hard bargain, Jane, but I’ll sign the contract.
examples: All right, sir, you drive a hard bargain.

drive away.monolingual: to leave some place driving a vehicle. _ They got in the car and drove away. _ They drove away and left us here.
examples: They got in the car and drove away.

drive back.monolingual: to go in a vehicle back to where it started. _ Mary drove back and parked the car where it had been when she started. _ You drive us there and I’ll drive back.
examples: Mary drove back and parked the car where it had been when she started.

drive off.monolingual: to leave somewhere, driving a vehicle. _ She got in her car and drove off. _ Please don’t drive off and leave me!
examples: She got in her car and drove off.

drive someone to drink.monolingual: Fig. [for someone or something] to cause someone to turn to alcohol as an escape from frustration. _ Being a Cubs fan is enough to drive you to drink. _ She was driven to drink by the problems she had with her teenage son.
examples: Being a Cubs fan is enough to drive you to drink.

drive someone up the wall.monolingual: Fig. to annoy or irritate someone. _ Stop whistling that tune. You’re driving me up the wall. _All his talk about moving to California nearly drove me up the wall.
examples: Stop whistling that tune.

drop a hint.monolingual: Fig. to give a tiny or careful hint about something. _ Mary dropped a hint that she wanted a new ring for her birthday.
examples: Mary dropped a hint that she wanted a new ring for her birthday.

drop away.monolingual: 1. Lit. to fall off; to fall away. _The leaves were still dropping away from the trees in November. _The dead branches dropped away from the tree.
examples: The leaves were still dropping away from the trees in November.

drop back.monolingual: 1. to fall back to an original position. _ His arm raised up and then dropped back. _ The lid dropped back to its original position as soon as we let go of it.
examples: His arm raised up and then dropped back.

drop down.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to fall down or stoop down. _ Suddenly, Ted dropped down, trying not to be seen by someone in a passing car. _ I dropped down as soon as I heard the loud sounds.
examples: Suddenly, Ted dropped down, trying not to be seen by someone in a passing car.

drop off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a part of something] to break away and fall off. _ The car’s bumper just dropped off—honest. _ I lifted boxes until I thought my arms would drop off.
examples: The car’s bumper just dropped off—honest.

drop the ball.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in a ball game of some type] to let the ball get away or fall out of one’s grasp. _ Good grief! Bill dropped the ball, just as he was about to score!
examples: Good grief! Bill dropped the ball, just as he was about to score! 2.

dry out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to become dry. _ The clothes finally dried out in the wet weather.
examples: The clothes finally dried out in the wet weather.

dry run.monolingual: Fig. an attempt; a practice or rehearsal. _We had better have a dry run for the official ceremony tomorrow. _ The children will need another dry run before their procession in the pageant.
examples: We had better have a dry run for the official ceremony tomorrow.

dry up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to dry away to nothing. _ Finally, the water on the track dried up, and the race was able to continue. _ When will the fields dry up so we can plant?
examples: Finally, the water on the track dried up, and the race was able to continue.

duck down.monolingual: to stoop down quickly, as if to avoid being hit. _ He ducked down when he heard the gunshot. _ Duck down and get out of the way.
examples: He ducked down when he heard the gunshot.

duck soup.monolingual: Fig. very easy; an easy thing to do. _For Maria, knitting a sweater is duck soup. _ Jill: This jar is stuck. Could you open it for me? Jane: Sure. Duck soup.
examples: For Maria, knitting a sweater is duck soup.

duke it out.monolingual: Sl. to have a fistfight. _ John told George to meet him in the alley so they could duke it out.
examples: John told George to meet him in the alley so they could duke it out.

dummy up.monolingual: Sl. to refuse to talk. _ Jill dummied up when they got her into the station. _John dummied up right away when the police arrived.
examples: Jill dummied up when they got her into the station.

eager beaver.monolingual: someone who is very enthusiastic; someone who works very hard. _ New volunteers are always eager beavers. _The young assistant gets to work very early. She’s a real eager beaver.
examples: New volunteers are always eager beavers.

eagle eye.monolingual: acute eyesight; an intently watchful eye. (From the sharp eyesight of the eagle.) _The students wrote their essays under the eagle eye of the headmaster. _The umpire kept his eagle eye on the tennis match.
examples: The students wrote their essays under the eagle eye of the headmaster.

early bird.monolingual: 1. Fig. a person who gets up early. _ I never miss sunrise. I’m an early bird. _ The early birds were up at dawn and ready for breakfast.
examples: I never miss sunrise.

ease off.monolingual: [for something] to diminish. _ The rain began to ease off. _ The storm seems to have eased off a little.
examples: The rain began to ease off.

easier said than done.monolingual: Cliché said of a task that is easier to talk about than to do. _ Yes, we must find a cure for cancer, but it’s easier said than done. _ Finding a good job is easier said than done.
examples: Yes, we must find a cure for cancer, but it’s easier said than done.

easy come, easy go.monolingual: Cliché said to explain the loss of something that required only a small amount of effort to acquire in the first place. _ Ann found twenty dollars in the morning and spent it foolishly at noon. “Easy come, easy go,” she said. _John spends his money a
examples: Ann found twenty dollars in the morning and spent it foolishly at noon.

easy pickings.monolingual: [of things] easy to get or steal; [of people] easy to get or persuade. _ The pickpockets found lots of easy pickings at the state fair.
examples: The pickpockets found lots of easy pickings at the state fair.

eat crow.monolingual: 1. Fig. to display total humility, especially when shown to be wrong. _ Well, it looks like I was wrong, and I’m going to have to eat crow. _ I’ll be eating crow if I’m not shown to be right.
examples: Well, it looks like I was wrong, and I’m going to have to eat crow.

eat humble pie.monolingual: to act very humble when one is shown to be wrong. _ I think I’m right, but if I’m wrong, I’ll eat humble pie. _ You think you’re so smart. I hope you have to eat humble pie.
examples: I think I’m right, but if I’m wrong, I’ll eat humble pie.

eat in.monolingual: to eat a meal at home. _ I really don’t want to eat in tonight. _ Let’s eat in. I’m tired.
examples: I really don’t want to eat in tonight.

eat out.monolingual: to eat a meal away from home, as at a restaurant. _ I just love to eat out every now and then. _ Let’s eat out tonight. I’m tired.
examples: I just love to eat out every now and then.

economical with the truth.monolingual: Euph. untruthful. _ The mayor was known to be economical with the truth. _I discovered that my boss had been economical with the truth when she said that the company was making money.
examples: The mayor was known to be economical with the truth.

elbow grease.monolingual: Fig. hard scrubbing. _ Tom: What did you use to get your car so shiny? Mary: Just regular wax and some elbow grease. _Joe put a lot of elbow grease into cleaning the kitchen.
examples: Tom: What did you use to get your car so shiny? Mary: Just regular wax and some elbow grease.

end up.monolingual: to come to an end. _ When will all this end up? _ I think that the party will have to end up about midnight.
examples: I think that the party will have to end up about midnight.

everything but the kitchen sink.monolingual: Cliché almost everything one can think of. _ When Sally went off to college, she took everything but the kitchen sink. _ John orders everything but the kitchen sink when he goes out to dinner, especially if someone else is paying for it.
examples: When Sally went off to college, she took everything but the kitchen sink.

face off.monolingual: 1. to begin a hockey game with two players facing one another. _ They faced off and the match was on.
examples: They faced off and the match was on.

face the music.monolingual: Fig. to receive punishment; to accept the unpleasant results of one’s actions. _ Mary broke a dining- room window and had to face the music when her father got home. _ After failing a math test, Tom had to go home and face the music.
examples: Mary broke a dining- room window and had to face the music when her father got home.

fair-haired boy.monolingual: Fig. a favored person. (Not necessarily young or a boy.) _ The teacher’s fair-haired boy always does well on tests. _The supervisor’s son was the fair-haired boy on the construction site.
examples: The teacher’s fair-haired boy always does well on tests.

fair-weather friend.monolingual: Fig. someone who is your friend only when things are pleasant or going well for you. _Bill stayed for lunch but he wouldn’t help me with the yard work. He’s just a fair-weather friend. _A fair-weather friend isn’t much help in an emergency.
examples: Bill stayed for lunch but he wouldn’t help me with the yard work.

fall asleep.monolingual: Fig. to go to sleep. _ I fell asleep while reading the very dull book. _ I got in bed and fell asleep at once.
examples: I fell asleep while reading the very dull book.

fall back.monolingual: to move back from something; to retreat from something. _ The gang members fell back, and I took that opportunity to get away. _ The troops fell back to regroup.
examples: The gang members fell back, and I took that opportunity to get away.

fall between two stools.monolingual: Fig. to come somewhere between two possibilities and so fail to meet the requirements of either. _ The material is not suitable for an academic book or for a popular one. It falls between two stools. _ He tries to be both teacher and friend, but fall
examples: The material is not suitable for an academic book or for a popular one.

fall down.monolingual: to drop or topple. _The baby fell down. _Walk carefully on this ice or you will fall down.
examples: The baby fell down.

fall from grace.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sin and get on the wrong side of God. (A Christian concept.) _ It was either fall from grace or starve from lack of money. That’s how thieves are made. _ Given the choice between falling from grace and starving, few people choose to starve
examples: It was either fall from grace or starve from lack of money.

fall in.monolingual: to line up in a row, standing shoulder to shoulder. _ The Boy Scouts were told to fall in behind the leader. _ The soldiers fell in quickly.
examples: The Boy Scouts were told to fall in behind the leader.

fall into the wrong hands.monolingual: Fig. to become associated with the wrong person; to become the possession of the wrong person. _ I don’t want these plans to fall into the wrong hands. _ This could be dangerous if it fell into the wrong hands.
examples: I don’t want these plans to fall into the wrong hands.

fall off.monolingual: to decline or diminish. _ Business falls off during the summer months. _My interest in school fell off when I became twenty.
examples: Business falls off during the summer months.

fall out.monolingual: 1. to happen; to result. _As things fell out, we had a wonderful trip. _ What fell out of our discussion was a decision to continue.
examples: As things fell out, we had a wonderful trip.

fall over.monolingual: to topple over and fall down. _The fence fell over and dented the car. _ I felt faint and almost fell over.
examples: The fence fell over and dented the car.

fall short.monolingual: to lack something; to lack enough of something, such as money, time, etc. _ We fell short of money at the end of the month. _ Tom fell short of cash and had to borrow from me.
examples: We fell short of money at the end of the month.

fall through.monolingual: [for something, such as plans] to fail. _Our party for next Saturday fell through. _ I hope our plans don’t fall through.
examples: Our party for next Saturday fell through.

fall to.monolingual: to begin doing something; to prepare to do something and go to work on it. _She asked for help, and everyone fell to. _ Fall to, you guys!
examples: She asked for help, and everyone fell to.

fan out.monolingual: Fig. to spread out over a wide area. _The searchers fanned out, looking for the child lost in the woods. _ Let’s fan out and search a wider area.
examples: The searchers fanned out, looking for the child lost in the woods.

fart around.monolingual: Fig. to waste time playing around. (Caution with fart, which is considered coarse.) _ Stop farting around and get the job started.
examples: Stop farting around and get the job started.

fast and furious.monolingual: Cliché very rapidly and with unrestrained energy. _ Her work in the kitchen was fast and furious, and it looked lovely when she finished. _ Everything was going so fast and furious at the store during the Christmas rush that we never had time to eat
examples: Her work in the kitchen was fast and furious, and it looked lovely when she finished.

fat chance.monolingual: Fig. very little likelihood. _ Fat chance he has of getting a promotion. _ You think she’ll lend you the money? Fat chance!
examples: Fat chance he has of getting a promotion.

fetch up.monolingual: Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _ I really felt like I was going to fetch up. _ Somebody fetched up in here and didn’t clean it up.
examples: I really felt like I was going to fetch up.

few and far between.monolingual: very few; few and widely scattered. _ Get some gasoline now. Service stations on this highway are few and far between. _ Some people think that good movies are few and far between.
examples: Get some gasoline now.

fill in.monolingual: [for an indentation, hole, etc.] to become full. _The scar filled in after a few months. _ Will this hole in the ground fill in by itself, or should I put some dirt in?
examples: The scar filled in after a few months.

fill out.monolingual: to become full; to gain weight. _ About a month after her debilitating illness, Maggie began to fill out again. _ The fruit on the trees began to fill out, and we knew it was going to ripen soon.
examples: About a month after her debilitating illness, Maggie began to fill out again.

fill up.monolingual: 1. to become full. _ The creek filled up after the heavy rain yesterday. _The rain barrel began to fill up during the storm.
examples: The creek filled up after the heavy rain yesterday.

filthy lucre.monolingual: money. _ I sure could use a little of that filthy lucre. _ I don’t want to touch any of your filthy lucre.
examples: I sure could use a little of that filthy lucre.

filthy rich.monolingual: 1. Fig. very wealthy. _ I wouldn’t mind being filthy rich. _ There are too many filthy rich people now.
examples: I wouldn’t mind being filthy rich.

fire up.monolingual: to light a cigarette, cigar, or pipe. _ One by one, the guests went outside and fired up. _ I have to get out of here and fire up.
examples: One by one, the guests went outside and fired up.

firm up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to develop better muscle tone; to become less flabby. _ I need to do some exercises so I can firm up. _You really ought to firm up.
examples: I need to do some exercises so I can firm up.

first of all.monolingual: as the very first thing; before anything else. _ First of all, put your name on this piece of paper. _ First of all, we’ll try to find a place to live.
examples: First of all, put your name on this piece of paper.

first off.monolingual: first; the first thing. (Almost the same as first of all.) _ He ordered soup first off. _ First off, we’ll find a place to live.
examples: He ordered soup first off.
