fish in troubled waters.monolingual: Fig. to involve oneself in a difficult, confused, or dangerous situation, especially with a view to gaining an advantage. _ Frank is fishing in troubled waters by buying more shares of that company. They are supposed to be in financial difficulties.
examples: Frank is fishing in troubled waters by buying more shares of that company.

fit to be tied.monolingual: angry and agitated. (As if needing to be restrained.) _ Joe was fit to be tied when his wife told him she was leaving. _ I was fit to be tied when Mary tried to be friendly, after three years of not speaking to me.
examples: Joe was fit to be tied when his wife told him she was leaving.

fit together.monolingual: [for things] to conform in shape to one another. _ All the pieces of the puzzle fit together. They really do. _ This nut and bolt just don’t fit together.
examples: All the pieces of the puzzle fit together.

fizzle out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a liquid] to lose its effervescence. _ This seltzer has fizzled out. I need a fresh glass of it.
examples: This seltzer has fizzled out.

flake down.monolingual: Sl. to go to bed and go to sleep. _ I’ve got to go home and flake down for a while. _Tom is flaked down for the night.
examples: I’ve got to go home and flake down for a while.

flame up.monolingual: 1. [for something] to catch fire and burst into flames. _ The trees flamed up one by one in the forest fire. _Suddenly the car flamed up and exploded.
examples: The trees flamed up one by one in the forest fire.

flare out.monolingual: to spread out; to widen. (Said especially of one opening of a tube or round-topped vessel.) _ The end of the pipe f lared out to a larger diameter. _ The top of the vase f lared out, and was decorated with little blobs of colored glass.
examples: The end of the pipe f lared out to a larger diameter.

flat out.monolingual: 1. clearly and definitely; holding nothing back. _ I told her f lat out that I didn’t like her. _ They reported f lat out that the operation was a failure.
examples: I told her f lat out that I didn’t like her.

flesh out.monolingual: to become more fleshy. _ She began to f lesh out at the age of thirteen. _ After his illness, Tom fleshed out and regained his strength.
examples: She began to f lesh out at the age of thirteen.

flight of fancy.monolingual: an idea or suggestion that is out of touch with reality or possibility. _What is the point in indulging in f lights of fancy about exotic vacations when you cannot even afford the rent?

flip out.monolingual: Sl. to lose control of oneself. _ After a sleepless night, Wally simply f lipped out. _ I felt like I was going to f lip out from the steady dripping of the faucet.
examples: After a sleepless night, Wally simply f lipped out.

flip over.monolingual: to turn over quickly. _ The fish f lipped over and f lipped back over again. _ The cat f lipped over and ran away.
examples: The fish f lipped over and f lipped back over again.

float around.monolingual: to float from here to there freely. _All sorts of paper and trash were f loating around on the surface of the pond. _Water hyacinths f loated around, making a very tropical scene.
examples: All sorts of paper and trash were f loating around on the surface of the pond.

flock together.monolingual: to gather together in great numbers. (Typically said of birds and sheep.) _A large number of blackbirds f locked together, making a lot of noise. _ Do sheep really f lock together in a storm?
examples: A large number of blackbirds f locked together, making a lot of noise.

floor it.monolingual: Fig. to press down hard and fast on the accelerator of a vehicle. _ She f loored it and sped off over the hill.
examples: She f loored it and sped off over the hill.

flop down.monolingual: to sit down heavily or awkwardly. _ Be graceful. Don’t just f lop down! _ When I reached the chair, all I could do was f lop down.
examples: When I reached the chair, all I could do was f lop down.

flub up.monolingual: to make an error. _ I f lubbed up again!

fly apart.monolingual: to break apart, throwing pieces around. _Don’t run the engine too fast or it will f ly apart! _ Mary’s bicycle wheel f lew apart during the race.
examples: Mary’s bicycle wheel f lew apart during the race.

fly by.monolingual: 1. Lit. to soar past, flying. _ Three jet fighters f lew by. _A huge hawk f lew by, frightening all the smaller birds.
examples: Three jet fighters f lew by.

fly off.monolingual: 1. Lit. to take to flight quickly. _ The stork f lew off before we got a good look at it. _ The little birds f lew off and things were quiet again.
examples: The stork f lew off before we got a good look at it.

fly off the handle.monolingual: Fig. to lose one’s temper. _Every time anyone mentions taxes, Mrs. Brown f lies off the handle. _ If she keeps f lying off the handle like that, she’ll have a heart attack.
examples: Every time anyone mentions taxes, Mrs.

foam up.monolingual: [for something, such as soap or milk] to make foam or lather. _ Milk will foam up when it is boiled. _ The boiling soup foamed up and slopped over the pot.
examples: Milk will foam up when it is boiled.

fog up.monolingual: [for something made of glass] to become partially or completely obscured by a film of water vapor. _ The glass fogged up, and we couldn’t see out.
examples: The glass fogged up, and we couldn’t see out.

fold up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to close by folding. _ The table just folded up with no warning, trapping my leg.
examples: The table just folded up with no warning, trapping my leg.

follow suit.monolingual: to follow in the same pattern; to follow someone else’s example. (From card games.) _ Mary went to work for a bank, and Jane followed suit. Now they are both head cashiers. _ The Smiths went out to dinner, but the Browns didn’t follow suit. They stay
examples: Mary went to work for a bank, and Jane followed suit.

follow the crowd.monolingual: to do what everyone else is doing. _ I am an independent thinker. I could never just follow the crowd. _When in doubt, I follow the crowd. At least I don’t stand out like a fool.
examples: I am an independent thinker.

food for thought.monolingual: Fig. something for someone to think about; issues to be considered. _ Your essay has provided me with some interesting food for thought. _ My adviser gave me some food for thought about job opportunities.
examples: Your essay has provided me with some interesting food for thought.

fool around.monolingual: to waste time doing something unnecessary or doing something amateurishly. _ Stop fooling around and clean your room as I told you. _I wish you didn’t spend so much time fooling around.
examples: Stop fooling around and clean your room as I told you.

foot-in-mouth disease.monolingual: the tendency to say the wrong thing at the wrong time. _I suffer a lot from foot-in-mouth disease. _ Well, Ralph has foot-in-mouth disease again.
examples: I suffer a lot from foot-in-mouth disease.

for all the world.monolingual: 1. exactly; precisely. (Especially with look.) _ She sat there looking for all the world as if she was going to cry. _ It started out seeming for all the world like a beautiful day. Then a storm came up.
examples: She sat there looking for all the world as if she was going to cry.

for good.monolingual: forever; permanently. _ I finally left home for good. _They tried to repair it many times before they fixed it for good.
examples: I finally left home for good.

for good measure.monolingual: as extra; (adding) a little more to make sure there is enough. _ When I bought a pound of nails, the clerk threw in a few extra nails for good measure. _ I always put a little extra salt in the soup for good measure.
examples: When I bought a pound of nails, the clerk threw in a few extra nails for good measure.

for keeps.monolingual: forever. _Does that mean I’m going to have this scar for keeps? _ This is yours for keeps. Enjoy it.
examples: This is yours for keeps.

for my money.monolingual: in my opinion (as regards value or worth). _ That’s the best brand of tools there is, for my money. _ For my money, you can’t go wrong with a pure wool sweater.
examples: That’s the best brand of tools there is, for my money.

for that matter.monolingual: besides; in addition. _ If you’re hungry, take one of my doughnuts. For that matter, take two. _ I don’t like this house. The roof leaks. For that matter, the whole place is falling apart. _ Tom is quite arrogant. So is his sister, for that matter.
examples: If you’re hungry, take one of my doughnuts.

for the asking.monolingual: if one just asks (for something); simply by asking; on request. _ Do you want to use my car? It’s yours for the asking. _ I have an extra winter coat that’s yours for the asking.
examples: Do you want to use my car? It’s yours for the asking.

for the birds.monolingual: worthless; undesirable. _This television program is for the birds. _ Winter weather is for the birds.
examples: This television program is for the birds.

for the most part.monolingual: mostly; in general. _For the most part, the class is enjoying geometry. _ I like working here for the most part.
examples: For the most part, the class is enjoying geometry.

forbidden fruit.monolingual: Fig. someone or something that one finds attractive or desirable partly because having the person or thing is immoral or illegal. (Biblical; from the apple in the Garden of Eden that was forbidden to Adam by God.) _ Jim flirts with his sister-in-law
examples: Jim flirts with his sister-in-law only because she’s forbidden fruit.

forget oneself.monolingual: to forget one’s manners or training. (Said in formal situations in reference to belching, bad table manners, and, in the case of very young children, pantswetting.) _ Sorry, Mother, I forgot myself. _ John, we are going out to dinner tonight. Please
examples: Sorry, Mother, I forgot myself.

forty winks.monolingual: Fig. a nap; some sleep. _ I could use forty winks before I have to get to work. _ I need forty winks before I get started again.
examples: I could use forty winks before I have to get to work.

foul up.monolingual: to blunder; to mess up. _Please don’t foul up this time. _The quarterback fouled up in the first quarter, and that lost us the game.
examples: Please don’t foul up this time.

free lunch.monolingual: Fig. something of value that is free. (Often negative. See also There’s no such thing as a free lunch.) _ There’s always somebody who’ll do anything to get a free lunch.
examples: There’s always somebody who’ll do anything to get a free lunch.

freeze over.monolingual: [for a body of water] to get cold and form a layer of ice on top. _The pond froze over, so we went skating.
examples: The pond froze over, so we went skating.

freeze up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to freeze and stop functioning. _ The joint froze up and wouldn’t move anymore.
examples: The joint froze up and wouldn’t move anymore.

freshen up.monolingual: to get cleaned up, rested up, or restored. _ I need a few minutes to freshen up before dinner.
examples: I need a few minutes to freshen up before dinner.

from hand to hand.monolingual: Fig. from one person to a series of other persons. _The book traveled from hand to hand until it got back to its owner. _ By the time the baby had been passed from hand to hand, it was crying.
examples: The book traveled from hand to hand until it got back to its owner.

from pillar to post.monolingual: Fig. from one place to a series of other places; (figuratively) from person to person, as with gossip. _ My father was in the army, and we moved from pillar to post year after year. _ After I told one person my secret, it went quickly from pillar to
examples: My father was in the army, and we moved from pillar to post year after year.

from stem to stern.monolingual: 1. Lit. from the front of a boat or ship to the back. _He inspected the boat from stem to stern and decided he wanted to buy it.
examples: He inspected the boat from stem to stern and decided he wanted to buy it.

from the ground up.monolingual: Fig. from the very beginning. _ We must plan our sales campaign carefully from the ground up. _ Sorry, but you’ll have to start all over again from the ground up.
examples: We must plan our sales campaign carefully from the ground up.

from the word go.monolingual: Cliché from the very beginning. _ I knew about the problem from the word go. _ She was failing the class from the word go.
examples: I knew about the problem from the word go.

from time to time.monolingual: irregularly; now and then; occasionally; sometimes; not predictably. _ From time to time, I like to go fishing instead of going to work. _ Bob visits us at our house from time to time.
examples: From time to time, I like to go fishing instead of going to work.

froth up.monolingual: [for something] to build up a froth when whipped, aerated, or boiled. _The mixture began to froth up as Dan beat it. _The milk frothed up as the steam went through it.
examples: The mixture began to froth up as Dan beat it.

fudge factor.monolingual: Fig. a margin of error. _ I never use a fudge factor. I measure correctly, and I cut the material exactly the way I measured it. _ I built in a fudge factor of three percent.
examples: I never use a fudge factor.

fuel up.monolingual: to fill one’s tank with fuel. _ Let’s stop here and fuel up. _ I need to fuel up at the next little town.
examples: Let’s stop here and fuel up.

fun and games.monolingual: Fig. playing around; doing worthless things. _All right, Bill, the fun and games are over. It’s time to get down to work. _This isn’t a serious course. It’s nothing but fun and games.
examples: All right, Bill, the fun and games are over.

futz around.monolingual: Sl. to waste time. _ Stop futzing around and get the job done. _ I wish you would stop futzing around!
examples: Stop futzing around and get the job done.

gas up.monolingual: to fill up one’s gasoline tank with gasoline. _I have to stop at the next service station and gas up. _ The next time you gas up, try some of the gasoline with alcohol in it.
examples: I have to stop at the next service station and gas up.

gather dust.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to sit unused for a long time. _ Most of my talent is just gathering dust because I don’t really have an opportunity to perform.
examples: Most of my talent is just gathering dust because I don’t really have an opportunity to perform.

get ahead of oneself.monolingual: Fig. [for someone] to do or say something sooner than it ought to be done so that the proper explanation or preparations have not been made. _I have to stick to my notes or I will get ahead of myself in my lecture. _When he bought a new little bicycl
examples: I have to stick to my notes or I will get ahead of myself in my lecture.

get along.monolingual: 1. [for people or animals] to be amiable with one another. _Those two just don’t get along. _They seem to get along just fine.
examples: Those two just don’t get along.

get away.monolingual: to move away. (Often a command.) _Get away! Don’t bother me! _ I tried to get away, but he wouldn’t let me.
examples: I tried to get away, but he wouldn’t let me.

get better.monolingual: to improve. _ I had a bad cold, but it’s getting better. _ Business was bad last year, but it’s getting better. _ I’m sorry you’re ill. I hope you get better.
examples: I had a bad cold, but it’s getting better.

get busy.monolingual: to start working; to work or appear to work harder or faster. _The boss is coming. You’d better get busy. _ I’ve got to get busy and clean this house up.
examples: The boss is coming.

get down.monolingual: 1. Sl. to lay one’s money on the table. (Gambling.) _Okay, everybody get down. _Get down, and let’s get going!
examples: Okay, everybody get down.

get down to brass tacks.monolingual: Fig. to begin to talk about important things; to get down to business. _ Let’s get down to brass tacks. We’ve wasted too much time chatting. _ Don’t you think that it’s about time to get down to brass tacks?
examples: Let’s get down to brass tacks.

get down to cases.monolingual: to begin to discuss specific matters; to get down to business. _When we’ve finished the general discussion, we’ll get down to cases. _ Now that everyone is here, we can get down to cases.
examples: When we’ve finished the general discussion, we’ll get down to cases.

get it on.monolingual: 1. Sl. to begin something. _ Time to go back to work. Let’s get it on! _ Get it on, you guys! Time to start your engines.
examples: Time to go back to work.

get lost.monolingual: 1. to become lost; to lose one’s way. _We got lost on the way home. _ Follow the path, or you might get lost.
examples: We got lost on the way home.

get moving.monolingual: to get busy; to get started; to work harder or faster. _ Come on, everybody. Get moving! _ The director is coming. You had better get moving.
examples: Come on, everybody.

get off.monolingual: 1. to start off (on a friendship). _ Tom and Bill had never met before. They seemed to get off all right, though. _ I’m glad they got off so well.
examples: Tom and Bill had never met before.

get out.monolingual: 1. [for someone or an animal] to depart to the outside or to escape. _ When did your dog get out and run away? _ When did he get out of jail?
examples: When did he get out of jail? 2.

get up.monolingual: to wake up and get out of bed. _ What time do you usually get up? _ I get up when I have to.
examples: I get up when I have to.

get well.monolingual: to become healthy again. _ Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well. _ Hurry up and get well!
examples: Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well.

get wet.monolingual: to become moist or soaked with water. _ Get out of the rain or you’ll get wet. _ Don’t get wet, or you’ll catch a cold.
examples: Get out of the rain or you’ll get wet.

get with it.monolingual: 1. Inf. to modernize one’s attitudes and behavior. _ Get with it, Martin. Go out and buy some new clothes! _ You really have to get with it, Ernie.
examples: Get with it, Martin.

get with the program.monolingual: Fig. follow the rules; do what you are supposed to do. (Implies that there is a clearly known method or “program” that is usually followed.) _ Come on, Mark. Get with the program. Do what you are told. _ Jane just can’t seem to get with the program.
examples: Come on, Mark. Get with the program.

gild the lily.monolingual: Fig. to add ornament or decoration to something that is pleasing in its original state; to attempt to improve something that is already fine the way it is. (Often refers to flattery or exaggeration.) _Your house has lovely brickwork. Don’t paint it.
examples: Your house has lovely brickwork.

give in.monolingual: cave in; to push in. _The rotting door gave in when we pushed, and we went inside. _ The wall gave in where I kicked it.
examples: The rotting door gave in when we pushed, and we went inside.

give of oneself.monolingual: to be generous with one’s time and concern. _ Tom is very good with children because he gives of himself. _ If you want to have more friends, you have to learn to give of yourself.
examples: Tom is very good with children because he gives of himself.

give out.monolingual: 1. to wear out and stop; to quit operating. _ My old bicycle finally gave out. _ I think that your shoes are about ready to give out.
examples: My old bicycle finally gave out.

give someone the eye.monolingual: Fig. to look at someone in a way that communicates romantic interest. _Ann gave John the eye. It really surprised him. _Tom kept giving Sally the eye. She finally got disgusted and left.
examples: Ann gave John the eye.

give someone the slip.monolingual: Sl. to escape from a pursuer. _ We were on his tail until he gave us the slip. _ I can give her the slip in no time at all.
examples: We were on his tail until he gave us the slip.

give the game away.monolingual: Fig. to reveal a plan or strategy. _ Now, all of you have to keep quiet. Please don’t give the game away. _ If you keep giving out hints, you’ll give the game away.
examples: Now, all of you have to keep quiet.

give up.monolingual: to quit; to quit trying. _I give up! I won’t press this further. _ Are you going to give up or keep fighting?
examples: I give up! I won’t press this further.

give up the ghost.monolingual: Euph. to die. (Fixed order. Often used to describe machines breaking down.) _The old man gave up the ghost. _ My poor old car finally gave up the ghost.
examples: The old man gave up the ghost.

glaze over.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to be covered over with a coat of something cloudy or ice. _The roads glazed over and became very dangerous. _ The street is glazed over badly.
examples: The roads glazed over and became very dangerous.

go along.monolingual: 1. to continue; to progress. _ Things are going along quite nicely in my new job. _ I hope everything is going along well.
examples: Things are going along quite nicely in my new job.

go back.monolingual: to return to the place of origin. _ That’s where I came from, and I’ll never go back. _I don’t want to go back.
examples: That’s where I came from, and I’ll never go back.

go bananas.monolingual: Sl. to go mildly crazy. _ Sorry, I just went bananas for a minute. _ I thought he was going to go bananas.
examples: Sorry, I just went bananas for a minute.

go begging.monolingual: Fig. to be left over, unwanted, or unused. (As if a thing were begging for an owner or a user.) _ There is still food left. A whole lobster is going begging. Please eat some more. _There are many excellent books in the library just going begging beca
examples: There is still food left.

go below.monolingual: to go beneath the main deck of a ship. (Nautical.) _ I will have to go below and fiddle with the engine. _ The captain went below to escape the worst of the storm.
examples: I will have to go below and fiddle with the engine.

go berserk.monolingual: to go crazy. _ She went berserk and strangled her cat.
examples: She went berserk and strangled her cat.

go by the board.monolingual: Fig. to get ruined or lost. (This is originally a nautical expression meaning “to fall or be washed overboard.”) _ I hate to see good food go by the board. Please eat up so we won’t have to throw it out. _ Your plan has gone by the board. The entire
examples: I hate to see good food go by the board.

go down.monolingual: 1. to sink below a normal or expected level or height. _The plane went down in f lames. _The ship went down with all hands aboard.
examples: The plane went down in f lames.

go down in flames.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plane] to crash. _ The enemy fighter planes went down in f lames, ending the battle. _The pilot and crew went down in f lames near the airport.
examples: The enemy fighter planes went down in f lames, ending the battle.

go downhill.monolingual: [for something] to decline and grow worse and worse. _ This industry is going downhill. We lose money every year. _As one gets older, one’s health tends to go downhill.
examples: This industry is going downhill.

go for broke.monolingual: to risk everything; to try as hard as possible. _ Okay, this is my last chance. I’m going for broke. _ Look at Mary starting to move in the final hundred yards of the race! She is really going for broke.
examples: Okay, this is my last chance.

go off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for an explosive device] to explode. _ The fireworks all went off as scheduled. _ The bomb went off and did a lot of damage.
examples: The fireworks all went off as scheduled.

go off half-cocked.monolingual: Fig. to go into action too early or without thinking. (Originally refers to a flintlock or matchlock gun firing prematurely, before the trigger was pulled.) _ Don’t go off half-cocked. Plan out what you’re going to do. _ Bill went off half-cocked and
examples: Don’t go off half-cocked.

go over.monolingual: Euph. to leave one’s country and go to ideologically opposed or enemy country; to defect. _ When the ballet company visited New York, two of the dancers went over. _ He had been spying for the Americans for many years, and he finally went over.
examples: When the ballet company visited New York, two of the dancers went over.

go overboard.monolingual: 1. Fig. to fall out of a boat or off of a ship; to fall overboard. _Be careful or you will go overboard. _ Someone went overboard in the fog.
examples: Be careful or you will go overboard.

go places.monolingual: to become very successful. _ I knew that Sally, with all her talent, would go places. _ I really want to go places in life.
examples: I knew that Sally, with all her talent, would go places.

go straight.monolingual: to stop breaking the law and lead a lawful life instead. _The judge encouraged the thief to go straight. _ After Bob was arrested, he promised his mother he would go straight.
examples: The judge encouraged the thief to go straight.

go the distance.monolingual: Fig. to do the whole amount; to play the entire game; to run the whole race. (Originally sports use.) _That horse runs fast. I hope it can go the distance. _This is going to be a long, hard project. I hope I can go the distance.
examples: That horse runs fast.

go the extra mile.monolingual: to try harder to please someone or to get the task done correctly; to do more than one is required to do to reach a goal. _I like doing business with that company. They always go the extra mile. _My teacher goes the extra mile to help us.
examples: I like doing business with that company.

go through.monolingual: to be approved; to succeed in getting through the approval process. _I sent the board of directors a proposal. I hope it goes through. _ We all hope that the new law goes through.
examples: I sent the board of directors a proposal.

go through the motions.monolingual: Fig. to make a feeble effort to do something; to do something insincerely or in cursory fashion. _Jane isn’t doing her best. She’s just going through the motions. _ Bill was supposed to be raking the yard, but he was just going through the motions.
examples: Jane isn’t doing her best.

go to sea.monolingual: to become a sailor. _ I went to sea at an early age. _ When I get older, I’m going to go to sea too.
examples: I went to sea at an early age.

go to the polls.monolingual: to go to a place to vote; to vote. _ What day do we go to the polls? _Our community goes to the polls in November.
examples: Our community goes to the polls in November.

go to town.monolingual: 1. Lit. to travel into town or a city. _ I have to go to town today.
examples: I have to go to town today.

go together.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two or more things] to look, sound, or taste good together. _ Do you think that this pink one and this purple one go together? _Milk and grapefruit don’t go together.
examples: Milk and grapefruit don’t go together.

go too far.monolingual: to do more than is acceptable. _ I didn’t mind at first, but now you’ve gone too far. _ If you go too far, I’ll slap you.
examples: I didn’t mind at first, but now you’ve gone too far.

go under.monolingual: 1. to sink beneath the surface of the water. _ After capsizing, the ship went under very slowly. _ I was afraid that our canoe would go under in the rapidly moving water.
examples: After capsizing, the ship went under very slowly.

go up.monolingual: [for something] to go higher. _ Gasoline prices are still going up. _ Prices keep going up and up, no matter what.
examples: Gasoline prices are still going up.

go wild.monolingual: Fig. to get very excited. _ At the end of the football game, the kick was good and the crowd went wild.
examples: At the end of the football game, the kick was good and the crowd went wild.

go wrong.monolingual: to fail; [for something bad] to happen. _ The project failed. I don’t know what went wrong. _ I’m afraid that everything will go wrong.
examples: The project failed.

gone with the wind.monolingual: Fig. gone as if taken away by the wind. (A phrase made famous by the Margaret Mitchell novel and subsequent film Gone with the Wind. The phrase is used to make gone have a stronger force.) _ Everything we worked for was gone with the wind.
examples: Everything we worked for was gone with the wind.

goof around.monolingual: to act silly. _ The kids were all goofing around, waiting for the bus. _ Stop goofing around!
examples: The kids were all goofing around, waiting for the bus.

goof off.monolingual: to waste time. _John is always goofing off. _Quit goofing off and get to work!
examples: John is always goofing off.

grease the skids.monolingual: Fig. to help prepare for or ease the way for the success or failure of someone or something. _Ray set out to grease the skids for the right things to happen. _ We need someone to grease the skids for the Wilson contract.
examples: Ray set out to grease the skids for the right things to happen.

a great deal.monolingual: much; a lot. _You can learn a great deal about nature by watching television. _ This is a serious problem and it worries me a great deal.
examples: You can learn a great deal about nature by watching television.

grin and bear it.monolingual: Fig. to endure something unpleasant in good humor. _ There is nothing you can do but grin and bear it. _ I hate having to work for rude people. I guess I have to grin and bear it.
examples: There is nothing you can do but grin and bear it.

grow out.monolingual: [for something that has been cut back] to regrow. _ Don’t worry, your hair will grow out again. _ Will the grass grow out again, do you think?
examples: Don’t worry, your hair will grow out again.

grow up.monolingual: to become mature; to become adult. _ All the children have grown up and the parents are left with a lot of debts.
examples: All the children have grown up and the parents are left with a lot of debts.

grunt work.monolingual: Fig. work that is menial and thankless. _During the summer, I earned money doing grunt work. _ I did all of the grunt work on the project, but my boss got all of the credit.
examples: During the summer, I earned money doing grunt work.

hack around.monolingual: Inf. to waste time. _I’m just hacking around and doing nothing. _Stop hacking around and get to work.
examples: I’m just hacking around and doing nothing.

hale and hearty.monolingual: Cliché healthy. _ The young infant was hale and hearty. _The calf—hale and hearty—ran around the barnyard.
examples: The young infant was hale and hearty.

hand over fist.monolingual: Fig. [for money and merchandise to be exchanged] very rapidly. _ What a busy day. We took in money hand over fist. _They were buying things hand over fist.
examples: What a busy day.

hand over hand.monolingual: Fig. [moving] one hand after the other (again and again). _ Sally pulled in the rope hand over hand. _ The man climbed up the rope hand over hand.
examples: Sally pulled in the rope hand over hand.

hands down.monolingual: easily; unquestionably. _ She won the contest hands down. _ They declared her the winner hands down.
examples: She won the contest hands down.

hang off.monolingual: to wait quietly to one side. _ The boys hung off a little, waiting to see what would happen next. _Hang off awhile and don’t do anything.
examples: The boys hung off a little, waiting to see what would happen next.

hang on.monolingual: 1. to wait awhile. _ Hang on a minute. I need to talk to you. _Hang on. Let me catch up with you.
examples: Hang on a minute.

hang together.monolingual: 1. Fig. [for something or a group of people] to hold together; to remain intact. _I hope our bridge group hangs together until we are old and gray. _ I don’t think that this car will hang together for another minute.
examples: I hope our bridge group hangs together until we are old and gray.

hang up.monolingual: 1. [for a machine or a computer] to grind to a halt; to stop because of some internal complication. _ Our computer hung up right in the middle of printing the report. _I was afraid that my computer would hang up permanently.
examples: Our computer hung up right in the middle of printing the report.

hard of hearing.monolingual: [of someone] unable to hear well or partially deaf. _ Please speak loudly. I am hard of hearing. _ Tom is hard of hearing, but is not totally deaf.
examples: Please speak loudly.

hatchet man.monolingual: a man who does the cruel or difficult things for someone else; someone who does someone else’s dirty work. _He served as the president’s hatchet man and ended up doing all the dirty work.
examples: He served as the president’s hatchet man and ended up doing all the dirty work.

have a ball.monolingual: to have an exciting time. _ I plan to have a ball while I’m on vacation. _ Come on, everybody! Let’s have a ball!
examples: I plan to have a ball while I’m on vacation.

have a heart.monolingual: Fig. to be compassionate; to be generous and forgiving; to have an especially compassionate heart. _ Oh, have a heart! Give me some help! _If Anne had a heart, she’d volunteer to help us on the charity drive.
examples: If Anne had a heart, she’d volunteer to help us on the charity drive.

have a seat.monolingual: to sit down. (Often a polite invitation to sit down.) _ Have a seat. I’ll be with you in a minute.
examples: Have a seat. I’ll be with you in a minute.

have an accident.monolingual: 1. to experience something that was not foreseen or intended. _ Traffic is very bad. I almost had an accident. _ Drive carefully. Try to avoid having an accident.
examples: Traffic is very bad.

have been around.monolingual: to be experienced in life. (Use with caution since this can also be taken to mean to be promiscuous.) _Ask Sally about how the government works. She’s been around the state capital for years. _ They all know a lot about life. They’ve been around.
examples: Ask Sally about how the government works.

have it both ways.monolingual: to have both of two incompatible things. _John wants the security of marriage and the freedom of being single. He wants to have it both ways. _ John thinks he can have it both ways—the wisdom of old age and the vigor of youth.
examples: John wants the security of marriage and the freedom of being single.

have none of something.monolingual: to tolerate or endure no amount of something. _ I’ll have none of your talk about quitting school. _ We’ll have none of your gossip. _ I wish to have none of the sweet potatoes, please.
examples: I’ll have none of your talk about quitting school.

have words.monolingual: Euph. to argue. _ From the sound of things, Bill and his father had words last night. _ We had words on the subject of money.
examples: From the sound of things, Bill and his father had words last night.

heads or tails.monolingual: the face of a coin or the other side of a coin. (Often used in an act of coin tossing, where one circumstance is valid if the front of a coin appears and another circumstance is valid if the other side appears.) _ Jim looked at Jane as he f lipped th
examples: Jim looked at Jane as he f lipped the coin into the air.

heads will roll.monolingual: Fig. people will get into severe trouble. _ When the company’s year-end results are known, heads will roll. _ Heads will roll when the principal sees the damaged classroom.
examples: When the company’s year-end results are known, heads will roll.

heal over.monolingual: [for the surface of a wound] to heal. _ The wound healed over very quickly, and there was very little scarring. _ I hope it will heal over without having to be stitched.
examples: The wound healed over very quickly, and there was very little scarring.

heal up.monolingual: [for an injury] to heal. _ The cut healed up in no time at all.
examples: The cut healed up in no time at all.

heat up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get warmer or hot. _ It really heats up in the afternoon around here. _ How soon will dinner be heated up?
examples: It really heats up in the afternoon around here.

heave to.monolingual: to stop a sailing ship by facing it directly into the wind. _ The captain gave the order to heave to. _ The ship hove to and everyone had a swim.
examples: The captain gave the order to heave to.

heavy going.monolingual: difficult to do, understand, or make progress with. _ Jim finds math heavy going. _ Talking to Mary is heavy going. She has nothing interesting to say.
examples: Jim finds math heavy going.

hell around.monolingual: Sl. to go around making trouble or noise. _ Who are those kids who are out there helling around every night? _ They hell around because it’s fun.
examples: They hell around because it’s fun.

hell on earth.monolingual: Fig. a very unpleasant situation, as if one were in hell. _That man made my life hell on earth! _The whole time I was there was just hell on earth.
examples: The whole time I was there was just hell on earth.

high and dry.monolingual: Fig. safe; unbothered by difficulties; unscathed. (As if someone or something were safe from a flood. See also leave someone high and dry.) _ While the riot was going on down on the streets, I was high and dry in my apartment. _Liz came out of the ar
examples: While the riot was going on down on the streets, I was high and dry in my apartment.

highway robbery.monolingual: outrageous overpricing; a bill that is much higher than normally acceptable but must be paid. (As if one had been accosted and robbed on the open road or in broad daylight.) _ Four thousand dollars! That’s highway robbery for one piece of furniture!

hit a snag.monolingual: Fig. to run into an unexpected problem. _ We’ve hit a snag with the building project. _I stopped working on the roof when I hit a snag.
examples: We’ve hit a snag with the building project.

hit pay dirt.monolingual: 1. Fig. to discover something of value. (Alludes to discovering valuable ore.) _Sally tried a number of different jobs until she hit pay dirt. _ I tried to borrow money from a lot of different people. They all said no. Then when I went to the bank, I
examples: Sally tried a number of different jobs until she hit pay dirt.

hit the fan.monolingual: Inf. Fig. to become publicly known; to become a scandal. (From the phrase when the shit hit the fan.) _ I wasn’t even in the country when it hit the fan. _It hit the fan, and within ten minutes the press had spread it all over the world.
examples: I wasn’t even in the country when it hit the fan.

hit the ground running.monolingual: Fig. to start the day very energetically. _ A decade ago I had a lot more energy. I would wake up, hit the ground running, and never stop until I went to bed again.
examples: A decade ago I had a lot more energy.

hit the jackpot.monolingual: 1. Lit. to win a large amount of money gambling or in a lottery. _ I hit the jackpot in the big contest. _ Sally hit the jackpot in the lottery.
examples: I hit the jackpot in the big contest.

hit the road.monolingual: Fig. to depart; to begin one’s journey, especially on a road trip; to leave for home. _ It’s time to hit the road. I’ll see you. _ We have to hit the road very early in the morning.
examples: It’s time to hit the road.

hit the skids.monolingual: Fig. to decline; to decrease in value or status. _ Jed hit the skids when he started drinking. _ The firm hit the skids when the dollar collapsed.
examples: Jed hit the skids when he started drinking.

hit the spot.monolingual: Inf. to be exactly right; to be refreshing. _ This cool drink really hits the spot. _ That was a delicious meal, dear. It hit the spot.
examples: This cool drink really hits the spot.

hold on.monolingual: to be patient. _ Just hold on. Everything will work out in good time. _ If you will just hold on, everything will probably be all right.
examples: Just hold on. Everything will work out in good time.

hold oneself together.monolingual: Fig. to maintain one’s calmness or sanity. _I don’t know if I can hold myself together through another horrible day like this one. _ I don’t know how she held herself together through all her troubles.
examples: I don’t know if I can hold myself together through another horrible day like this one.

hold together.monolingual: [for something] to keep from falling apart. _ Don’t run the engine too fast because it won’t hold together. _ Do you think that this book will hold together much longer?
examples: Don’t run the engine too fast because it won’t hold together.

hole in one.monolingual: 1. Lit. an instance of hitting a golf ball from the tee to the hole in only one try. (From the game of golf.) _ John made a hole in one yesterday. _ I’ve never gotten a hole in one.
examples: John made a hole in one yesterday.

hopping mad.monolingual: Fig. very angry. _Joe got hopping mad when the salesclerk was rude to him. _ The student’s practical jokes made the teacher hopping mad.
examples: Joe got hopping mad when the salesclerk was rude to him.

hot and bothered.monolingual: 1. Fig. excited; anxious. _ Now don’t get hot and bothered. Take it easy. _ John is hot and bothered about the tax increase.
examples: Now don’t get hot and bothered.

hot and heavy.monolingual: Fig. referring to serious passion or emotions. _ Things were getting a little hot and heavy so Ellen asked to be taken home. _The movie had one hot and heavy scene after another. Pretty soon it got to be a joke.
examples: Things were getting a little hot and heavy so Ellen asked to be taken home.

hot under the collar.monolingual: Fig. very angry. _ The boss was really hot under the collar when you told him you lost the contract. _ I get hot under the collar every time I think about it.
examples: The boss was really hot under the collar when you told him you lost the contract.

hunch over.monolingual: [for someone] to bend over. _ The wounded man hunched over and staggered to the window. _ He was hunched over with pain.
examples: The wounded man hunched over and staggered to the window.

hurry up and wait.monolingual: Fig. to do some things in a series fast and then have to wait a long time to do the next things in the series. (Originally military.) _ That’s all we ever do. Rush to stand in line somewhere. We just hurry up and wait all day long. _Hurry up and wait
examples: That’s all we ever do.

hush up.monolingual: to be quiet; to get quiet; to stop talking. _ You talk too much. Hush up! _ I want you to hush up and sit down!
examples: You talk too much.

hustle and bustle.monolingual: Fig. confusion and business. _I can’t stand the hustle and bustle of big cities. _ There is a lot of hustle and bustle in this office at the end of the fiscal year.
examples: I can’t stand the hustle and bustle of big cities.

hustle up.monolingual: to hurry up. _ Hustle up, you guys. We have to get moving. _ Hustle up. We are almost late.
examples: Hustle up, you guys.

ice over.monolingual: [for water] to freeze and develop a covering of ice. _ I can’t wait for the river to ice over so we can do some ice fishing.
examples: I can’t wait for the river to ice over so we can do some ice fishing.

ice up.monolingual: to become icy. _ Are the roads icing up?

in a big way.monolingual: very much; intensely. _ I’m really interested in her in a big way. _ He plays to win—in a big way.
examples: I’m really interested in her in a big way.

in a flash.monolingual: Fig. quickly; immediately. _ I’ll be there in a f lash. _ It happened in a f lash. Suddenly my wallet was gone.
examples: I’ll be there in a f lash.

in a heartbeat.monolingual: Fig. almost immediately. _ If I had the money, I would go back to college in a heartbeat. _ Just tell me that you need me and I’ll come there in a heartbeat.
examples: If I had the money, I would go back to college in a heartbeat.

in a nutshell.monolingual: Fig. [of news or information] in a (figurative) capsule; in summary. _ This cable channel provides the latest news in a nutshell. _In a nutshell, what happened at work today?
examples: This cable channel provides the latest news in a nutshell.

in a pinch.monolingual: as a substitute. _A piece of clothing can be used as a bandage in a pinch. _ In a pinch, you can use folded paper to prop up the table leg so the table won’t rock.
examples: A piece of clothing can be used as a bandage in a pinch.

in and of itself.monolingual: considering it alone. _ The idea in and of itself is not bad, but the side issues introduce many difficulties. _ Her action, in and of itself, caused us no problem.
examples: The idea in and of itself is not bad, but the side issues introduce many difficulties.

in business.monolingual: operating; equipped or ready to operate. _ We’re in business now, and things are running smoothly. _ Now it works. Now we’re in business.
examples: We’re in business now, and things are running smoothly.

in character.monolingual: Fig. typical of someone’s behavior. _ For Tom to shout that way wasn’t at all in character. He’s usually quite pleasant. _ It was quite in character for Sally to walk away angry.
examples: For Tom to shout that way wasn’t at all in character.

in cold blood.monolingual: Fig. without feeling; with cruel intent. (Frequently said of a crime, especially murder.) _ The killer walked up and shot the woman in cold blood. _How insulting! For a person to say something like that in cold blood is just horrible.
examples: The killer walked up and shot the woman in cold blood.

in deep.monolingual: 1. Fig. deeply involved (with someone or something). _Mary and Sam are in deep. _Wilbur got in deep with the mob.
examples: Mary and Sam are in deep.

in detail.monolingual: with lots of details; giving all the details. (Often used with an adjective showing the level of detail, such as great, enormous, etc., as in the second example.) _ I explained the policy to the customer in detail. _We planned the entire project in g
examples: I explained the policy to the customer in detail.

in droves.monolingual: Fig. in large numbers. _ The settlers arrived on the prairie in droves.
examples: The settlers arrived on the prairie in droves.

in high dudgeon.monolingual: Fig. feeling or exhibiting great resentment; taking great offense at something. (Often with leave.) _ After the rude remarks, the person who was insulted left in high dudgeon. _ Dennis strode from the room in high dudgeon, and we knew he would get hi
examples: After the rude remarks, the person who was insulted left in high dudgeon.

in kind.monolingual: 1. in goods rather than in money. _ The country doctor was usually paid in kind. He accepted two pigs as payment for an operation. _Do you have to pay tax on payments made in kind?
examples: The country doctor was usually paid in kind.

in no uncertain terms.monolingual: Cliché in very specific and direct language. _ I was so mad. I told her in no uncertain terms to leave and never come back. _ I told him in no uncertain terms to stop calling me.
examples: I was so mad. I told her in no uncertain terms to leave and never come back.

in other words.monolingual: a phrase introducing a restatement of what has just been said. _ Henry: Sure I want to do it, but how much do I get paid? Andrew: In other words, you’re just doing it for the money. _Bill: Well, I suppose I really should prepare my entourage for depa
examples: Henry: Sure I want to do it, but how much do I get paid? Andrew: In other words, you’re just doing it for the money.

in rare form.monolingual: 1. Fig. well prepared for a good performance; at one’s best. _ The goalie is in rare form today; that’s his third great save already. _ We are not exactly in rare form on Monday mornings.
examples: The goalie is in rare form today; that’s his third great save already.

in reality.monolingual: viewing things realistically; really. _ Jane dreamed it was snowing, but in reality, it was very warm. _ John looks happy, but in reality, he is miserable.
examples: Jane dreamed it was snowing, but in reality, it was very warm.

in recent memory.monolingual: Fig. the period of time in which things are still remembered and discussed. _ Never in recent memory has there been this much snow! _ I haven’t been this happy in recent memory!

in spades.monolingual: in the best or most extreme way possible; extravagantly. _ He f lunked the test in spades. _ He succeeded at life in spades—honors degree, great career, rich wife, lovely children, and early retirement.
examples: He f lunked the test in spades.

in stitches.monolingual: Fig. laughing very hard. _ Charlie had us in stitches with all his jokes. _ The movie sure was funny. I was in stitches!
examples: Charlie had us in stitches with all his jokes.

in the air.monolingual: Fig. everywhere; all about. _There is such a feeling of joy in the air. _ We felt a sense of tension in the air.
examples: There is such a feeling of joy in the air.

in the black.monolingual: Fig. not in debt; in a financially profitable condition. (As opposed to in the red.) _ I wish my accounts were in the black. _Sally moved the company into the black.
examples: I wish my accounts were in the black.

in the hopper.monolingual: Fig. in process; in line to be processed. (A hopper is a chute for incoming work or material to be processed.) _ It’s in the hopper. I’ll get to it. _ Your job is in the hopper, and your turn is next.
examples: It’s in the hopper.

in the know.monolingual: knowledgeable. _ Let’s ask Bob. He’s in the know. _ I have no knowledge of how to work this machine. I think I can get myself in the know very quickly though.
examples: Let’s ask Bob. He’s in the know.

in the line of duty.monolingual: Fig. as part of one’s expected duties. _When soldiers fight people in a war, it’s in the line of duty. _ Police officers have to do things they may not like in the line of duty.
examples: When soldiers fight people in a war, it’s in the line of duty.

in the making.monolingual: in development; in the process of developing. _ This is a real problem in the making. Let’s try to keep it from getting any worse.
examples: This is a real problem in the making.

in the money.monolingual: 1. Fig. wealthy. _John is really in the money. He’s worth millions. _If I am ever in the money, I’ll be generous.
examples: John is really in the money.

in the offing.monolingual: happening at some time in the future. _ There is a big investigation in the offing, but I don’t know when. _It’s hard to tell what’s in the offing if you don’t keep track of things.
examples: There is a big investigation in the offing, but I don’t know when.

in the pipeline.monolingual: Fig. backed up somewhere in a process; in process; in a queue. _ There’s a lot of goods still in the pipeline. That means no more new orders will be shipped for a while. _Your papers are in the pipeline somewhere. You’ll just have to wait.
examples: There’s a lot of goods still in the pipeline.

in the running.monolingual: Fig. in competition; competing and having a chance to win. _ Is Tom still in the running? Does he still have a chance to be elected? _I don’t know about Tom, but Gladys is definitely still in the running.
examples: I don’t know about Tom, but Gladys is definitely still in the running.

in the same breath.monolingual: Fig. [stated or said] almost at the same time. _ He told me I was lazy, but then in the same breath he said I was doing a good job. _ The teacher said that the students were working hard and, in the same breath, that they were not working hard enough
examples: He told me I was lazy, but then in the same breath he said I was doing a good job.

in the wind.monolingual: Fig. about to happen. _There are some major changes in the wind. Expect these changes to happen soon. _ There is something in the wind. We’ll find out what it is soon.
examples: There are some major changes in the wind.

in the works.monolingual: Fig. being prepared; being planned; being done. _ There are some new laws in the works that will affect all of us. _ I have some ideas in the works that you might be interested in.
examples: There are some new laws in the works that will affect all of us.

in the worst way.monolingual: Fig. very much. _ I want a new car in the worst way. _ Bob wants to retire in the worst way.
examples: I want a new car in the worst way.

in this day and age.monolingual: Fig. now; in these modern times. _ Bill: Ted f lunked out of school. Mother: Imagine that! Especially in this day and age. _ Bill: Taxes keep going up and up. Bob: What do you expect in this day and age?
examples: Bill: Ted f lunked out of school.

in vain.monolingual: for no purpose; [done] as a failure. _ They rushed her to the hospital, but they did it in vain. _ We tried in vain to get her there on time.
examples: They rushed her to the hospital, but they did it in vain.

inch back.monolingual: to move back very slowly. _ The trainer inched back from the angry tiger. _ The tiger inched back and sprang.
examples: The trainer inched back from the angry tiger.

inch by inch.monolingual: Fig. one inch at a time; little by little. _Traffic moved along inch by inch. _ Inch by inch, the snail moved across the stone.
examples: Traffic moved along inch by inch.

inch forward.monolingual: to move forward very slowly. _ Inch forward very slowly, and try not to make any noise. _ The cat inched forward, taking care not to alert the bird to its presence.
examples: Inch forward very slowly, and try not to make any noise.

jack of all trades.monolingual: someone who can do several different jobs instead of specializing in one. _ John can do plumbing, carpentry, and roofing—a real jack of all trades. He isn’t very good at any of them. _ Take your car to a certified engine mechanic, not a jack of all t
examples: John can do plumbing, carpentry, and roofing—a real jack of all trades.

join hands.monolingual: [for people] to hold hands so that each person is holding the hands of two other people; [for two people] to hold each other’s hands. _ Let us join hands and pray together. _The dancers joined hands and formed a circle that moved to the left.
examples: Let us join hands and pray together.

join up.monolingual: to join some organization. _ The club has opened its membership rolls again. Are you going to join up? _ I can’t afford to join up.
examples: The club has opened its membership rolls again.

joined at the hip.monolingual: Sl. closely connected; always together. _Those two are joined at the hip. They are always together. _ Sam and Martha are joined at the hip.
examples: Those two are joined at the hip.

juice up.monolingual: Sl. to drink one or more alcoholic drinks. _Hey, man, let’s go out and juice up tonight. _ Stop juicing up every night.
examples: Hey, man, let’s go out and juice up tonight.

jump the gun.monolingual: Fig. to start before the starting signal. (Originally used in sports contests that are started by firing a gun.) _We all had to start the race again because Jane jumped the gun. _When we took the test, Tom jumped the gun and started early.
examples: We all had to start the race again because Jane jumped the gun.

just a minute.monolingual: only a short time; [wait] a short period of time. _ I’m almost done. I’ll be there in just a minute! _ Could I have just a minute of your time?
examples: I’m almost done.

just like that.monolingual: in just the way it happened or was stated; without any [further] discussion or comment. _Sue: You can’t walk out on me just like that. John: I can too. Just watch! _ Mary: And then she slapped him in the face, just like that! Sally: She can be so rud
examples: Sue: You can’t walk out on me just like that.

keel over.monolingual: [for a person] to fall over or fall down in a faint or in death. _ It was so hot in the room that two people just keeled over.
examples: It was so hot in the room that two people just keeled over.

keep good time.monolingual: [for a watch or clock] to be accurate. _ I have to return my watch to the store because it doesn’t keep good time. _ Mine keeps good time.
examples: I have to return my watch to the store because it doesn’t keep good time.

keep house.monolingual: to manage a household. _ I hate to keep house. I’d rather live in a tent than keep house. _My grandmother kept house for nearly sixty years.
examples: I hate to keep house.

keep oneself to oneself.monolingual: to remain aloof. _ He does tend to keep himself to himself. _ Keep yourself to yourself, and you’ll be all right there.
examples: He does tend to keep himself to himself.

keep someone company.monolingual: to sit or stay with someone, especially someone who is lonely. _ I kept my uncle company for a few hours. _He was very grateful for someone to keep him company. He gets very lonely.
examples: I kept my uncle company for a few hours.

keep someone posted.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone informed (of what is happening); to keep someone up to date. _ If the price of corn goes up, I need to know. Please keep me posted. _ Keep her posted about the patient’s status.
examples: If the price of corn goes up, I need to know.

keep the ball rolling.monolingual: 1. Lit. to keep a rolling ball moving. _ You have to throw hard enough to keep the ball rolling all the way to the bowling pins.
examples: You have to throw hard enough to keep the ball rolling all the way to the bowling pins.

keep the home fires burning.monolingual: Fig. to keep things going at one’s home or other central location. (From a World War I song.) _My uncle kept the home fires burning when my sister and I went to school. _ The manager stays at the office and keeps the home fires burning while I’m out
examples: My uncle kept the home fires burning when my sister and I went to school.

keep to oneself.monolingual: to be solitary; to stay away from other people. _ Ann tends to keep to herself. She doesn’t have many friends. _ I try to keep to myself each morning so I can get some work done.
examples: Ann tends to keep to herself.

keep together.monolingual: to remain as a group. _ We will keep together to the very end. _ Our group decided to keep together.
examples: We will keep together to the very end.

keep up appearances.monolingual: to make things look all right whether they are or not. _ We must keep up appearances even if it means little sacrifices here and there. _ Things may be unpleasant, but we will keep up appearances.
examples: We must keep up appearances even if it means little sacrifices here and there.

keep up with the times.monolingual: Fig. to work to appear contemporary and fashionable. _ I am too old-fashioned. I have to keep up with the times better. _ I don’t care about keeping up with the times.
examples: I am too old-fashioned.

kick back.monolingual: 1. Inf. to relax; to lean back and relax. _ I really like to kick back and relax. _ It’s time to kick back and enjoy life.
examples: I really like to kick back and relax.

kick up.monolingual: to cause trouble or discomfort. _ The ignition in my car is kicking up again. I will have to have it looked into. _ Aunt Jane’s arthritis is kicking up. She needs to see the doctor again.
examples: The ignition in my car is kicking up again.

kill the fatted calf.monolingual: Fig. to prepare an elaborate banquet (in someone’s honor). (From the biblical story recounting the return of the prodigal son.) _When Bob got back from college, his parents killed the fatted calf and threw a great party. _ Sorry this meal isn’t much,
examples: When Bob got back from college, his parents killed the fatted calf and threw a great party.

killer instinct.monolingual: Cliché an inborn desire or ability to be ruthless. _ Fred has a real killer instinct. He’s a difficult boss to work for.
examples: Fred has a real killer instinct.

kiss and make up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for two people who have been arguing] to kiss each other and apologize. _ John apologized to his wife for disagreeing with her, and they finally kissed and made up.
examples: John apologized to his wife for disagreeing with her, and they finally kissed and made up.

kiss and tell.monolingual: Fig. to participate in something secret and private, and then tell other people about it. (In actual use, it usually refers to a person of the opposite sex even when it does not refer to actual kissing.) _The project was supposed to be a secret betwe
examples: The project was supposed to be a secret between Jane and me, but she spread it all around.

kiss off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to die. _ The cat is going to have to kiss off one of these days soon. _ The cat kissed off after eighteen years of joy and devotion.
examples: The cat is going to have to kiss off one of these days soon.

kneel down.monolingual: to get down on one’s knees. _ Please kneel down and fold your hands. _You should at least kneel down and be quiet.
examples: Please kneel down and fold your hands.

knit together.monolingual: [for broken bones] to join or grow together. _ The bones are knitting together exactly as expected. _ If the bones don’t knit together properly, we will have to do something a little more drastic.
examples: The bones are knitting together exactly as expected.

knock on wood.monolingual: to rap on something made of wood. (Said as a wish for good luck. Usually a phrase attached to another statement. Sometime said while knocking or rapping on real wood.) _ I think I am well at last—knock on wood. _ I knock on wood when I wish something
examples: I think I am well at last—knock on wood.

last out.monolingual: to hold out; to endure. _ How long can you last out? _ I don’t think we can last out much longer without food and water.
examples: I don’t think we can last out much longer without food and water.

lay an egg.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a hen, etc.] to deposit an egg. _ Old Red stopped laying eggs, so we stewed her for Sunday dinner.
examples: Old Red stopped laying eggs, so we stewed her for Sunday dinner.

lay down.monolingual: to give up. _Do you expect me to just lay down? _You really think I should just lay down and let them walk all over me?

lay to.monolingual: to begin doing something, such as fighting or eating. _ All right, you guys. Lay to. The stuff will get cold if you don’t eat it. _ Lay to! Let’s get on with it.
examples: All right, you guys.

lead off.monolingual: to be the first one to go or leave. _ You lead off. I’ll follow. _ Mary led off and the others followed closely behind.
examples: You lead off. I’ll follow.

lead on.monolingual: to continue to lead onward. _ The guide led on and we followed. _Lead on, my friend. We are right behind you!
examples: The guide led on and we followed.

leaf out.monolingual: [for a plant] to open its leaf buds. _ Most of the bushes leaf out in mid-April. _ The trees leafed out early this year.
examples: Most of the bushes leaf out in mid-April.

leak out.monolingual: [for information] to become known unofficially. _ I hope that news of the new building does not leak out before the contract is signed. _ When the story leaked out, my telephone would not stop ringing.
examples: I hope that news of the new building does not leak out before the contract is signed.

leap up.monolingual: to jump upwards. _ The dog leapt up and licked my cheek. _ I leapt up so I could see over the wall for just a second.
examples: The dog leapt up and licked my cheek.

leave it at that.monolingual: to leave a situation as it is. _ This is the best we can do. We’ll have to leave it at that. _ I can do no more. I will have to leave it at that.
examples: This is the best we can do.

leave no stone unturned.monolingual: Fig. to search in all possible places. (As if one might search under every rock.) _Don’t worry. We’ll find your stolen car. We’ll leave no stone unturned. _ In searching for a nice place to live, we left no stone unturned.
examples: Don’t worry. We’ll find your stolen car.

leave someone high and dry.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for water] to recede and leave someone untouched. _ The waters receded and left us high and dry.
examples: The waters receded and left us high and dry.

leave someone in the lurch.monolingual: Fig. to leave someone waiting for or anticipating your actions. _ Where were you, John? You really left me in the lurch. _I didn’t mean to leave you in the lurch. I thought we had canceled our meeting.
examples: Where were you, John? You really left me in the lurch.

lengthen out.monolingual: to stretch or grow longer. _The days began to lengthen out and we knew summer was upon us. _As we approached the end of the trail, the distance seemed to lengthen out.
examples: The days began to lengthen out and we knew summer was upon us.

let down.monolingual: to relax one’s efforts or vigilance. _ Now is no time to let down. Keep on your guard. _ After the contest was over, Jane let down a bit so she could relax.
examples: Now is no time to let down.

let it all hang out.monolingual: Inf. to be yourself, assuming that you generally are not; to become totally relaxed and unpretentious. _ Come on. Relax! Let it all hang out. _ I tried to let it all hang out, but I still felt out of place.
examples: Come on. Relax! Let it all hang out.

let oneself go.monolingual: 1. Fig. to become less constrained; to get excited and have a good time. _ I love to dance and just let myself go. _ Let yourself go, John. Learn to enjoy life.
examples: I love to dance and just let myself go.

let out.monolingual: [for an event that includes many people] to end. (The people are then permitted to come out.) _ What time does the movie let out? I have to meet someone in the lobby. _ The meeting let out at about seven o’clock. _ School lets out in June.
examples: What time does the movie let out? I have to meet someone in the lobby.

let someone go.monolingual: Euph. to fire someone. _ They let Jane go from her job. _ I’m afraid we’re going to have to let you go.
examples: They let Jane go from her job.

let up.monolingual: 1. to diminish. _I hope this rain lets up a little soon. _When the snow lets up so I can see, I will drive to the store.
examples: I hope this rain lets up a little soon.

level off.monolingual: [for variation or fluctuation in the motion of something] to diminish; [for a rate] to stop increasing or decreasing. _ The plane leveled off at 10,000 feet. _ After a while the workload will level off. _ Things will level off after we get through th
examples: The plane leveled off at 10,000 feet.

level out.monolingual: [for something that was going up and down] to assume a more level course or path. _The road leveled out after a while and driving was easier. _As we got down into the valley, the land leveled out and traveling was easier.
examples: The road leveled out after a while and driving was easier.

lie back.monolingual: to relax; to lean back in a chair and relax. _ Just lie back and try to get comfortable. _ I really need to get home and lie back and relax.
examples: Just lie back and try to get comfortable.

lie down.monolingual: to recline. _ Why don’t you lie down for a while? _ I need to lie down and have a little snooze.
examples: I need to lie down and have a little snooze.

lie in.monolingual: [for a woman] to lie in bed awaiting the birth of her child. _ The child is due soon, and the mother is lying in at the present time. _ She did not lie in at all. She worked right up to the onset of labor pains.
examples: The child is due soon, and the mother is lying in at the present time.

lift off.monolingual: [for a plane or rocket] to move upward, leaving the ground. _ The rocket lifted off exactly on time.
examples: The rocket lifted off exactly on time.

lift up.monolingual: to raise up. _ Suddenly, the top of the box lifted up and a hand reached out. _Bill’s hand lifted up and fell back again.
examples: Suddenly, the top of the box lifted up and a hand reached out.

light up.monolingual: 1. to become brighter. _ Suddenly, the sky lit up like day. _ The room lit up as the fire suddenly came back to life.
examples: Suddenly, the sky lit up like day.

lighten up.monolingual: to become lighter or brighter. _We applied a new coat of white paint to the walls, and the room lightened up considerably. _ The sky is beginning to lighten up a little.
examples: We applied a new coat of white paint to the walls, and the room lightened up considerably.

like father, like son.monolingual: Prov. Fathers and sons resemble each other, and sons tend to do what their fathers did before them. _ Jill: George’s father smoked all the time, and now George is smoking excessively, too. Jane: Like father, like son, eh? _ I think my son will grow u
examples: Jill: George’s father smoked all the time, and now George is smoking excessively, too.

line up.monolingual: to form a line; to get into a line. _All right, everyone, line up!

linger on.monolingual: to remain for a long time; to exist longer than would have been thought. _ This cold of mine just keeps lingering on. _Some of the guests lingered on for a long time after the party was over.
examples: This cold of mine just keeps lingering on.

liquor up.monolingual: to drink an alcoholic beverage, especially to excess. _Sam sat around all evening liquoring up. _They seem to liquor up almost every night of the week.
examples: Sam sat around all evening liquoring up.

listen up.monolingual: to listen carefully. (Usually a command.) _Now, listen up! This is important. _ Listen up, you guys!
examples: Now, listen up! This is important.

live and let live.monolingual: Cliché not to interfere with other people’s business or preferences. _ I don’t care what they do! Live and let live, I always say. _ Your parents are strict. Mine just live and let live.
examples: I don’t care what they do! Live and let live, I always say.

live in.monolingual: to live at the residence at which one works. _ In order to be here early enough to prepare breakfast, the cook has to live in. _ Mr. Simpson has a valet, but he doesn’t live in.
examples: In order to be here early enough to prepare breakfast, the cook has to live in.

live in sin.monolingual: to live with and have sex with someone to whom one is not married. (Sometimes serious and sometimes jocular.) _Would you like to get married, or would you prefer that we live in sin for a few more years? _ Let’s live in sin. There’s no risk of divorc
examples: Let’s live in sin.

live in the past.monolingual: Fig. to live while dwelling on past memories without participating in the present or planning for the future. _ You are just living in the past. Join us in the twenty-first century. _Living in the past has its advantages.
examples: You are just living in the past.

live it up.monolingual: to have an exciting time; to do what one pleases—regardless of cost—to please oneself. _ At the party, John was really living it up. _ Come on! Have fun! Live it up!
examples: At the party, John was really living it up.

live large.monolingual: to live in luxury; to spend time in grand style. _ George loved to live large, dining at fine French restaurants.
examples: George loved to live large, dining at fine French restaurants.

live together.monolingual: 1. [for two people] to dwell in the same place. _ I live together with my sister in the house my parents left us. _ Henry and Jill live together in their parents’ house.
examples: I live together with my sister in the house my parents left us.

loaded for bear.monolingual: 1. Inf. angry. _He left here in a rage. He was really loaded for bear. _ When I got home from work, I was really loaded for bear. What a horrible day!
examples: He left here in a rage.

loaf around.monolingual: to waste time; to idle the time away doing almost nothing. _ Every time I see you, you are just loafing around. _ I enjoy loafing around on the weekend.
examples: Every time I see you, you are just loafing around.

log on.monolingual: to begin to use a computer system, as by entering a password, etc. (This action may be recorded, or logged, automatically in the computer’s memory.) _ What time did you log on to the system this morning? _ I always log on before I get my first cup of
examples: I always log on before I get my first cup of coffee.

loll around.monolingual: to roll, flop, or hang around. _ The dog’s tongue lolled around as it rolled on its back, trying to keep cool. _ Stop lolling around and get to work.
examples: The dog’s tongue lolled around as it rolled on its back, trying to keep cool.

long in the tooth.monolingual: Fig. old. _ That actor is getting a little long in the tooth to play the romantic lead. _I may be long in the tooth, but I’m not stupid.
examples: That actor is getting a little long in the tooth to play the romantic lead.

long story short.monolingual: Sl. to make a long story short. _Okay, long story short: everything that goes up comes down, okay? _ Then the guy comes over, and—long story short—“You got a match?”

look here.monolingual: a phrase emphasizing the point that follows. (Can show some impatience.) _Henry: Look here, I want to try to help you, but you’re not making it easy for me. Rachel: I’m just so upset. _ Andy: Look here, I just asked you a simple question! Bob: As I t
examples: Henry: Look here, I want to try to help you, but you’re not making it easy for me.

look on.monolingual: to be a spectator and watch what is happening without participating. _ The beating took place while a policeman looked on. _While the kittens played, the mother cat looked on contentedly.
examples: The beating took place while a policeman looked on.

look on the bright side.monolingual: Fig. consider the positive aspects of a negative situation. _ Look on the bright side. Things could have been much worse than they are.
examples: Look on the bright side.

look the other way.monolingual: 1. Lit. to look in the opposite direction. _ To make sure it’s safe to cross the street, look the other way before you step off the curb.
examples: To make sure it’s safe to cross the street, look the other way before you step off the curb.

look up.monolingual: to show promise of improving. _My prospects for a job are looking up. _ Conditions are looking up.
examples: My prospects for a job are looking up.

loosen up.monolingual: to become loose or relaxed. _Loosen up. Relax. _We tried to get Mary to loosen up, but she did not respond.
examples: Loosen up. Relax.

lose face.monolingual: Fig. to lose status; to become less respectable. _ John is more afraid of losing face than losing money. _ Things will go better if you can explain to him where he was wrong without making him lose face.
examples: John is more afraid of losing face than losing money.

lose it.monolingual: 1. Sl. to empty one’s stomach; to vomit. _Oh, God! I think I’m going to lose it! _ Go lose it in the bushes.
examples: Go lose it in the bushes.

lose out.monolingual: to lose in competition; to lose one’s expected reward. _Our team lost out because our quarterback broke his leg. _I ran my best race, but I still lost out.
examples: Our team lost out because our quarterback broke his leg.

love at first sight.monolingual: Fig. love established when two people first see one another. _Bill was standing at the door when Ann opened it. It was love at first sight. _It was love at first sight when they met, but it didn’t last long.
examples: Bill was standing at the door when Ann opened it.

low-hanging fruit.monolingual: Fig. the easiest person(s) to sell something to, to convince of something, or to fool. (From the much older easy pickings.) _ People who always want to be the first to buy something, they’re low-hanging fruit for this product. _ Don’t be satisfied wi
examples: People who always want to be the first to buy something, they’re low-hanging fruit for this product.

luck out.monolingual: to be fortunate; to strike it lucky. _I really lucked out when I ordered the duck. It’s excellent. _ I didn’t luck out at all. I rarely make the right choice.
examples: I really lucked out when I ordered the duck.

lunch out.monolingual: to eat lunch away from one’s home or away from one’s place of work. _I think I’ll lunch out today. I’m tired of carrying lunches. _ I want to lunch out today.
examples: I think I’ll lunch out today.

made for each other.monolingual: [of two people] very well suited romantically. _ Bill and Jane were made for each other. _ Mr. and Mrs. Smith were not exactly made for each other. They really don’t get along.
examples: Bill and Jane were made for each other.

make a killing.monolingual: Fig. to have a great success, especially in making money. _John has got a job selling insurance. He’s not exactly making a killing. _ Bill made a killing at the racetrack yesterday.
examples: John has got a job selling insurance.

make a night of it.monolingual: Fig. to spend the entire evening or night doing something. (Especially when one had intended to devote only a little time to the outing.) _ We went out to have a bite to eat and were having such a good time that we decided to make a night of it. _I d
examples: We went out to have a bite to eat and were having such a good time that we decided to make a night of it.

make a pig of oneself.monolingual: Fig. to eat too much, too fast, or noisily; to eat more than one’s share. _ Don’t make a pig of yourself! _ Sam is making a pig of himself and taking more than his share.
examples: Sam is making a pig of himself and taking more than his share.

make a run for it.monolingual: Fig. to run fast to get away or get somewhere. _When the guard wasn’t looking, the prisoner made a run for it. _ In the baseball game, the player on first base made a run for it, but he didn’t make it to second base.
examples: When the guard wasn’t looking, the prisoner made a run for it.

make a virtue of necessity.monolingual: Prov. to do what you have to do cheerfully or willingly. _When Bill’s mother became sick, there was no one but Bill to take care of her, so Bill made a virtue of necessity and resolved to enjoy their time together.
examples: When Bill’s mother became sick, there was no one but Bill to take care of her, so Bill made a virtue of necessity and resolved to enjoy their time together.

make an appearance.monolingual: to appear; to appear in a performance. _We waited for thirty minutes for the professor to make an appearance, then we went home. _ The famous singing star made an appearance in Detroit last August.
examples: We waited for thirty minutes for the professor to make an appearance, then we went home.

make an exhibition of oneself.monolingual: to show off; to try to get a lot of attention for oneself. _She is not just dancing, she is making an exhibition of herself. _ Whenever Rudy drinks, he makes an exhibition of himself.
examples: She is not just dancing, she is making an exhibition of herself.

make oneself at home.monolingual: to make oneself comfortable as if one were in one’s own home. _ Please come in and make yourself at home. _I’m glad you’re here. During your visit, just make yourself at home.
examples: Please come in and make yourself at home.

make out like a bandit.monolingual: Rur. to make a large profit. _ Joe’s making out like a bandit, selling expensive cameras. _ Mary made out like a bandit, playing twenty-one in Las Vegas.
examples: Joe’s making out like a bandit, selling expensive cameras.

make sense.monolingual: to be understandable. _ John doesn’t make sense. _ What John says makes sense to me.
examples: John doesn’t make sense.

make the grade.monolingual: to be satisfactory; to be what is expected. _ I’m sorry, but your work doesn’t exactly make the grade. _ This meal doesn’t just make the grade. It is excellent.
examples: I’m sorry, but your work doesn’t exactly make the grade.

make up.monolingual: to put on makeup. _ I have to go make up before Joe comes to pick me up.
examples: I have to go make up before Joe comes to pick me up.

make waves.monolingual: Sl. to cause difficulty. (Often in the negative.) _Just relax. Don’t make waves. _If you make waves too much around here, you won’t last long.
examples: Just relax. Don’t make waves.
