man about town.monolingual: a fashionable man who leads a sophisticated life. _ He prefers a nightclub to a quiet night at home—a man about town. _ Bob’s too much of a man about town to go to a football game.
examples: He prefers a nightclub to a quiet night at home—a man about town.

march on.monolingual: 1. Lit. to continue marching. _ Please march on. Don’t stop here; there are other parts of the parade coming along behind you. _Let’s march on. We have a long way to go.
examples: Please march on.

match up.monolingual: [for things or people] to match, be equal, or complementary. _ These match up. See how they are the same length? _ Sorry, but these two parts don’t match up.
examples: These match up.

max out.monolingual: to reach one’s maximum in something, such as weight in weight lifting or credit on a credit card. _Andy finally maxed out at 300 pounds. _ Randy just knew when he had maxed out. Something in his body told him to stop.
examples: Andy finally maxed out at 300 pounds.

mean business.monolingual: to be very, very serious. _Stop laughing! I mean business. _I could tell from the look on her face that she meant business.
examples: Stop laughing! I mean business.

mellow out.monolingual: 1. to become less angry. _When you mellow out, maybe we can talk. _ Come on, man, stop yelling and mellow out!
examples: When you mellow out, maybe we can talk.

melt away.monolingual: to melt into a liquid. _ The ice cubes melted away quickly in the intense heat. _ When the wax candles melted away, they ruined the lace tablecloth.
examples: The ice cubes melted away quickly in the intense heat.

melt down.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something frozen] to melt. _ The glacier melted down little by little. _ When the ice on the streets melted down, it was safe to drive again.
examples: The glacier melted down little by little.

mind you.monolingual: a phrase introducing something that should be taken into consideration. _ He’s very well dressed, but mind you, he’s got plenty of money to buy clothes. _ Lisa is unfriendly to me, but mind you, she’s never very nice to anyone.
examples: He’s very well dressed, but mind you, he’s got plenty of money to buy clothes.

mope around.monolingual: to go about in a depressed state. _ Since her dog ran away, Sally mopes around all day. _Don’t mope around. Cheer up!
examples: Since her dog ran away, Sally mopes around all day.

more often than not.monolingual: Fig. usually. _ These f lowers will live through the winter more often than not. _This kind of dog will grow up to be a good watchdog more often than not.
examples: These f lowers will live through the winter more often than not.

more than one bargained for.monolingual: more than one thought one would get. (Usually in reference to trouble or difficulty.) _ When Betsy brought home the sweet little puppy for a companion, she got more than she bargained for. That animal has cost her hundreds of dollars in bills. _I got
examples: When Betsy brought home the sweet little puppy for a companion, she got more than she bargained for.

the more the merrier.monolingual: Cliché the more people there are, the happier the situation will be. _Of course you can have a ride with us! The more the merrier. _The manager hired a new employee even though there’s not enough work for all of us now. Oh, well, the more the merrier
examples: Of course you can have a ride with us! The more the merrier.

mount up.monolingual: 1. to get up on a horse. _ Mount up and let’s get out of here! _ Please mount up so we can leave.
examples: Please mount up so we can leave.

mouth off.monolingual: to speak out of turn; to backtalk. _ If you mouth off, I will ground you for three weeks. _Don’t mouth off at me, buster!
examples: If you mouth off, I will ground you for three weeks.

move along.monolingual: to continue to move; to start moving out of the way. (Often a command.) _ The crowd moved along slowly. _ Please just move along. There is nothing to see here.
examples: The crowd moved along slowly.

move down.monolingual: to move oneself farther down a line of things. _ Someone else needs to sit on this bench. Please move down. _Could you move down a little so we can have some more room?
examples: Someone else needs to sit on this bench.

move on.monolingual: to continue moving; to travel on; to move along and not stop or tarry. _Move on! Don’t stop here! _Please move on!

move over.monolingual: to move a bit [away from the speaker]. _Move over. I need some space. _ Please move over. Part of this space is mine.
examples: Move over. I need some space.

move someone to tears.monolingual: to bring someone to the point of crying. _The story moved me to tears. _As she recounted the accident, she moved herself to tears.
examples: The story moved me to tears.

move up.monolingual: to advance; to go higher. _Isn’t it about time that I move up? I’ve been an office clerk for over a year. _ I had hoped that I would move up faster than this.
examples: Isn’t it about time that I move up? I’ve been an office clerk for over a year.

much ado about nothing.monolingual: Cliché a furor over something unimportant. (The name of a Shakespeare play.) _All this arguing is much ado about nothing.
examples: All this arguing is much ado about nothing.

much of a muchness.monolingual: too much of something that there is generally a lot of. _ All this talk about e-commerce and business-2-business is too much of a muchness.
examples: All this talk about e-commerce and business-2-business is too much of a muchness.

muddle along.monolingual: to progress in confusion; to continue awkwardly. _I will just have to muddle along as best I can until things get straightened out. _ The project muddled along until the new manager got hold of it.
examples: I will just have to muddle along as best I can until things get straightened out.

neck and neck.monolingual: Fig. exactly even, especially in a race or a contest. _ John and Tom finished the race neck and neck. _ Mary and Ann were neck and neck in the spelling contest. Their scores were tied.
examples: John and Tom finished the race neck and neck.

needless to say.monolingual: It is so obvious that it doesn’t need to be said, but.... _Needless to say, I should have spent more time on the report, but I just didn’t have it.
examples: Needless to say, I should have spent more time on the report, but I just didn’t have it.

neither fish nor fowl.monolingual: Cliché not any recognizable thing. _ The car that they drove up in was neither fish nor fowl. It must have been made out of spare parts. _This proposal is neither fish nor fowl. I can’t tell what you’re proposing.
examples: The car that they drove up in was neither fish nor fowl.

neither here nor there.monolingual: Cliché of no consequence or meaning; irrelevant and immaterial. _ Whether you go to the movie or stay at home is neither here nor there. _ Your comment—though interesting—is neither here nor there.
examples: Whether you go to the movie or stay at home is neither here nor there.

nerves of steel.monolingual: Fig. very steady nerves; great patience and courage. _ I was scared to death, but Fred, who has nerves of steel, faced the thugs bravely.
examples: I was scared to death, but Fred, who has nerves of steel, faced the thugs bravely.

nest together.monolingual: to fit together or within one another compactly. _ These mixing bowls nest together. _ I want some of those Russian wooden dolls that nest together.
examples: These mixing bowls nest together.

new kid on the block.monolingual: 1. Lit. a child who has just moved to a certain neighborhood. _ The new kid on the block turned out to be a really good baseball player.
examples: The new kid on the block turned out to be a really good baseball player.

night owl.monolingual: Fig. someone who stays up at night; someone who works at night. _ My roommate is a night owl and usually reads until 5:00 a.m. _ A few night owls stayed at the café all night long.
examples: My roommate is a night owl and usually reads until 5:00 a.

nine times out of ten.monolingual: Fig. usually; almost always. _ Nine times out of ten people will choose coffee rather than tea.
examples: Nine times out of ten people will choose coffee rather than tea.

nip and tuck.monolingual: Fig. almost even; almost tied. _ The horses ran nip and tuck for the first half of the race. Then my horse pulled ahead. _ In the football game last Saturday, both teams were nip and tuck throughout the game.
examples: The horses ran nip and tuck for the first half of the race.

no dice.monolingual: Inf. no; not possible. _When I asked about a loan, he said, “No dice.” _ No. It can’t be done, no dice.
examples: When I asked about a loan, he said, “No dice.

no go.monolingual: Inf. negative; inopportune. (This is hyphenated before a nominal.) _We’re in a no-go situation. _ Is it go or no go?
examples: We’re in a no-go situation.

no great shakes.monolingual: Inf. someone or something that is not very good. (There is no affirmative version of this.) _ Your idea is no great shakes, but we’ll try it anyway. _ Ted is no great shakes when it comes to brains.
examples: Your idea is no great shakes, but we’ll try it anyway.

no soap.monolingual: Inf. no. _I can’t do it. No soap. _No soap, I don’t lend anyone money.
examples: I can’t do it. No soap.

no spring chicken.monolingual: Fig. a person well past youth; an old person. _ That actress is no spring chicken, but she does a pretty good job of playing a twenty-year-old girl. _ Jane: How old do you think Robert is? Jill: Well, he’s certainly no spring chicken.
examples: That actress is no spring chicken, but she does a pretty good job of playing a twenty-year-old girl.

no two ways about it.monolingual: no choice about it; no other interpretation of it. (Note the form there’s rather than there are.) _ You have to go to the doctor whether you like it or not. There’s no two ways about it. _This letter means you’re in trouble with the tax people. There
examples: You have to go to the doctor whether you like it or not.

nod off.monolingual: to fall asleep, usually while sitting up. _Jack nodded off during the minister’s sermon. _Father always nods off after Sunday lunch.
examples: Jack nodded off during the minister’s sermon.

none other than.monolingual: Cliché the very [person]. (Expresses surprise.) _ The new building was opened by none other than the president. _Bob’s wife turned out to be none other than my cousin.
examples: The new building was opened by none other than the president.

none the wiser.monolingual: not knowing any more in spite of events or exposure to facts. _ I was none the wiser about black holes after the lecture. It was a complete waste of time. _ Anne tried to explain the situation tactfully to Bob, but in the end, he was none the wiser.
examples: I was none the wiser about black holes after the lecture.

not grow on trees.monolingual: Fig. not to be abundant; not to be expendable. (Usually said about money.) _ I can’t afford that. Money doesn’t grow on trees, you know. _Don’t waste the glue. That stuff doesn’t grow on trees, you know.
examples: I can’t afford that.

not long for this world.monolingual: Fig. about to die. _ Our dog is nearly twelve years old and not long for this world. _ I’m so tired. I think I’m not long for this world.
examples: Our dog is nearly twelve years old and not long for this world.

nothing to write home about.monolingual: Fig. mediocre; not as good as you expected. _I went to that new restaurant last night. It’s nothing to write home about. _ Jill: I went to see a movie last night. Jane: How was it? Jill: Nothing to write home about.
examples: I went to that new restaurant last night.

now and then.monolingual: sometimes; occasionally. now and then.) _ I like to go to a movie now and then. _ We visit my parents now and then, but we rarely see our other relatives.
examples: I like to go to a movie now and then.

null and void.monolingual: Cliché without legal force; having no legal effect. _ The court declared the law to be null and void. _ The millionaire’s will was null and void because it was unsigned.
examples: The court declared the law to be null and void.

nut up.monolingual: Sl. to go crazy. _I knew I would nut up if I didn’t quit that job. _ I almost nutted up at the last place I worked.
examples: I knew I would nut up if I didn’t quit that job.

nuts and bolts.monolingual: 1. Fig. the mundane workings of something; the basics of something. _ I want you to learn how to write well. You have to know the nuts and bolts of writing. _ She’s got a lot of good, general ideas, but when it comes to the nuts and bolts of getting
examples: I want you to learn how to write well.

odds and ends.monolingual: miscellaneous things. _ There were lots of odds and ends in the attic, but nothing of real value. _ I had the whole house cleaned out except for a few odds and ends that you might want to keep.
examples: There were lots of odds and ends in the attic, but nothing of real value.

of late.monolingual: lately. _ Have you seen Sally of late? _ We haven’t had an opportunity to eat out of late.
examples: We haven’t had an opportunity to eat out of late.

of the first water.monolingual: Fig. of the finest quality. _ This is a very fine pearl—a pearl of the first water. _ Tom is of the first water—a true gentleman.
examples: This is a very fine pearl—a pearl of the first water.

off and running.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of horses, dogs, or people] having started racing. _ It’s a beautiful day at the races, and, yes, they’re off and running!
examples: It’s a beautiful day at the races, and, yes, they’re off and running! 2.

off chance.monolingual: slight possibility. _I need your phone number on the off chance I need more help. _ There’s an off chance that we might be hiring next month.
examples: I need your phone number on the off chance I need more help.

off to the races.monolingual: Fig. an expression characterizing the activity or excitement that is just beginning; [we are] leaving for something interesting or exciting. _ The tour bus is out in front waiting and we’ve said goodbye to everyone. Looks like we’re off to the races.
examples: The tour bus is out in front waiting and we’ve said goodbye to everyone.

oink out.monolingual: Sl. to overeat. _I oink out every time we have chocolate cake. _ This Thursday starts a four-day weekend, and I plan to oink out every day.
examples: I oink out every time we have chocolate cake.

old hat.monolingual: Fig. old-fashioned; outmoded. _That’s a silly idea. It’s old hat. _ Hardly anybody uses typewriters anymore. That’s just old hat.
examples: That’s a silly idea.

on a shoestring.monolingual: Fig. with a very small amount of money. _ We lived on a shoestring for years before I got a goodpaying job. _ John traveled to Florida on a shoestring.
examples: We lived on a shoestring for years before I got a goodpaying job.

on all fours.monolingual: on one’s hands and knees. _I dropped a contact lens and spent an hour on all fours looking for it. _The baby can walk, but is on all fours most of the time anyway.
examples: I dropped a contact lens and spent an hour on all fours looking for it.

on board.monolingual: 1. Lit. aboard (on or in) a ship, bus, airplane, etc. _ Is there a doctor on board? We have a sick passenger. _ When everyone is on board, we will leave.
examples: Is there a doctor on board? We have a sick passenger.

on cloud nine.monolingual: Fig. very happy. _ When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine. _When the check came, I was on cloud nine for days.
examples: When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine.

on edge.monolingual: 1. Lit. on something’s own edge. _Can you stand a dime on edge? _ You should store these crates on edge, not lying f lat.
examples: You should store these crates on edge, not lying f lat.

on fire.monolingual: 1. Lit. burning; being burned with flames. _Help! My car is on fire! _ That house on the corner is on fire!
examples: That house on the corner is on fire! 2.

on hold.monolingual: 1. Lit. waiting; temporarily halted. _ The building project is on hold while we try to find money to complete it. _ We put our wedding plans on hold until we finished school.
examples: The building project is on hold while we try to find money to complete it.

on ice.monolingual: 1. Lit. stored or preserved on ice or under refrigeration. _ I have a lot of root beer on ice for the picnic. _ All the soft drinks are on ice.
examples: I have a lot of root beer on ice for the picnic.

on pins and needles.monolingual: Fig. anxious; in suspense. _ I’ve been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news. _ We were on pins and needles until we heard that your plane had landed safely.
examples: I’ve been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news.

on purpose.monolingual: intentionally; in a way that is meant or intended; not an accident. _ The bully stepped on my foot on purpose. _ Jealously, Jimmy destroyed Billy’s sand castle on purpose.
examples: The bully stepped on my foot on purpose.

on second thought.monolingual: Fig. having given something more thought; having reconsidered something. _ On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment. _On second thought, let’s not go to a movie.
examples: On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment.

on the ball.monolingual: Inf. knowledgeable; competent; attentive. _ This guy is really on the ball. _ If you were on the ball, this wouldn’t have happened.
examples: This guy is really on the ball.

on the button.monolingual: exactly right; in exactly the right place; at exactly the right time. _ That’s it! You’re right on the button. _ He got here at one o’clock on the button.
examples: That’s it! You’re right on the button.

on the double.monolingual: very fast; twice as fast as normal. (Originally military. Alludes to “double time” in marching.) _ Get over here right now—on the double! _ She wants to see you in her office on the double.
examples: She wants to see you in her office on the double.

on the face of it.monolingual: Fig. superficially; from the way it looks. _This looks like a serious problem on the face of it. It probably is minor, however. _ On the face of it, it seems worthless.
examples: This looks like a serious problem on the face of it.

on the fly.monolingual: [done] while something or someone is operating or moving. _ I’ll try to capture the data on the f ly. _ Please try to buy some aspirin somewhere on the f ly today.
examples: I’ll try to capture the data on the f ly.

on the go.monolingual: busy; moving about busily. _ I’m usually on the go all day long. _ I hate being on the go all the time.
examples: I’m usually on the go all day long.

on the house.monolingual: [of something] given away free by a merchant. _ “Here,” said the waiter, “have a cup of coffee on the house.” _ I went to a restaurant last night. I was the ten thousandth customer, so my dinner was on the house.
examples: “Here,” said the waiter, “have a cup of coffee on the house.

on the lam.monolingual: running from the police. (Underworld.) _ Richard has been on the lam for a week now. _ The gang leader broke out of prison and is still on the lam.
examples: Richard has been on the lam for a week now.

on the level.monolingual: honest; straightforward. _Come on now, on the level, tell me the truth. _ Is the ad on the level?
examples: Come on now, on the level, tell me the truth.

on the loose.monolingual: running around free. _ Look out! There is a bear on the loose from the zoo. _ Most kids enjoy being on the loose when they go to college.
examples: Look out! There is a bear on the loose from the zoo.

on the mark.monolingual: Fig. right on the measurement point; showing just the right anount. _ It’s exactly one quart, right on the mark.
examples: It’s exactly one quart, right on the mark.

on the move.monolingual: 1. moving from place to place. _ Are the cattle on the move now, or are they still grazing?
examples: Are the cattle on the move now, or are they still grazing? 2.

on the other hand.monolingual: Fig. a phrase introducing an alternate view. _ John: I’m ready to go; on the other hand, I’m perfectly comfortable here. Sally: I’ll let you know when I’m ready, then. _ Mary: I like this one. On the other hand, this is nice too. Sue: Why not get bot
examples: John: I’m ready to go; on the other hand, I’m perfectly comfortable here.

on the pill.monolingual: taking birth control pills. _Is it true that Mary is on the pill? _ She was on the pill, but she isn’t now.
examples: She was on the pill, but she isn’t now.

on the prowl.monolingual: looking for someone for sexual purposes. (Alludes to a prowling cat.) _ Tom looks like he is on the prowl again tonight. _ That whole gang of boys is on the prowl. Watch out.
examples: Tom looks like he is on the prowl again tonight.

on the rag.monolingual: 1. Sl.menstruating. (Potentially offensive. Use with caution.) _ Kim’s on the rag and in a bad mood. _ Sue doesn’t go swimming when she’s on the rag.
examples: Kim’s on the rag and in a bad mood.

on the rise.monolingual: Fig. increasing in frequency or intensity. _ The number of auto thefts in Cook County is on the rise again.
examples: The number of auto thefts in Cook County is on the rise again.

on the run.monolingual: 1. Fig. while one is moving from place to place. _ I will try to pick up some aspirin today on the run. _ I will think about it on the run.
examples: I will try to pick up some aspirin today on the run.

on the same wavelength.monolingual: Fig. thinking in the same pattern. _ We’re not on the same wavelength. Let’s try again. _ We kept talking until we got on the same wavelength.
examples: We’re not on the same wavelength.

on the shelf.monolingual: 1. Fig. not active socially; left to oneself in social matters. (Alludes to being left or stored on a shelf.) _ I’ve been on the shelf long enough. I’m going to make some friends. _ She likes being on the shelf.
examples: I’ve been on the shelf long enough.

on the skids.monolingual: Sl. on the decline. _ My newly started business is on the skids. _ Her health is really on the skids, but she stays cheery anyway.
examples: My newly started business is on the skids.

on the sly.monolingual: Fig. secretly and deceptively. _ She was stealing little bits of money on the sly. _ Martin was having an affair with the maid on the sly.
examples: She was stealing little bits of money on the sly.

on the spot.monolingual: 1. Lit. at exactly the right place; at exactly the right time. _ It’s noon, and I’m glad you’re all here on the spot. Now we can begin. _I expect you to be on the spot when and where trouble arises.
examples: It’s noon, and I’m glad you’re all here on the spot.

on the street.monolingual: 1. Fig. widely known. _ Sue put it on the street, and now everyone knows. _ It’s on the street. There isn’t anyone who hasn’t heard it.
examples: Sue put it on the street, and now everyone knows.

on the table.monolingual: Fig. subject to discussion by the group; submitted as a point of discussion. _ The chairman said we could not discuss salaries since the topic was no longer on the table.
examples: The chairman said we could not discuss salaries since the topic was no longer on the table.

on the up-and-up.monolingual: legitimate; open and aboveboard. _ Is this deal on the up-and-up? What’s the catch? _ Everything I do is on the up-and-up. I am totally honest.
examples: Everything I do is on the up-and-up.

on the wagon.monolingual: Fig. not drinking alcohol. _ No, I don’t care for a cocktail. I’m on the wagon. _ Bob’s old drinking buddies complained that he was no fun when he went on the wagon.
examples: No, I don’t care for a cocktail.

on the wane.monolingual: becoming less; fading away. _Her inf luence in on the wane, but she is still the boss.
examples: Her inf luence in on the wane, but she is still the boss.

on the warpath.monolingual: very angry. _The boss is on the warpath again. Watch out! _I am on the warpath about setting goals and standards again.
examples: The boss is on the warpath again.

on the whole.monolingual: generally; considering everything. _ On the whole, this was a very good day. _ Your work—on the whole—is quite good.
examples: On the whole, this was a very good day.

on thin ice.monolingual: 1. Lit. on ice that is too thin to support one. _ Billy is on thin ice and is in great danger.
examples: Billy is on thin ice and is in great danger.

on top of the world.monolingual: Fig. feeling wonderful; glorious; ecstatic. _ Wow, I feel on top of the world. _ Since he got a new job, he’s on top of the world.
examples: Wow, I feel on top of the world.

once and for all.monolingual: finally; permanently. _ Sue: I’m going to get this place organized once and for all! Alice: That’ll be the day! _ “We need to get this straightened out once and for all,” said Bob, for the fourth time today.
examples: “We need to get this straightened out once and for all,” said Bob, for the fourth time today.

once in a blue moon.monolingual: Cliché very seldom. _ Jill: Does your husband ever bring you f lowers? Ellen: Once in a blue moon. _ Once in a blue moon, I buy a fashion magazine, just to see what people are wearing.
examples: Jill: Does your husband ever bring you f lowers? Ellen: Once in a blue moon.

one and all.monolingual: everyone. _ “Good morning to one and all,” said Jane as she walked through the outer office. _Let’s hope that this turns out to be a wonderful party for one and all.
examples: “Good morning to one and all,” said Jane as she walked through the outer office.

one and the same.monolingual: Cliché the very same person or thing. _ John Jones and J. Jones are one and the same. _ Men’s socks and men’s stockings are almost one and the same.
examples: John Jones and J.

the one that got away.monolingual: Fig. the big fish that got away, especially as the subject of a fisherman’s story. _ The one that got away is always bigger than the one that got caught.
examples: The one that got away is always bigger than the one that got caught.

one too many.monolingual: Euph. one drink of liquor too many, implying drunkenness. _I think I’ve had one too many. It’s time to stop drinking. _ Don’t drive if you’ve had one too many.
examples: I think I’ve had one too many.

one-horse town.monolingual: Fig. a very small town; a small and backward town. _ I refuse to spend a whole week in that onehorse town! _ I grew up in a one-horse town, and I liked it very much.
examples: I grew up in a one-horse town, and I liked it very much.

one-night stand.monolingual: 1. Lit. a performance lasting only one night. _ The band did a series of one-night stands down the East Coast. _ You can’t make a living doing one-night stands.
examples: The band did a series of one-night stands down the East Coast.

one-track mind.monolingual: Fig. a mind that thinks entirely or almost entirely about one subject. _ Adolescent boys often have one-track minds. All they’re interested in is the opposite sex. _ Bob has a one-track mind. He can only talk about football.
examples: Adolescent boys often have one-track minds.

open up.monolingual: 1. Lit. open your door; open your mouth. (Usually Open up!) _ I want in. Open up! _ Open up! This is the police.
examples: Open up! This is the police.

or else.monolingual: or suffer the consequences. (An inspecific threat of bad consequences.) _ Do what I tell you, or else. _ Don’t be late for work, or else!
examples: Do what I tell you, or else.

or words to that effect.monolingual: Fig. or similar words meaning the same thing. _ John: It says right here in the contract, “You are expected to attend without fail,” or words to that effect. Mary: That means I have to be there, huh? John: You got it! _ Sally: She said that I wasn’t
examples: John: It says right here in the contract, “You are expected to attend without fail,” or words to that effect.

out for blood.monolingual: Fig. aggressively seeking to harm or get revenge; angry and looking for the cause of one’s distress. _ The opposite team is out for blood, but we have a good defense.
examples: The opposite team is out for blood, but we have a good defense.

out of character.monolingual: 1. unlike one’s usual behavior. _Ann’s remark was quite out of character. _ It was out of character for Ann to act so stubborn.
examples: Ann’s remark was quite out of character.

out of luck.monolingual: without good luck; having bad fortune. _ If you wanted some ice cream, you’re out of luck. _ I was out of luck. I got there too late to get a seat.
examples: If you wanted some ice cream, you’re out of luck.

out of order.monolingual: 1. Lit. [of something or things] out of the proper sequence. _ She noticed that the books on the shelf were out of order. _ All these cards were alphabetized, and now they’re out of order.
examples: She noticed that the books on the shelf were out of order.

out of season.monolingual: 1. not now available for sale. _Sorry, oysters are out of season. We don’t have any. _ Watermelon is out of season in the winter.
examples: Sorry, oysters are out of season.

out of the ordinary.monolingual: unusual. _ It was a good meal, but not out of the ordinary. _ Your report was nicely done, but nothing out of the ordinary.
examples: It was a good meal, but not out of the ordinary.

out of the picture.monolingual: Fig. no longer relevant to a situation; departed; dead. _ Now that Tom is out of the picture, we needn’t concern ourselves about his objections. _ With her husband out of the picture, she can begin living as she pleases.
examples: Now that Tom is out of the picture, we needn’t concern ourselves about his objections.

out of the question.monolingual: Fig. not allowed; not permitted. _ I’m sorry, but your taking my car is out of the question. _ You can’t go to Florida this spring. We can’t afford it. It’s out of the question.
examples: I’m sorry, but your taking my car is out of the question.

out of the running.monolingual: Fig. no longer being considered; eliminated from a contest. _ After the first part of the diving meet, three members of our team were out of the running. _ After the scandal was made public, I was out of the running. I pulled out of the election.
examples: After the first part of the diving meet, three members of our team were out of the running.

out of the woods.monolingual: Fig. past a critical phase; out of the unknown. _When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed. _ I can give you a better prediction for your future health when you are out of the woods.
examples: When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed.

out of thin air.monolingual: Fig. out of nowhere; out of nothing. _ Suddenly—out of thin air—the messenger appeared. _You just made that excuse up out of thin air.
examples: Suddenly—out of thin air—the messenger appeared.

out of this world.monolingual: 1. Fig. wonderful and exciting. _This pie is out of this world. _ My boyfriend is just out of this world.
examples: This pie is out of this world.

over the hump.monolingual: 1. Fig. over the hard part; past the midpoint. _ Things should be easy from now on. We finally got over the hump. _ When you get over the hump, life is much better.
examples: Things should be easy from now on.

over the top.monolingual: 1. Fig. having gained more than one’s goal. _Our fund-raising campaign went over the top by $3,000. _We didn’t go over the top. We didn’t even get half of what we set out to collect.
examples: Our fund-raising campaign went over the top by $3,000.

pack it in.monolingual: 1. Fig. to quit trying to do something; to give up trying something and quit. _ I was so distressed that I almost packed it in. _ I’ve had enough! I’m going to pack it in.
examples: I was so distressed that I almost packed it in.

pack up.monolingual: to prepare one’s belongings to be transported by placing them into a container; to gather one’s things together for one’s departure. _ If we are going to leave in the morning, we should pack up now. _ I think you should pack up and be ready to leave
examples: If we are going to leave in the morning, we should pack up now.

pad out.monolingual: Sl. to go to bed or to sleep. _ Man, if I don’t pad out by midnight, I’m a zombie. _ Why don’t you people go home so I can pad out?
examples: Man, if I don’t pad out by midnight, I’m a zombie.

pair off.monolingual: [for two people or other creatures] to form a couple or pair. _ All of them paired off and worked as teams to solve the puzzle. _ Everyone should pair off and discuss the issue for a while.
examples: All of them paired off and worked as teams to solve the puzzle.

par for the course.monolingual: typical; about what one could expect. (This refers to golf courses, not school courses.) _ So he went off and left you? Well that’s about par for the course. He’s no friend. _ I worked for days on this proposal, but it was rejected. That’s par for th
examples: So he went off and left you? Well that’s about par for the course.

pass muster.monolingual: Fig. to measure up to the required standards. _ I tried, but my efforts didn’t pass muster. _ If you don’t wear a jacket and tie, you won’t pass muster at that fancy restaurant. They won’t let you in.
examples: I tried, but my efforts didn’t pass muster.

pass out.monolingual: to faint; to lose consciousness. _ Oh, look! Tom has passed out. _ When he got the news, he passed out.
examples: Oh, look! Tom has passed out.

pass the buck.monolingual: Fig. to pass the blame (to someone else); to give the responsibility (to someone else). _ Don’t try to pass the buck! It’s your fault, and everybody knows it. _ Some people try to pass the buck whenever they can.
examples: Don’t try to pass the buck! It’s your fault, and everybody knows it.

pay off.monolingual: to yield profits; to result in benefits. _ My investment in those stocks has really paid off. _ The time I spent in school paid off in later years.
examples: My investment in those stocks has really paid off.

pay the penalty.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay a fine for doing something wrong. _ You ran the red light and now you will have to pay the penalty.
examples: You ran the red light and now you will have to pay the penalty.

pay the piper.monolingual: Fig. to face the results of one’s actions; to receive punishment for something. _You can put off paying your debts only so long. Eventually you’ll have to pay the piper. _ You can’t get away with that forever. You’ll have to pay the piper someday.
examples: You can put off paying your debts only so long.

pay the price.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pay the price that is asked for goods or services. (Usually implying that the price is high.) _If this is the quality of goods that you require, you will have to pay the price.
examples: If this is the quality of goods that you require, you will have to pay the price.

pay up.monolingual: to pay what is owed. (Often a command: Pay up!) _ I want my money now. Pay up! _ If you don’t pay up, I’ll take you to court.
examples: I want my money now.

peace of mind.monolingual: Fig. a tranquility that results from not having worries, guilt, or problems. _If peace of mind is more important to you than earning a lot of money, maybe you should consider teaching.
examples: If peace of mind is more important to you than earning a lot of money, maybe you should consider teaching.

peal out.monolingual: [for bells or voices] to sound forth musically. _ The bells pealed out to announce that the wedding had taken place. _ All six of the bells seemed to peal out at once.
examples: The bells pealed out to announce that the wedding had taken place.

peel out.monolingual: [for a driver] to speed off in a car with a screeching of tires. _ Dave got in his car and peeled out, waking the neighbors. _ I wish he would stop peeling out!
examples: Dave got in his car and peeled out, waking the neighbors.

peg out.monolingual: Sl. to die. _ I was so scared, I thought I would peg out for sure. _ Uncle Herman almost pegged out last week.
examples: I was so scared, I thought I would peg out for sure.

perk up.monolingual: to become invigorated; to become more active. _After a bit of water, the plants perked up nicely. _About noon, Andy perked up and looked wide-awake.
examples: After a bit of water, the plants perked up nicely.

pet peeve.monolingual: Fig. a frequent annoyance; one’s “favorite” or most often encountered annoyance. _ My pet peeve is someone who always comes into the theater after the show has started. _Drivers who don’t signal are John’s pet peeve.
examples: My pet peeve is someone who always comes into the theater after the show has started.

peter out.monolingual: [for something] to die or dwindle away; [for something] to become exhausted gradually. _ When the fire petered out, I went to bed. _My money finally petered out, and I had to come home.
examples: When the fire petered out, I went to bed.

pick up.monolingual: 1. to tidy up. _ When you finish playing, you have to pick up. _ Please pick up after yourself.
examples: When you finish playing, you have to pick up.

pick up the pace.monolingual: to speed up the tempo; to increase the rate that something is being done. _We are going to have to pick up the pace of activity around here if we are to get the job done.
examples: We are going to have to pick up the pace of activity around here if we are to get the job done.

pie in the sky.monolingual: 1. Fig. a future reward after death, considered as a replacement for a reward not received on earth. _ Don’t hold out for pie in the sky. Get realistic. _ If he didn’t hope for some heavenly pie in the sky, he would probably be a real crook.
examples: Don’t hold out for pie in the sky.

piece of cake.monolingual: Fig. something easy to do. _ No problem. When you know what you’re doing, it’s a piece of cake. _ Glad to help. It was a piece of cake. _ Rescuing frightened cats is my specialty. Piece of cake!
examples: No problem. When you know what you’re doing, it’s a piece of cake.

pile up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for things] to gather or accumulate. _The newspapers began to pile up after a few days. _ Work is really piling up around here.
examples: The newspapers began to pile up after a few days.

pipe down.monolingual: to become quiet; to cease making noise; to shut up. (Especially as a rude command.) _ Pipe down! I’m trying to sleep. _ Come on! Pipe down and get back to work!
examples: Pipe down! I’m trying to sleep.

piping hot.monolingual: [of food] extremely hot. _ On a cold day, I like to eat piping hot soup. _ Be careful! This coffee is piping hot!
examples: On a cold day, I like to eat piping hot soup.

place of business.monolingual: a place where business is done; a factory or office. _ Our place of business opens at 9:00 a.m. each day. _ You will have to come to our place of business to make a purchase.
examples: Our place of business opens at 9:00 a.

play for time.monolingual: Fig. to stall; to act in such a way as to gain time. _ I’ll play for time while you sneak out the window. _ The lawyers for the defense were playing for time while they looked for a witness.
examples: I’ll play for time while you sneak out the window.

play hard to get.monolingual: Fig. to be coy, intentionally shy, and fickle. (Usually refers to someone of the opposite sex.) _ Why can’t we go out? Why do you play hard to get? _ Sally annoys all the boys because she plays hard to get.
examples: Sally annoys all the boys because she plays hard to get.

play hooky.monolingual: to fail to attend school or some other event. _ Why aren’t you in school? Are you playing hooky? _ I don’t have time for the sales meeting today, so I think I’ll just play hooky.
examples: I don’t have time for the sales meeting today, so I think I’ll just play hooky.

play it cool.monolingual: 1. Inf. to do something while not revealing insecurities or incompetence; to act blasé. _ Play it cool, man. Look like you belong there. _If the boss walks in, just play it cool.
examples: Play it cool, man.

play on.monolingual: to continue to play. _ The band played on and the dance continued until the wee hours of the morning. _ We played on and on until the last guests left the party.
examples: The band played on and the dance continued until the wee hours of the morning.

play out.monolingual: [for a process] to run out; to finish. _ The whole incident is about to play out. Then it all will be forgotten. _ When the event plays out, everything will return to normal.
examples: The whole incident is about to play out.

play politics.monolingual: 1. Lit. to negotiate politically. _ Everybody at city hall is playing politics as usual. _If you’re elected as a member of a political party, you’ll have to play politics.
examples: Everybody at city hall is playing politics as usual.

play possum.monolingual: Fig. to pretend to be inactive, unobservant, asleep, or dead. (The possum refers to an opossum.) _ I knew that Bob wasn’t asleep. He was just playing possum. _ I can’t tell if this animal is dead or just playing possum.
examples: I knew that Bob wasn’t asleep.

play the field.monolingual: to date many different people rather than just one. _ When Tom told Ann good-bye, he said he wanted to play the field. _ He said he wanted to play the field while he was still young.
examples: When Tom told Ann good-bye, he said he wanted to play the field.

play the fool.monolingual: Fig. to act in a silly manner in order to amuse other people. _ The teacher told Tom to stop playing the fool and sit down. _ Fred likes playing the fool, but we didn’t find him funny last night.
examples: The teacher told Tom to stop playing the fool and sit down.

play through.monolingual: [for golfers] to pass someone on the golf course. _ Do you mind if we play through? We have to get back to the courtroom by two o’clock. _ We let them play through because they were moving so fast.
examples: Do you mind if we play through? We have to get back to the courtroom by two o’clock.

play with a full deck.monolingual: 1. Lit. to play cards with a complete deck, containing all the cards. _Are we playing with a full deck or did some card drop on the f loor? I haven’t seen the three of hearts all evening!
examples: Are we playing with a full deck or did some card drop on the f loor? I haven’t seen the three of hearts all evening! 2.

play with fire.monolingual: 1. Lit. to use fire as a toy; to experiment with flames and fire. _ Jimmy! I’ve told you never to play with fire!
examples: Jimmy! I’ve told you never to play with fire! 2.

poke along.monolingual: to move along slowly; to lag or tarry. _ Get moving. Stop poking along. _ I was just poking along, taking my time, not paying attention to what was going on around me.
examples: Get moving. Stop poking along.

pooch out.monolingual: to stick or bulge out, as with a belly. _ His chubby tummy pooched out when he relaxed.
examples: His chubby tummy pooched out when he relaxed.

poop out.monolingual: Inf. to quit; to wear out and stop. _ He pooped out after about an hour of hard work. _ I think I’m going to poop out pretty soon.
examples: He pooped out after about an hour of hard work.

pop off.monolingual: 1. Sl. to make an unnecessary remark; to interrupt with a remark; to sound off. _ Please don’t pop off all the time. _ Bob keeps popping off when he should be listening.
examples: Please don’t pop off all the time.

pop the question.monolingual: [for a man] to ask a woman to marry him. (Could also be used by a woman asking a man.) _ She waited for years for him to pop the question. _ Finally she popped the question.
examples: She waited for years for him to pop the question.

pop up.monolingual: 1. [for a baseball batter] to hit a baseball that goes high upward rather than outward. _ The catcher came to bat and popped up. _I hope I don’t pop up this time.
examples: The catcher came to bat and popped up.

pound a beat.monolingual: Fig. to walk a regular route. _ The cop pounded the same beat for years and years. _ Pounding a beat will wreck your feet.
examples: The cop pounded the same beat for years and years.

pound the pavement.monolingual: Fig. to walk through the streets looking for a job. _I spent two months pounding the pavement after the factory I worked for closed. _Hey, Bob. You’d better get busy pounding those nails unless you want to be out pounding the pavement.
examples: I spent two months pounding the pavement after the factory I worked for closed.

pour forth.monolingual: to gush out; to gush forth. _ The milk gushed out of the hole in the container. _A tremendous amount of water poured forth when the fire hydrant was knocked over.
examples: The milk gushed out of the hole in the container.

power up.monolingual: to start an engine. _ Well, let’s power up so we will be ready to leave with the others. _ It’s time to power up and get going.
examples: Well, let’s power up so we will be ready to leave with the others.

pray to the porcelain god.monolingual: Sl. to kneel at the toilet bowl and vomit from drunkenness. _Wally spent a while praying to the porcelain god last night. _ I think I have to go pray to the porcelain god.
examples: Wally spent a while praying to the porcelain god last night.

psych out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to have a nervous or emotional trauma; to go mad for a brief time. _ Another day like this one and I’ll psych out for sure. _ He looked at the bill and psyched out.
examples: Another day like this one and I’ll psych out for sure.

psych up.monolingual: Inf. to get mentally ready for something. _I have to psych up before the big game tonight. _We want to psych up so we can play a good game.
examples: I have to psych up before the big game tonight.

pucker up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to tighten one’s lips together into a circle as if to kiss. _He puckered up and kissed her once, and then again.
examples: He puckered up and kissed her once, and then again.

puff out.monolingual: to swell out. _ The frog’s throat puffed out, and we expected to hear a croak. _ The sail puffed out, and the boat began to move.
examples: The frog’s throat puffed out, and we expected to hear a croak.

puff up.monolingual: to swell up. _Her finger puffed up and she thought she might have an infection. _ His eyelids had puffed up during the night.
examples: Her finger puffed up and she thought she might have an infection.

pull a fast one.monolingual: Inf. to succeed in an act of deception. _ She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home. _ Don’t try to pull a fast one with me! I know what you’re doing.
examples: She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home.

pull oneself together.monolingual: 1. Fig. to compose oneself; to gather one’s wits about one. _ I have to pull myself together and try it again. _ Now try to pull yourself together and get through this crisis.
examples: I have to pull myself together and try it again.

pull up stakes.monolingual: 1. Lit. to pull up tent stakes to take down a tent in preparation to leaving. _ Let’s pull up stakes and head home before the storm hits.
examples: Let’s pull up stakes and head home before the storm hits.

punch in.monolingual: to record one’s arrival at one’s workplace at a certain time. _ What time did you punch in? _ I punched in at the regular time.
examples: I punched in at the regular time.

punch out.monolingual: to record that one has left one’s workplace at a certain time. _ Why didn’t you punch out when you left last night? _ I punched out at the regular time.
examples: I punched out at the regular time.

punk out.monolingual: Sl. to chicken out (of something); to withdraw from something in cowardice. _He was supposed to ask her out, but he punked out at the last minute. _ Come on! Stick with it! Don’t punk out!
examples: He was supposed to ask her out, but he punked out at the last minute.

push along.monolingual: to move along; to travel along as with a purpose. _We must push along. We have a long way to travel before morning. _ They pushed along at a steady clip until they arrived at their destination.
examples: We must push along.

push out.monolingual: to spread out; to expand outward. _ The sides of the box pushed out, and I was afraid it would break. _ His little tummy pushed out when he was full.
examples: The sides of the box pushed out, and I was afraid it would break.

push the envelope.monolingual: Fig. to expand the definition, categorization, dimensions, or perimeters of something. _ The engineers wanted to completely redesign the product, but couldn’t push the envelope because of a very restricted budget.
examples: The engineers wanted to completely redesign the product, but couldn’t push the envelope because of a very restricted budget.

put oneself out.monolingual: to inconvenience oneself. _ I just don’t know why I put myself out for you! _ No, I did not put myself out at all. It was no trouble, in fact.
examples: No, I did not put myself out at all.

put out.monolingual: to generate [lots of something]. _ What a great machine. It really puts out! _ The new laser printer really puts out!
examples: What a great machine.

put something behind one.monolingual: Fig. to try to forget about something. _ I look forward to putting all my problems behind me. _ She will be happier when all this can be put behind her.
examples: I look forward to putting all my problems behind me.

put two and two together.monolingual: to figure something out from the information available. _Well, I put two and two together and came up with an idea of who did it. _ Don’t worry. John won’t figure it out. He can’t put two and two together.
examples: Well, I put two and two together and came up with an idea of who did it.

putz around.monolingual: Inf. to fiddle around; to mess around. _Stop putzing around and get to work. _ Those guys spend most of their time just putzing around.
examples: Stop putzing around and get to work.

quick off the mark.monolingual: quick starting or reacting. (Compare this with slow off the mark.) _ Boy, you were quick off the mark there! _ If you can be really quick off the mark, you can soon find the answer.
examples: If you can be really quick off the mark, you can soon find the answer.

quick on the uptake.monolingual: quick to understand or learn something. _Just because I’m not quick on the uptake, it doesn’t mean I’m stupid. _Mary understands jokes before anyone else because she’s so quick on the uptake.
examples: Just because I’m not quick on the uptake, it doesn’t mean I’m stupid.

quiet down.monolingual: to become quiet; to become less noisy. _ Please quiet down. _ Ask them to quiet down.
examples: Please quiet down.

quit while one is ahead.monolingual: to stop doing something while one is still successful. _When will I learn to quit while I’m ahead? _ Get into the market. Make some money and get out. Quit while you’re ahead.
examples: Get into the market.

race against time.monolingual: 1. a rush; a rush to beat a deadline. _ We were in a race against time to beat the deadline. _It was a race against time, but we made it.
examples: We were in a race against time to beat the deadline.

rack out.monolingual: Sl. to go to bed and to sleep. _ I’m really tired. I’ve got to go rack out for a while. _I racked out until nearly noon.
examples: I’m really tired.

rag out.monolingual: Sl. to dress up. _ I like to rag out and go to parties. _ I hate to rag out. I like comfortable clothes.
examples: I like to rag out and go to parties.

rain cats and dogs.monolingual: Fig. to rain very hard. _ It’s raining cats and dogs. Look at it pour! _ I’m not going out in that storm. It’s raining cats and dogs.
examples: It’s raining cats and dogs.

rain or shine.monolingual: no matter whether it rains or the sun shines. _ Don’t worry. I’ll be there rain or shine. _ We’ll hold the picnic—rain or shine.
examples: Don’t worry. I’ll be there rain or shine.

raise the bar.monolingual: Fig. to make a task a little more difficult. (As with raising the bar in high jumping or pole vaulting.) _ Just as I was getting accustomed to my job, the manager raised the bar and I had to perform even better.
examples: Just as I was getting accustomed to my job, the manager raised the bar and I had to perform even better.

raise up.monolingual: to lift oneself up; to get up or begin to get up. _ She raised up and then fell back onto her bed. She was too weak to get up. _ I could not raise up enough to see out the window.
examples: She raised up and then fell back onto her bed.

rank and file.monolingual: 1. Lit. regular soldiers, not the officers. _ I think there is low morale among the rank and file, sir. _ The rank and file usually do exactly as they are told.
examples: I think there is low morale among the rank and file, sir.

rat out.monolingual: Sl. to quit; to fink out (on someone or something). _ It’s too late to rat out. _ He tried to rat out at the last minute.
examples: It’s too late to rat out.

reach down.monolingual: to extend downward. _ The stems of the plant reached down almost to the f loor. _The drapes don’t quite reach down to the f loor.
examples: The stems of the plant reached down almost to the f loor.

reach out.monolingual: 1. Lit. to extend one’s grasp outward. _ He reached out, but there was no one to take hold of. _I reached out and grabbed onto the first thing I could get hold of.
examples: He reached out, but there was no one to take hold of.

read between the lines.monolingual: Fig. to infer something (from something else); to try to understand what is meant by something that is not written explicitly or openly. _After listening to what she said, if you read between the lines, you can begin to see what she really means. _ D
examples: After listening to what she said, if you read between the lines, you can begin to see what she really means.

rear back.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a horse] to pull back and up onto its hind legs in an effort to move backwards rapidly or throw a rider. _ The animal reared back in terror. _ The horse reared back and almost threw its rider.
examples: The animal reared back in terror.

rear up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a horse] to lean back on its hind legs and raise its front legs, assuming a threatening posture or avoiding something on the ground such as a snake. _ The horse reared up suddenly, throwing the rider onto the ground. _ When the horse rea
examples: The horse reared up suddenly, throwing the rider onto the ground.

red ink.monolingual: Fig. debt; indebtedness as shown in red ink on a financial statement. _ There is too much red ink in my financial statement. _ Too much red ink and the company will collapse.
examples: There is too much red ink in my financial statement.

red tape.monolingual: Fig. over-strict attention to the wording and details of rules and regulations, especially by government workers. (From the color of the tape used by government departments in England to tie up bundles of documents.) _Because of red tape, Frank took
examples: Because of red tape, Frank took weeks to get a visa.

reduce someone to tears.monolingual: to cause a person to cry through insults, frustration, and belittling. _ He scolded her so much that she was reduced to tears by the end of the meeting.
examples: He scolded her so much that she was reduced to tears by the end of the meeting.

rein up.monolingual: [for a horse rider] to stop. _The equestrian reined up and dismounted. _We all reined up and waited for the cars to pass by.
examples: The equestrian reined up and dismounted.

reinvent the wheel.monolingual: Fig. to make unnecessary or redundant preparations. _ You don’t need to reinvent the wheel. Read up on what others have done. _ I don’t have to reinvent the wheel, but I will be cautious before I act.
examples: You don’t need to reinvent the wheel.

rest assured.monolingual: to be assured; to be certain. _ Rest assured that you’ll receive the best of care. _Please rest assured that we will do everything possible to help.
examples: Rest assured that you’ll receive the best of care.

return the favor.monolingual: to do a good deed for someone who has done a good deed for you. _ You helped me last week, so I’ll return the favor and help you this week. _ There is no point in helping Bill. He’ll never return the favor.
examples: You helped me last week, so I’ll return the favor and help you this week.

rev up.monolingual: to increase in amount or activity. _ Production revved up after the strike. _We’re hoping business will rev up soon.
examples: Production revved up after the strike.

ride off.monolingual: to depart, riding something such as a horse or a bicycle. _Betty said good-bye and rode off. _We rode off, each one in a different direction.
examples: Betty said good-bye and rode off.

ride on.monolingual: to continue to ride, traveling onward. _ We rode on for at least an hour before finding a rest stop. _ They rode on for a while.
examples: We rode on for at least an hour before finding a rest stop.

ring a bell.monolingual: Fig. [for something] to cause someone to remember something or for it to seem familiar. _ I’ve never met John Franklin, but his name rings a bell. _ Whenever I see a bee, it rings a bell. I remember when I was stung by one.
examples: I’ve never met John Franklin, but his name rings a bell.

ring back.monolingual: to call back on the telephone. _ No, there’s no message. I’ll ring back later. _ She’s not here now. I suggest you ring back after dinner.
examples: No, there’s no message.

ring off the hook.monolingual: Fig. [for a telephone] to ring incessantly and repeatedly. _ What a busy day! The telephone has been ringing off the hook all day long. _The telephone has been ringing off the hook ever since the ad appeared in the paper.
examples: What a busy day! The telephone has been ringing off the hook all day long.

ring out.monolingual: [for a loud sound] to go out. _ The bells rang out at the end of the wedding ceremony. _Loud cheers rang out at the end of the game. _A shot rang out and started all the dogs barking.
examples: The bells rang out at the end of the wedding ceremony.

ring true.monolingual: Fig. to sound or seem true or likely. (From testing the quality of metal or glass by striking it and evaluating the sound made.) _ The student’s excuse for being late doesn’t ring true. _ Do you think that Mary’s explanation for her absence rang true
examples: The student’s excuse for being late doesn’t ring true.

rip off.monolingual: [for something] to tear or peel off. _ My pocket ripped off, and my money is gone now! _ A piece of the bumper ripped off my car.
examples: A piece of the bumper ripped off my car.

rise from the ashes.monolingual: Fig. [for a structure] to be rebuilt after destruction. _ The entire west section of the city was destroyed and a group of new buildings rose from the ashes in only a few months. _ Will the city rise again from the ashes? No one knows.
examples: The entire west section of the city was destroyed and a group of new buildings rose from the ashes in only a few months.

rise to the challenge.monolingual: Fig. to accept a challenge. (Usually in reference to success with the challenge.) _You can depend on Kelly to rise to the challenge. _We were not able to rise to the challenge and we lost the contract.
examples: You can depend on Kelly to rise to the challenge.

rise to the occasion.monolingual: Fig. to meet the challenge of an event; to try extra hard to do a task. _ John was able to rise to the occasion and make the conference a success. _ It was a big challenge, but he rose to the occasion.
examples: John was able to rise to the occasion and make the conference a success.

rise up.monolingual: 1. to come up; to ascend. _ The water is rising up fast. You had better get to higher ground. _ As the water rose up, it covered the fields and streets.
examples: The water is rising up fast.

road hog.monolingual: Fig. someone who drives carelessly and selfishly. _ Look at that road hog driving in the middle of the road and stopping other drivers from passing him. _ That road hog nearly knocked the children over. He was driving too fast.
examples: Look at that road hog driving in the middle of the road and stopping other drivers from passing him.

roar away.monolingual: to speed away, making a loud clamor. _ The car roared away into the night with tires screeching. _ The train roared away, carrying Andy to Canada.
examples: The car roared away into the night with tires screeching.

rob the cradle.monolingual: Fig. to marry or date someone who is much younger than oneself. _ I hear that Bill is dating Ann. Isn’t that sort of robbing the cradle? She’s much younger than he is. _ Uncle Bill—who is nearly eighty—married a thirty-year-old woman. That is really
examples: I hear that Bill is dating Ann.

rock the boat.monolingual: 1. Lit. to do something to move a boat from side to side, causing it to rock. (Often in a negative sense.) _ Sit down and stop rocking the boat. You’ll turn it over!
examples: Sit down and stop rocking the boat.

roll about.monolingual: to move about, turning or rotating, as a wheel or a ball. _ The ball rolled about awhile and then came to rest. _His eyes rolled about in amazement before he spoke.
examples: The ball rolled about awhile and then came to rest.

roll around.monolingual: to move about, rotating, turning over, turning, or moving on wheels. _The baby rolled around on the f loor, giggling and cooing. _The toy truck won’t roll around anymore.
examples: The baby rolled around on the f loor, giggling and cooing.

roll away.monolingual: to move away, rotating, turning over, turning, or moving on wheels. _The ball rolled away and fell down a storm sewer. _The cart rolled away, and we had to chase it down the hill.
examples: The ball rolled away and fell down a storm sewer.

roll back.monolingual: [for something] to return, rotating or turning or moving on wheels. _ I rolled the ball away, thinking it would roll back. It didn’t. _ I struck the golf ball out of the sand trap, but it rolled back.
examples: I rolled the ball away, thinking it would roll back.

roll down.monolingual: to move downward, rotating, as a wheel or a ball, or to move downward on wheels. _ I pushed the wagon up the driveway, and it rolled down again. _ Don’t place the cart at the top of the hill. It will roll down.
examples: I pushed the wagon up the driveway, and it rolled down again.

roll in.monolingual: Fig. to come in large numbers or amounts, easily, as if rolling. (Alludes to the arrival of many wheeled conveyances.) _We didn’t expect many people at the party, but they just kept rolling in. _Money is simply rolling in for our charity.
examples: We didn’t expect many people at the party, but they just kept rolling in.

roll on.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to continue rolling. _ The ball rolled on and on. _ The cart came rolling down the hill and rolled on for a few yards at the bottom.
examples: The ball rolled on and on.

roll over.monolingual: to turn over; to rotate one half turn. _ The old man rolled over and started snoring again. _Please roll over and give me some more space in the bed.
examples: The old man rolled over and started snoring again.

rot away.monolingual: to decompose; to decompose and fall away. _ The fallen trees rotted away and surrendered their nutrients to the soil. _ As the wood rotted away, it became rich humus.
examples: The fallen trees rotted away and surrendered their nutrients to the soil.

rot off.monolingual: to decompose. _If you don’t clean and repaint that old windowsill, it will rot off. _ A few old branches finally rotted off, but the ancient tree looked as if it would survive the wet spell.
examples: If you don’t clean and repaint that old windowsill, it will rot off.

rule the roost.monolingual: Fig. to be the boss or manager, especially at home. _ Who rules the roost at your house? _ Our new office manager really rules the roost.
examples: Our new office manager really rules the roost.

run along.monolingual: to leave. _Please run along and leave me alone. _ I have to run along now. Good-bye.
examples: Please run along and leave me alone.

run around.monolingual: 1. to run here and there. _Why are you running around? Sit down and be quiet. _Please stop running around. You are making me nervous.
examples: Why are you running around? Sit down and be quiet.

run back.monolingual: to come back, running. _ She ran to the barn and then ran back. _ Tom ran back, very much afraid.
examples: She ran to the barn and then ran back.

run behind.monolingual: to be late; to run late. _ We are running behind. You had better hurry. _Things are running behind, and we will not finish on time.
examples: We are running behind.

run down.monolingual: 1. to come down, running or very quickly; to go down, running or very quickly. _ I need to talk to you down here. Can you run down? _I will run down and talk to you.
examples: I need to talk to you down here.

run for it.monolingual: to escape by running. _ The dogs were coming after me fast. There was nothing I could do but run for it. _ I ran for it when I saw the police coming.
examples: The dogs were coming after me fast.

run in the family.monolingual: [for a characteristic] to appear in many (or all) members of a family. _My grandparents lived well into their nineties, and it runs in the family. _ My brothers and I have red hair. It runs in the family.
examples: My grandparents lived well into their nineties, and it runs in the family.

run off.monolingual: 1. to flee. _The children rang our doorbell and then ran off. _They ran off as fast as they could.
examples: The children rang our doorbell and then ran off.

run off at the mouth.monolingual: Sl. to talk too much. _ I wish you would stop running off at the mouth. _Tom runs off at the mouth too much. I wish he would temper his remarks.
examples: I wish you would stop running off at the mouth.

run on.monolingual: 1. to continue running. _I wanted to stop her and ask her something, but she just ran on. _ The joggers had a chance to stop and rest, but they just ran on.
examples: I wanted to stop her and ask her something, but she just ran on.

run out of steam.monolingual: Fig. to lose momentum and fail. _ Toward the end of the lecture, he seemed to run out of steam, leaving us with no summary or conclusion.
examples: Toward the end of the lecture, he seemed to run out of steam, leaving us with no summary or conclusion.

run over.monolingual: 1. to come by for a quick visit. _ Can you run over for a minute after work? _I will run over for a minute as soon as I can.
examples: I will run over for a minute as soon as I can.

run rampant.monolingual: to run, develop, or grow out of control. _ The children ran rampant through the house. _Weeds have run rampant around the abandoned house.
examples: The children ran rampant through the house.

run scared.monolingual: to behave as if one were going to fail. _ The mayor was running scared, but won anyway. _ When we lost that big contract, everyone in the office was running scared. We thought we’d be fired.
examples: The mayor was running scared, but won anyway.

run someone ragged.monolingual: Fig. to keep someone or something very busy. _ This busy season is running us all ragged at the store. _ What a busy day. I ran myself ragged.
examples: This busy season is running us all ragged at the store.

run the gamut.monolingual: to cover a wide range [from one thing to another]. _ She wants to buy the house, but her requests run the gamut from expensive new carpeting to completely new landscaping. _ His hobbies run the gamut from piano repair to portrait painting.
examples: She wants to buy the house, but her requests run the gamut from expensive new carpeting to completely new landscaping.

run the show.monolingual: to be in charge; to be in command. _Who’s running this show? _ No, I don’t want to have to run the show again.
examples: No, I don’t want to have to run the show again.

rush hour.monolingual: the period of time when heavy traffic is moving into or out of a city. _ This is the slowest rush hour I have ever been in. Traffic is almost in gridlock.
examples: This is the slowest rush hour I have ever been in.

rust out.monolingual: to develop holes or weak places owing to rust. _ Our hot water heater rusted out and f looded the basement.
examples: Our hot water heater rusted out and f looded the basement.

sack out.monolingual: to go to bed or go to sleep. _ It’s time for me to sack out. _ Let’s sack out early tonight.
examples: It’s time for me to sack out.

sacked out.monolingual: asleep. _ Mary is sacked out in her room. _ Here it is ten o’clock, and you are still sacked out!
examples: Mary is sacked out in her room.

sacred cow.monolingual: Fig. something that is regarded by some people with such respect and veneration that they do not like it being criticized by anyone in any way. (From the fact that the cow is regarded as sacred in India and is not eaten or mistreated.) _A university
examples: A university education is a sacred cow in the Smith family.

saddle up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to prepare one’s horse for riding by putting a saddle on it. _ Let’s saddle up and go for a ride.
examples: Let’s saddle up and go for a ride.

safe and sound.monolingual: unharmed and whole or healthy. _ It was a rough trip, but we got there safe and sound. _ I’m glad to see you here safe and sound.
examples: It was a rough trip, but we got there safe and sound.

sail under false colors.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sail with false identification. (Pirates often sailed under the national flag of the ship they planned on attacking.) _ The ship, sailing under false colors, suddenly started to pursue our ship. _ Bluebeard the pirate was known for sailing
examples: The ship, sailing under false colors, suddenly started to pursue our ship.

sally forth.monolingual: to go forth; to leave and go out. _ The soldiers sallied forth from behind the stone wall. _Well, it’s time to sally forth and drive to work.
examples: The soldiers sallied forth from behind the stone wall.

same difference.monolingual: the same; no difference at all. _ Pink, fuchsia, what does it matter? Same difference. _ Whether you go or I go, it’s the same difference.
examples: Pink, fuchsia, what does it matter? Same difference.

save the day.monolingual: to produce a good result when a bad result was expected. _ The team was expected to lose, but Sally made three points and saved the day. _ Your excellent speech calmed the crowd and saved the day.
examples: The team was expected to lose, but Sally made three points and saved the day.

saved by the bell.monolingual: Cliché saved by the timely intervention of someone or something. (Alludes to a boxer who is saved from being counted out by the bell that ends a round.) _ I was going to have to do my part, but someone knocked on the door and I didn’t have to do it.
examples: I was going to have to do my part, but someone knocked on the door and I didn’t have to do it.

say grace.monolingual: to say a prayer of gratitude before or after a meal. _ Grandfather always says grace at Thanksgiving. _ A local preacher said grace at the banquet.
examples: Grandfather always says grace at Thanksgiving.

say the word.monolingual: to give a signal to begin; to say yes or okay. _ I’m ready to start any time you say the word. _ We’ll all shout “Happy Birthday!” when I say the word.
examples: I’m ready to start any time you say the word.

scoot over.monolingual: to slide sideways while seated. _Scoot over and let me sit down. _If you scoot over, we can get another person in this row.
examples: Scoot over and let me sit down.

scratch the surface.monolingual: 1. Lit. to scratch something just on the surface, not extending the mark below the finish into the wood, stone, marble, below. _There is no serious damage done to the bench. You only scratched the surface.
examples: There is no serious damage done to the bench.

screw around.monolingual: 1. Inf. to mess around; to waste time. _ Stop screwing around and get to work! _ I’m not screwing around, I’m thinking.
examples: I’m not screwing around, I’m thinking.

screw off.monolingual: Inf. to waste time. _ Stop screwing off and get busy! _ I’m not screwing off. This is my lunch hour.
examples: I’m not screwing off.

screw up.monolingual: 1. Inf. to mess up. _ I hope I don’t screw up this time. _The waiter screwed up again.
examples: I hope I don’t screw up this time.

screwed up.monolingual: Inf. ruined; messed up. _ This is a really screwed up schedule. Let’s start over again. _ Your schedule is completely screwed up.
examples: This is a really screwed up schedule.

scrub up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to clean oneself up. _ You have to scrub up before dinner. _ Please go scrub up before you come to the table.
examples: You have to scrub up before dinner.

see red.monolingual: to be angry. _ Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red. _Bill really saw red when the tax bill arrived.
examples: Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red.

see stars.monolingual: Fig. to seem to see flashing lights after receiving a blow to the head. _ I saw stars when I bumped my head on the attic ceiling. _ The little boy saw stars when he fell headfirst onto the concrete.
examples: I saw stars when I bumped my head on the attic ceiling.

see the light.monolingual: Fig. to understand something clearly at last. _ After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light. _ I know that geometry is difficult. Keep working at it. You’ll see the light pretty soon.
examples: After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light.

seize the opportunity.monolingual: to take advantage of an opportunity when offered. _ My uncle offered me a trip to Europe, so I seized the opportunity. _ Whenever you have a chance, you should seize the opportunity.
examples: My uncle offered me a trip to Europe, so I seized the opportunity.

seize up.monolingual: to freeze or halt; to grind suddenly to a stop. _ The engine seized up, and the car coasted to a stop. _ My knee seized up in the middle of a football game.
examples: The engine seized up, and the car coasted to a stop.

sell out.monolingual: [for an item] to be sold until there is no more. _ All the plastic hangers have sold out.
examples: All the plastic hangers have sold out.

send someone packing.monolingual: Fig. to send someone away; to dismiss someone, possibly rudely. _I couldn’t stand him anymore, so I sent him packing. _ The maid proved to be so incompetent that I had to send her packing.
examples: I couldn’t stand him anymore, so I sent him packing.

serve someone right.monolingual: [for an act or event] to punish someone fairly (for doing something). _John copied off my test paper. It would serve him right if he fails the test. _ It’d serve John right if he got arrested.
examples: John copied off my test paper.

serve time.monolingual: to spend a certain amount of time in jail. _ The criminal served ten years in jail. _ After the felon served his time, he was released from prison.
examples: The criminal served ten years in jail.

set for life.monolingual: prepared to exist for the rest of one’s life; having adequate supplies for the rest of one’s life. _ As soon as I win the lottery, I will be set for life. I’ll never have to work again!
examples: As soon as I win the lottery, I will be set for life.

set in.monolingual: to begin; to become fixed for a period of time. _ A severe cold spell set in early in November. _When high temperatures set in, the use of electricity went up considerably.
examples: A severe cold spell set in early in November.

set the record straight.monolingual: Fig. to put right a mistake or misunderstanding; to make sure that an account, etc., is correct. _The manager thought Jean was to blame, but she soon set the record straight. _Jane’s mother heard that Tom is a married man, but he set the record strai
examples: The manager thought Jean was to blame, but she soon set the record straight.

set the world on fire.monolingual: Fig. to do exciting things that bring fame and glory. (Frequently with the negative.) _I’m not very ambitious. I don’t want to set the world on fire. _ You don’t have to set the world on fire. Just do a good job.
examples: I’m not very ambitious.

set to.monolingual: to begin to fight; to attack or commence someone or something. _The two boys set to almost as soon as they met each other. _They set to and fought for about ten minutes, cursing and screaming.
examples: The two boys set to almost as soon as they met each other.

settle down.monolingual: 1. to calm down. _ Now, children, it’s time to settle down and start class. _ If you don’t settle down, I’ll send you all home.
examples: Now, children, it’s time to settle down and start class.

settle in.monolingual: to become accustomed to one’s new surroundings; to get used to living in a place or a new dwelling. _ I need a little time to settle in, then I can think about buying a car.
examples: I need a little time to settle in, then I can think about buying a car.

shake a leg.monolingual: 1. to hurry; to move faster. (Often as a command.) _ Let’s shake a leg, you guys. We gotta be there in twenty minutes. _ She told me to shake a leg, so I hurried the best I could.
examples: Let’s shake a leg, you guys.

shape up.monolingual: 1. to improve; to reform. _ I want to get things shaped up around here. _ I guess I’d better shape up if I want to stay in school.
examples: I want to get things shaped up around here.

share and share alike.monolingual: Cliché having or taking equal shares. _I kept five and gave the other five to Mary—share and share alike. _ The two roommates agreed that they would divide expenses—share and share alike.
examples: I kept five and gave the other five to Mary—share and share alike.

shoot oneself in the foot.monolingual: Fig. to cause oneself difficulty; to be the author of one’s own misfortune. _ I am a master at shooting myself in the foot. _ Again, he shot himself in the foot by saying too much to the press.
examples: I am a master at shooting myself in the foot.

shoot the breeze.monolingual: Fig. to chat casually and without purpose. _ We spent the entire afternoon just shooting the breeze. _ It was good to shoot the breeze with you, Mary.
examples: We spent the entire afternoon just shooting the breeze.

shoot up.monolingual: Sl. to take drugs by injection. _ Wallace was caught by the cops shooting up in the high school rest room.
examples: Wallace was caught by the cops shooting up in the high school rest room.

show off.monolingual: to do things in a way that is meant to attract attention. _Please stop showing off! You embarrass me. _ John is always showing off to his girlfriend.
examples: Please stop showing off! You embarrass me.

show up.monolingual: to appear; to arrive. _ Where is John? I hope he shows up soon. _ When will the bus show up? _ Weeds began to show up in the garden.
examples: Where is John? I hope he shows up soon.

shuffle off this mortal coil.monolingual: Euph. to die. (Often jocular or formal euphemism. Not often used in consoling someone.) _Cousin Fred shuff led off this mortal coil after suffering a heart attack. _ When I shuff le off this mortal coil, I want to go out in style—bells, f lowers, and
examples: Cousin Fred shuff led off this mortal coil after suffering a heart attack.

sign in.monolingual: to indicate that one has arrived somewhere and at what time by signing a piece of paper or a list. _ Please sign in so we will know you are here. _ Did you remember to sign in this time?
examples: Please sign in so we will know you are here.
