sign off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a broadcaster] to announce the end of programming for the day; [for an amateur radio operator] to announce the end of a transmission. _Wally signed off and turned the transmitter off. _ Channel 43 failed to sign off at the scheduled time
examples: Wally signed off and turned the transmitter off.

sign on.monolingual: to announce the beginning of a broadcast transmission. _The announcer signed on and then played “The Star-Spangled Banner.” _ We usually sign on at six in the morning.
examples: The announcer signed on and then played “The Star-Spangled Banner.

sign on the dotted line.monolingual: 1. Lit. to indicate one’s agreement or assent by placing one’s signature on a special line provided for that purpose. (The line may be solid or dotted.) _ I agreed to the contract, but I haven’t signed on the dotted line yet. _When you have signed on
examples: I agreed to the contract, but I haven’t signed on the dotted line yet.

sign out.monolingual: to indicate that one is leaving a place or going out temporarily by signing a piece of paper or a list. _ I forgot to sign out when I left. _ Please sign out every time you leave.
examples: I forgot to sign out when I left.

silt up.monolingual: [for a body of water] to become filled with silt. _ The river moved too fast to silt up. _ The lake silted up in a very few years.
examples: The river moved too fast to silt up.

simmer down.monolingual: 1. Lit. to decrease in intensity. (As boiling dies down when the heat is lowered or removed.) _ The hectic activity of the day finally simmered down. _ When things simmer down in the fall, this is a much nicer place.
examples: The hectic activity of the day finally simmered down.

sing out.monolingual: to sing louder. _ Sing out, please. This is a very large hall. _ The sopranos will have to sing out more.
examples: Sing out, please.

sink in.monolingual: 1. Lit. to sink, submerge, or descend into something. _ How long will it take the water to sink in? _ It might take days for the oil to sink in, so you have time to clean it up.
examples: It might take days for the oil to sink in, so you have time to clean it up.

sit around.monolingual: to relax sitting; to waste time sitting. _ Don’t just sit around! Get moving! _ I need to sit around every now and then and reorganize my thoughts.
examples: I need to sit around every now and then and reorganize my thoughts.

sit back.monolingual: to push oneself back in one’s seat; to lean against the back of one’s seat. _ Please sit back. I can’t see around you. _ I sat back and made myself comfortable, assuming that the movie would bore me to sleep.
examples: Please sit back.

sit down.monolingual: to be seated; to sit on something, such as a chair. _ Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. _ Can I sit down here?
examples: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

sit on the fence.monolingual: Fig. not to take sides in a dispute; not to make a clear choice between two possibilities. (Fig. on the image of someone straddling a fence, representing indecision.) _When Jane and Tom argue, it is best to sit on the fence and not make either of the
examples: When Jane and Tom argue, it is best to sit on the fence and not make either of them angry.

sit out.monolingual: to elect not to participate in something. _ I think I will not join in this game. I’ll sit out. _ I’ll sit out for this round.
examples: I think I will not join in this game.

sit tight.monolingual: to wait; to wait patiently. (This does not necessarily refer to sitting.) _Just relax and sit tight. I’ll be right with you. _ We were waiting in line for the gates to open when someone came out and told us to sit tight because it wouldn’t be much lo
examples: Just relax and sit tight.

sit up.monolingual: 1. to rise from a lying to a sitting position. _ When the alarm went off, he sat up and put his feet on the f loor. _ She couldn’t sleep, so she sat up and read a book.
examples: When the alarm went off, he sat up and put his feet on the f loor.

six feet under.monolingual: Fig. dead and buried. _ Fred died and is six feet under. _They put him six feet under two days after he died.
examples: Fred died and is six feet under.

skate around.monolingual: to skate here and there in no particular direction. _ Let’s go over to the pond and skate around. _ We will skate around for a while until we get too cold.
examples: Let’s go over to the pond and skate around.

skate on thin ice.monolingual: Fig. to be in a risky situation. (Fig. on the image of someone taking the risk of ice skating on thin ice.) _ I try to stay well informed so I don’t end up skating on thin ice when the teacher asks me a question. _ You are skating on thin ice when yo
examples: I try to stay well informed so I don’t end up skating on thin ice when the teacher asks me a question.

skip rope.monolingual: to jump over an arc of rope that is swung beneath one’s feet then over one’s head, repeatedly. _The children skipped rope on the playground. _ The boxer skipped rope while training.
examples: The children skipped rope on the playground.

slack off.monolingual: 1. to taper off; to reduce gradually. _ Business tends to slack off during the winter months. _ The storms begin to slack off in April.
examples: Business tends to slack off during the winter months.

slam dunk.monolingual: 1. Lit. [in basketball] a goal scored by shooting the ball down from above the rim. _He was wide open and scored on an easy slam dunk.
examples: He was wide open and scored on an easy slam dunk.

sleep in.monolingual: to oversleep; to sleep late in the morning. _If you sleep in again, you’ll get fired. _ I really felt like sleeping in this morning.
examples: If you sleep in again, you’ll get fired.

sleep out.monolingual: to sleep outside or away from one’s home. _ Can I sleep out tonight? _ Didn’t you sleep out last night?

sleep together.monolingual: 1. [for two or more people] to share a bed. _ Do you mean that Fred and Dave have to sleep together? _My brother and I used to have to sleep together.
examples: My brother and I used to have to sleep together.

slim down.monolingual: to become thinner; to lose weight. _You have really slimmed down a lot since I last saw you. _ I need to eat less so I can slim down. _ He slimmed down quite a bit after he had his health problem.
examples: You have really slimmed down a lot since I last saw you.

slip down.monolingual: to slide or glide downward. _ His socks kept slipping down. _ He lost so much weight that his pants almost slipped down.
examples: His socks kept slipping down.

slip out.monolingual: 1. [for someone] to exit quietly without bothering anyone. _ I slipped out during intermission.
examples: I slipped out during intermission.

slip up.monolingual: to make an error. _ I hope you don’t slip up again. Try to be more careful.
examples: I hope you don’t slip up again.

slow down.monolingual: to decrease speed; to go slower. _Please slow down. You are going too fast.
examples: Please slow down.

slow off the mark.monolingual: 1. Lit. slow in starting or reacting. (Compare this with quick off the mark.) _ If you are always that slow off the mark you will never win the race. _ Boy, you were slow off the mark there!
examples: If you are always that slow off the mark you will never win the race.

slow up.monolingual: to go slower; to reduce speed in order for someone or something to catch up. _ Slow up a little! I can’t keep up with you! _ Please slow up. I can’t follow your lecture when you talk so fast.
examples: Please slow up.

slug it out.monolingual: to fight something out; to argue intensely about something. _ They finally went outside to slug it out. _ We’ll just have to sit down in the conference room and slug it out.
examples: They finally went outside to slug it out.

slump down.monolingual: [for someone] to collapse and fall down; [for someone] to crumple. _The shot hit Max and he slumped down. _ Suddenly, Mr. Wilson slumped down in pain.
examples: The shot hit Max and he slumped down.

slush up.monolingual: to become messy with slush. _ As the winter storm increases in intensity, the roads will slush up and become impassable. _ After an hour of snow and rain, the roads were so slushed up that we could not travel.
examples: As the winter storm increases in intensity, the roads will slush up and become impassable.

small change.monolingual: Fig. an insignificant person. (Also a rude term of address.) _Look, small change, why don’t you just move along? _ The guy you think is small change happens to own this building you seem to be guarding so well.
examples: The guy you think is small change happens to own this building you seem to be guarding so well.

small fry.monolingual: 1. Lit. newly hatched fish; small, juvenile fish. _ The catch was bad today. Nothing but small fry.
examples: The catch was bad today.

small potatoes.monolingual: something or someone insignificant; small fry. _ This contract is small potatoes, but it keeps us in business till we get into the real money. _Small potatoes are better than no potatoes at all.
examples: This contract is small potatoes, but it keeps us in business till we get into the real money.

smarten up.monolingual: to get smarter; to become more alert and knowing. _ You had better smarten up if you want to survive around here. _ I knew he would smarten up sooner or later.
examples: You had better smarten up if you want to survive around here.

smell a rat.monolingual: to suspect that something is wrong; to sense that someone has caused something wrong. _I don’t think this was an accident. I smell a rat. Bob had something to do with this. _ The minute I came in, I smelled a rat. Sure enough, I had been robbed.
examples: I don’t think this was an accident.

smell blood.monolingual: Fig. to be ready for a fight; to be ready to attack; to be ready to act. (Like sharks, which are sent into a frenzy by the smell of blood.) _ Lefty was surrounded, and you could tell that the guys from the other gang smelled blood. _ The lawyer heard
examples: Lefty was surrounded, and you could tell that the guys from the other gang smelled blood.

smell fishy.monolingual: to seem suspicious. _ Barlowe squinted a bit. Something smells fishy here, he thought. _Something about the deal smelled fishy—too good to be true.
examples: Barlowe squinted a bit.

smell like a rose.monolingual: Fig. to seem innocent. _ I came out of the whole mess smelling like a rose, even though I caused all the trouble. _ The politician survived the scandal smelling like a rose, but I knew different.
examples: I came out of the whole mess smelling like a rose, even though I caused all the trouble.

smoke like a chimney.monolingual: to smoke a great deal of tobacco or other smokable substances. _ My uncle smoked like a chimney when he was living. _ Somebody who smokes like a chimney in a restaurant ought to be thrown out.
examples: My uncle smoked like a chimney when he was living.

smoke-filled room.monolingual: a room where a small group of people make important decisions. (Usually used in reference to political parties.) _The smoke-filled rooms are still producing the candidates for most offices, despite all the political reforms. _ The deal was cut in a s
examples: The smoke-filled rooms are still producing the candidates for most offices, despite all the political reforms.

snowed under.monolingual: overworked; exceptionally busy. _ Look, I’m really snowed under at the moment. Can this wait? _ He really has been snowed under with work.
examples: Look, I’m really snowed under at the moment.

soaked to the skin.monolingual: wet clear through one’s clothing to the skin. _ I was caught in the rain and got soaked to the skin. _ Oh, come in and dry off! You must be soaked to the skin.
examples: I was caught in the rain and got soaked to the skin.

sob story.monolingual: Fig. a sad story that is likely to draw tears. _I’ve heard nothing but sob stories today. Isn’t anybody happy? _ She had quite a sob story, and I listened to the whole thing.
examples: I’ve heard nothing but sob stories today.

sober up.monolingual: to recover from alcohol or drug intoxication. _ Barlowe had one hour to sober up and get to the station. _ It took him a while to sober up.
examples: Barlowe had one hour to sober up and get to the station.

soft touch.monolingual: 1. a gentle way of handling someone or something. _ Bess has a soft touch and can bring both sides together. _Kelly lacks the kind of soft touch needed for this kind of negotiation.
examples: Bess has a soft touch and can bring both sides together.

soften up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to become softer. _The butter softened up in the heat of the day. _ The candles will probably soften up and bend over in this hot weather.
examples: The butter softened up in the heat of the day.

sort oneself out.monolingual: to pull oneself together; to figure out what to do about one’s problems. (Fig. on sort something out W.) _ I need a few days to sort myself out. _ I need some time to sort myself out.
examples: I need a few days to sort myself out.

sound asleep.monolingual: completely asleep; in a deep sleep. _ I was sound asleep when the fire broke out.
examples: I was sound asleep when the fire broke out.

sound off.monolingual: to speak something loudly; to call out one’s name or one’s place in a numerical sequence. _ All right, sound off, you guys! _ Each one sounded off.
examples: Each one sounded off.

sour grapes.monolingual: Fig. something that one cannot have and so disparages as if it were never desirable. _ Of course you want to buy this expensive jacket. Criticizing it is just sour grapes, but you still really want it.
examples: Of course you want to buy this expensive jacket.

space out.monolingual: to become giddy or disoriented. _ Judy spaced out during the meeting and I didn’t understand a word she said. _ I have a tendency to space out at the end of a hard day.
examples: Judy spaced out during the meeting and I didn’t understand a word she said.

spaz out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to overreact to something; to become overly excited about something. _ I knew you would spaz out! But my grades are not that bad! _Come on, don’t spaz out!
examples: Come on, don’t spaz out! 2.

speak for oneself.monolingual: to speak on one’s own behalf. _ I can speak for myself. I don’t need you to speak for me. _ Speak for yourself. What you say does not represent my thinking.
examples: I can speak for myself.

speak out.monolingual: to speak loudly; to speak to be heard. _ Please speak out. We need to hear you. _They won’t hear you in the back row if you don’t speak out.
examples: Please speak out.

speak up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to speak more loudly. _ They can’t hear you in the back of the room. Please speak up. _What? Speak up, please. I’m hard of hearing.
examples: They can’t hear you in the back of the room.

speak with a forked tongue.monolingual: Fig. to tell lies; to try to deceive someone. _ Jean’s mother sounds very charming, but she speaks with a forked tongue. _People tend to believe Fred because he seems plausible, but we know he speaks with a forked tongue.
examples: Jean’s mother sounds very charming, but she speaks with a forked tongue.

speed up.monolingual: to go faster. _ Please speed up. We are late.
examples: Please speed up.

spill over.monolingual: 1. [for a container] to overflow. _ I hope your bucket of water doesn’t spill over. _ The milk glass spilled over because it was filled too full.
examples: I hope your bucket of water doesn’t spill over.

spin a yarn.monolingual: Fig. to tell a tale. _ Grandpa spun an unbelievable yarn for us. _ My uncle is always spinning yarns about his childhood.
examples: Grandpa spun an unbelievable yarn for us.

spin doctor.monolingual: someone who gives a twisted or deviously deceptive version of an event. (Usually in the context of manipulating the news for political reasons.) _ Things were going bad for the candidate, so he got himself a new spin doctor. _A good spin doctor could
examples: Things were going bad for the candidate, so he got himself a new spin doctor.

spin off.monolingual: [for something] to part and fly away from something that is spinning; [for something] to detach or break loose from something. _ The blade of the lawn mower spun off, but fortunately no one was injured. _The rustedon nut spun off easily after I got i
examples: The blade of the lawn mower spun off, but fortunately no one was injured.

spin out.monolingual: [for a vehicle] to go out of control, spinning. _ You nearly spun out on that last turn! _Cars were spinning out all over the highway when the ice storm hit.
examples: Cars were spinning out all over the highway when the ice storm hit.

spit up.monolingual: Euph. to vomit. _ The food was so bad, she was afraid she would spit up. _ Mommy, I have to spit up!
examples: The food was so bad, she was afraid she would spit up.

splash down.monolingual: [for a space capsule] to land in the water. _ The capsule splashed down very close to the pickup ship.
examples: The capsule splashed down very close to the pickup ship.

split hairs.monolingual: Fig. to quibble; to try to make petty distinctions. _ They don’t have any serious differences. They are just splitting hairs. _ Don’t waste time splitting hairs. Accept it the way it is.
examples: They don’t have any serious differences.

split the difference.monolingual: to divide the difference evenly (with someone else). _ You want to sell for $120, and I want to buy for $100. Let’s split the difference and close the deal at $110. _ I don’t want to split the difference. I want $120.
examples: You want to sell for $120, and I want to buy for $100.

spread out.monolingual: to separate and distribute over a wide area. _ The sheriff told the members of the posse to spread out and continue their search. _The wine spread out and stained a large area of the carpet.
examples: The sheriff told the members of the posse to spread out and continue their search.

spread the word.monolingual: to tell many people some kind of information. _I need to spread the word that the meeting is canceled for this afternoon.
examples: I need to spread the word that the meeting is canceled for this afternoon.

spring to life.monolingual: Fig. to become suddenly alive or more alive. _The party sprang to life after midnight. _The city sprang to life at dawn.
examples: The party sprang to life after midnight.

spring up.monolingual: to appear or develop suddenly; to sprout, as with a seedling. _ We knew it was really spring when all the f lowers sprang up. _It seems as if the tulips sprang up overnight. _ The dog’s ears sprang up when the refrigerator opened.
examples: We knew it was really spring when all the f lowers sprang up.

sprout up.monolingual: to grow upward quickly, as do newly sprouted seedlings. _ The seeds sprouted up in the warm rains. _ Many of the newly planted seeds failed to sprout up on time.
examples: The seeds sprouted up in the warm rains.

sputter out.monolingual: [for a flame] to go out in little puffs. _ The candle f lame f lickered and sputtered out. _ The fire sputtered out after midnight and we all got very cold before down.
examples: The candle f lame f lickered and sputtered out.

stack up.monolingual: [for something] to accumulate, as in stacks. _ Your work is stacking up. You will have to work late to finish it. _I hate to let my work stack up. I have to do it sooner or later.
examples: Your work is stacking up.

stall for time.monolingual: to cause a delay intentionally. _You are just stalling for time. Please hurry. _ She is stalling for time, hoping someone will rescue her.
examples: You are just stalling for time.

stand and deliver.monolingual: to give up something to someone who demands it. (Originally used by highway robbers asking for passengers’ valuables.) _ And when the tax agent says “Stand and deliver” you have to be prepared to pay what is demanded. _The robber stopped the coach an
examples: And when the tax agent says “Stand and deliver” you have to be prepared to pay what is demanded.

stand around.monolingual: to wait around, standing; to loiter. _Please don’t stand around. Get busy! _ Why are all these people standing around doing nothing?
examples: Please don’t stand around.

stand aside.monolingual: 1. Lit. to step aside; to get out of the way. _ Please stand aside while the bridal party passes by. _ The guests stood aside while the bride and groom left.
examples: Please stand aside while the bridal party passes by.

stand by.monolingual: to wait and remain ready. (Generally heard in communication, such as broadcasting, telephones, etc.) _ Your transatlantic telephone call is almost ready. Please stand by. _ Is everyone ready for the telecast? Only ten seconds— stand by.
examples: Your transatlantic telephone call is almost ready.

stand corrected.monolingual: to admit that one has been wrong. _ I realize that I accused him wrongly. I stand corrected. _ We appreciate now that our conclusions were wrong. We stand corrected.
examples: I realize that I accused him wrongly.

stand down.monolingual: 1. to step down, particularly from the witness stand in a courtroom. _ The bailiff told the witness to stand down. _ Please stand down and take your seat.
examples: The bailiff told the witness to stand down.

stand on ceremony.monolingual: to hold rigidly to protocol or formal manners. (Often in the negative.) _Please help yourself to more. Don’t stand on ceremony. _We are very informal around here. Hardly anyone stands on ceremony.
examples: Please help yourself to more.

stand tall.monolingual: to be brave and proud. _ I can still stand tall. I’m innocent. _ Our athletes stand tall in the knowledge that they did their best.
examples: I can still stand tall.

stand the test of time.monolingual: Prov. to be well regarded; to last for a long time. _Bill and Nancy just celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary. Their marriage has stood the test of time. _The singer’s work was not popular while she was alive, but it has stood the test of ti
examples: Bill and Nancy just celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary.

stand to reason.monolingual: to seem reasonable. _ It stands to reason that it’ll be colder in January than it is in November. _ It stands to reason that Bill left in a hurry, although no one saw him go.
examples: It stands to reason that it’ll be colder in January than it is in November.

stand together.monolingual: 1. to stand in a group. _ All the members of the family stood together for a photograph. _Please stand together so I can count you.
examples: All the members of the family stood together for a photograph.

stand trial.monolingual: to be the accused person in a trial before a judge; to be on trial. _ He had to stand trial for perjury and obstruction of justice.
examples: He had to stand trial for perjury and obstruction of justice.

stand up.monolingual: 1. to arise from a sitting or reclining position. _He stood up and looked across the valley. _She had been sitting for so long that it was a pleasure to stand up.
examples: He stood up and looked across the valley.

stand up and be counted.monolingual: to state one’s support (for someone or something). _ If you believe in more government help for farmers, write your representative—stand up and be counted. _ I’m generally in favor of what you propose, but not enough to stand up and be counted.
examples: If you believe in more government help for farmers, write your representative—stand up and be counted.

start off.monolingual: to begin; to set out on a journey. _ When do you want to start off ? _ We will start off as soon as we can get everything packed.
examples: We will start off as soon as we can get everything packed.

start out.monolingual: to begin. _Whenever you are ready, we will start out. _ We can’t start out until Tom is here.
examples: Whenever you are ready, we will start out.

start over.monolingual: to begin again. _I have messed this up so much that there is nothing to do now but start over. _ When you start over, try to do it right this time.
examples: I have messed this up so much that there is nothing to do now but start over.

start up.monolingual: to begin; to begin running, as with an engine. _ The car started up without a problem. _The engines of the plane started up one by one.
examples: The car started up without a problem.

stay behind.monolingual: [for someone] to remain in a place when others have left. _ I will stay behind and tell the late arrivers where you have gone. _Fred always stayed behind to clean up.
examples: I will stay behind and tell the late arrivers where you have gone.

stay put.monolingual: not to move; to stay where one is. _We’ve decided to stay put and not to move to Florida. _If the children just stay put, their parents will come for them soon.
examples: We’ve decided to stay put and not to move to Florida.

steam up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to become covered with a film of steam or water vapor. _ The windows steamed up and we had to wipe them so we could see out. _ The window has steamed up, and I can’t see.
examples: The windows steamed up and we had to wipe them so we could see out.

step forward.monolingual: 1. Lit. to move forward one step or several steps. _ The volunteer stepped forward. _ I stepped forward and someone moved up behind me immediately.
examples: The volunteer stepped forward.

step off.monolingual: to come off something by taking a step. _ She came to the bottom step and stepped off. _ Ed was afraid to dive in from the side of the pool, so he just stepped off.
examples: She came to the bottom step and stepped off.

step up.monolingual: to increase. _ Industrial production stepped up a large amount this last quarter. _ Traffic has stepped up since the road was paved.
examples: Industrial production stepped up a large amount this last quarter.

step up to the plate.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a batter in baseball] to move near home plate in preparation for striking the ball when it is pitched. _The batter stepped up to the plate and glared at the pitcher.
examples: The batter stepped up to the plate and glared at the pitcher.

stick around.monolingual: [for a person] to remain in a place. _ The kids stuck around for a time after the party was over. _Oh, Ann. Please stick around for a while. I want to talk to you later.
examples: The kids stuck around for a time after the party was over.

stick out.monolingual: to project outward. _ You can’t lock your suitcase because there is a bit of cloth sticking out. _Some cloth stuck out of the top of the drawer.
examples: You can’t lock your suitcase because there is a bit of cloth sticking out.

stick out a mile.monolingual: Fig. to project outward very obviously. _My nose sticks out a mile! I hate it! _ His stomach sticks out a mile. What do you suppose is in there?
examples: His stomach sticks out a mile.

stick together.monolingual: 1. Lit. to adhere to one another. _ The noodles are sticking together. What shall I do? _ You need to keep the pieces separate while you fry them or else they will stick together.
examples: The noodles are sticking together.

stick up.monolingual: to stand upright or on end; to thrust upward. _ The ugly red f lower stuck up from the bouquet. _ Why is the worst-looking f lower sticking up above all the rest?
examples: The ugly red f lower stuck up from the bouquet.

stiffen up.monolingual: to become stiff. _ The bread dough stiffened up as it got cold. _ My knees began to stiffen up after I sat still for an hour.
examples: The bread dough stiffened up as it got cold.

stink on ice.monolingual: Sl. to be really rotten. (So rotten as to reek even when frozen.) _This show stinks on ice. _The whole idea stank on ice.
examples: This show stinks on ice.

stone dead.monolingual: Rur. dead; unquestionably dead; long dead. _ The cat was stone dead and stiff as a board by the time we got to him. _ Old Tom is stone dead and in the ground.
examples: The cat was stone dead and stiff as a board by the time we got to him.

stop up.monolingual: [for something] to become clogged. _ The sink stopped up again!

stow away.monolingual: to conceal oneself in a vehicle, originally a ship, in order to travel without paying. _ Don got to this country by stowing away on a cargo ship.
examples: Don got to this country by stowing away on a cargo ship.

straight from the shoulder.monolingual: Fig. very direct, without attenuation or embellishment. _ Okay, I’ll give it to you straight from the shoulder. _Right straight from the shoulder: clean out your desk; you’re through.
examples: Okay, I’ll give it to you straight from the shoulder.

straight man.monolingual: someone who sets up jokes or gags so that someone else can say the punch line. _ I need a straight man to set up all my jokes. _ I’m tired of being a straight man for a has-been comic.
examples: I need a straight man to set up all my jokes.

straight shooter.monolingual: Fig. an honest person. _ I trust Mike; he’s a straight shooter. _We need a straight shooter in office who will work for the people rather than some lobbyists.
examples: I trust Mike; he’s a straight shooter.

straighten out.monolingual: 1. to become straight. _ The road finally straightened out. _The train tracks straightened out on the plain.
examples: The road finally straightened out.

straighten up.monolingual: 1. to sit or stand more straight. _ Billy’s mother told him to straighten up or he’d fall out of his chair. _John straightened up so he’d look taller.
examples: Billy’s mother told him to straighten up or he’d fall out of his chair.

straighten up and fly right.monolingual: Fig. to improve one’s behavior or attitude and perform better. (Originally referred to an airplane.) _ If you want to keep out of trouble, you had better straighten up and f ly right. _ Straighten up and f ly right or I will send you to the principal
examples: If you want to keep out of trouble, you had better straighten up and f ly right.

strain at the leash.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a dog] to pull very hard on its leash. _ It’s hard to walk Fido, because he is always straining at the leash. _I wish that this dog would not strain at the leash. It’s very hard on me.
examples: It’s hard to walk Fido, because he is always straining at the leash.

stretch out.monolingual: [for one] to extend and stretch one’s body to its full length. _ She lay down, stretched out, and relaxed for the first time in days. _I need a bigger bed. I can’t stretch out in this one.
examples: She lay down, stretched out, and relaxed for the first time in days.

strike it rich.monolingual: to acquire wealth suddenly. _If I could strike it rich, I wouldn’t have to work anymore. _ Sally ordered a dozen oysters and found a huge pearl in one of them. She struck it rich!
examples: If I could strike it rich, I wouldn’t have to work anymore.

strike out.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a baseball batter] to be declared out after making three strikes. (Baseball.) _And so Drew Wilson strikes out for his second time in this game! _He struck out in the second inning, and the manager took him out then.
examples: He struck out in the second inning, and the manager took him out then.

strip down.monolingual: to remove one’s clothing. _ The doctor told Joe to strip down for his examination. _ Joe stripped down for the examination.
examples: The doctor told Joe to strip down for his examination.

strung out.monolingual: 1. extended in time; overly long. _ Why was that lecture so strung out? She talked and talked. _ It was strung out because there was very little to be said.
examples: Why was that lecture so strung out? She talked and talked.

stuff the ballot box.monolingual: to fill a ballot box with illegal votes or with more votes than the number of actual voters. _ The politician was charged with stuffing the ballot box. _ The ballot box was stuffed with lots of votes for the crooked politician.
examples: The politician was charged with stuffing the ballot box.

swan song.monolingual: Fig. the last work or performance of a playwright, musician, actor, etc., before death or retirement. _ His portrayal of Lear was the actor’s swan song. _ We didn’t know that her performance last night was the singer’s swan song.
examples: His portrayal of Lear was the actor’s swan song.

sweep along.monolingual: to glide along smoothly, as if flying. _ The sailboat swept along, pushed by the strong wind. _ The fallen leaves blew up against the fence, swept along by a strong wind.
examples: The sailboat swept along, pushed by the strong wind.

sweep up.monolingual: to clean up by sweeping. _ Would you sweep up this time? _ Please give me a few minutes to sweep up before you come to visit.
examples: Please give me a few minutes to sweep up before you come to visit.

sweet nothings.monolingual: affectionate but unimportant or meaningless words spoken to a loved one. _ Jack was whispering sweet nothings in Joan’s ear when they were dancing. _ The two lovers sat in the cinema exchanging sweet nothings.
examples: Jack was whispering sweet nothings in Joan’s ear when they were dancing.

sweeten the pot.monolingual: Fig. to increase the amount of money bet in a card game with hopes of encouraging other players to bet more enthusiastically. _ John sweetened the pot hoping others would follow.
examples: John sweetened the pot hoping others would follow.

swell out.monolingual: to bulge outward; to expand outward. _ The sides of the box swelled out because it was too full. _ The west wall of the garage swelled out just before the building collapsed.
examples: The sides of the box swelled out because it was too full.

swell up.monolingual: to enlarge; to inflate; to bulge out. _ I struck my thumb with a hammer and it swelled up something awful.
examples: I struck my thumb with a hammer and it swelled up something awful.

switch off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to turn itself off. _ At midnight, all the lights switched off automatically. _ The television switched off after I went to sleep.
examples: At midnight, all the lights switched off automatically.

switch on.monolingual: 1. [for something] to turn itself on. _ Exactly at midnight, the lights switched on. _ The radio switched on early in the morning to wake us up.
examples: Exactly at midnight, the lights switched on.

tail off.monolingual: to dwindle to nothing. _The number of people filing for unemployment insurance is beginning to tail off. _ As the storms tailed off, we began to realize how much damage had been done.
examples: The number of people filing for unemployment insurance is beginning to tail off.

take a bow.monolingual: to bow and acknowledge credit for a good performance. _At the end of the concerto, the pianist rose and took a bow. _ The audience applauded wildly and demanded that the conductor come out and take a bow again.
examples: At the end of the concerto, the pianist rose and took a bow.

take a nap.monolingual: to have a brief period of sleep. _I took a short nap just after lunch. _The baby takes a long nap each afternoon.
examples: I took a short nap just after lunch.

take a powder.monolingual: Sl. to leave; to leave town. (Underworld.) _ Why don’t you take a powder? Go on! Beat it! _ Willie took a powder and will lie low for a while.
examples: Willie took a powder and will lie low for a while.

take cover.monolingual: to seek shelter from gunfire or other projectiles. _ As soon as the firing started, we took cover behind a huge boulder.
examples: As soon as the firing started, we took cover behind a huge boulder.

take it on the lam.monolingual: Sl. to get out of town; to run away. (Underworld.) _ Both crooks took it on the lam when things got hot. _Walt knew that the time had come to take it on the lam.
examples: Both crooks took it on the lam when things got hot.

take no prisoners.monolingual: 1. Lit. to kill the enemy rather than seize the enemy as prisoners. _ The soldiers’ orders were to take no prisoners.
examples: The soldiers’ orders were to take no prisoners.

take off.monolingual: 1. Fig. to leave the ground and begin to fly. (As with a bird or an airplane.) _ When do we take off ? _ The eagle took off and headed toward the mountains.
examples: The eagle took off and headed toward the mountains.

take sides.monolingual: to choose one side of an argument. _ They were arguing, but I didn’t want to take sides, so I left. _ I don’t mind taking sides on important issues.
examples: They were arguing, but I didn’t want to take sides, so I left.

take the cure.monolingual: to enter into any treatment program or treatment center. (Especially those dealing with drugs and alcohol.) _ I wanted to take the cure, but I just couldn’t bring myself to do it. _ It’s hard to get those addicted to realize that they are the ones wh
examples: I wanted to take the cure, but I just couldn’t bring myself to do it.

take the fall.monolingual: Sl. to get arrested for a particular crime. (Especially when others are going unpunished for the same crime. _ Walt and Tony pulled the job off together, but Tony took the fall. _You did it, and I won’t take the fall!
examples: Walt and Tony pulled the job off together, but Tony took the fall.

take the plunge.monolingual: to marry someone. _ I’m not ready to take the plunge yet. _ Sam and Mary took the plunge.
examples: I’m not ready to take the plunge yet.

take the stand.monolingual: to go to and sit in the witness chair in a courtroom. _ I was in court all day, waiting to take the stand. _ The lawyer asked the witness to take the stand.
examples: I was in court all day, waiting to take the stand.

take time out.monolingual: to spend time away from studying or working. _ He’s taking time out between high school and starting at the university. _Mary’s taking time out from her job to work abroad for a year.
examples: He’s taking time out between high school and starting at the university.

talk a blue streak.monolingual: Fig. to talk very much and very rapidly. _ Billy didn’t talk until he was two, and then he started talking a blue streak. _ I can’t understand anything Bob says. He talks a blue streak, and I can’t follow his thinking.
examples: Billy didn’t talk until he was two, and then he started talking a blue streak.

talk in circles.monolingual: Fig. to talk in a confusing or roundabout manner. _I couldn’t understand a thing he said. All he did was talk in circles. _We argued for a long time and finally decided that we were talking in circles.
examples: I couldn’t understand a thing he said.

talk turkey.monolingual: Fig. to talk business; to talk frankly. _ Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss. Let’s talk turkey. _ John wanted to talk turkey, but Jane just wanted to joke around.
examples: Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss.

tap out.monolingual: 1. Sl. to lose one’s money in gambling or in the securities markets. _I’m gonna tap out in about three more rolls—just watch. _ I really tapped out on that gold-mining stock.
examples: I’m gonna tap out in about three more rolls—just watch.

teach someone a lesson.monolingual: to get even with someone for bad behavior. _John tripped me, so I punched him. That ought to teach him a lesson. _ That taught me a lesson. I won’t do it again.
examples: John tripped me, so I punched him.

tear along.monolingual: to go along very fast, as in running, driving, cycling, etc. _The cars tore along the road, raising dust and making noise. _ Andy tore along on his bicycle, trying to see how fast he could go.
examples: The cars tore along the road, raising dust and making noise.

tee off.monolingual: 1. Lit. to start the first hole in a game of golf. _ It’s time to tee off. Let’s get on the course. _ What time do we tee off ?
examples: It’s time to tee off.

teed off.monolingual: Inf. angry. _I’m not teed off! I’m enraged. _I was so teed off I could have spit!
examples: I’m not teed off! I’m enraged.

teething troubles.monolingual: 1. Lit. pain and crying on the part of a baby whose teeth are growing in. _Billy has been whining because of teething troubles.
examples: Billy has been whining because of teething troubles.

tell all.monolingual: to tell everything, even the secrets. _Some reporter got hold of the actress’s maid who offered to tell all for a fee.
examples: Some reporter got hold of the actress’s maid who offered to tell all for a fee.

tell tales out of school.monolingual: to tell secrets or spread rumors. _ I wish that John would keep quiet. He’s telling tales out of school again. _ If you tell tales out of school a lot, people won’t know when to believe you.
examples: I wish that John would keep quiet.

thanks a bunch.monolingual: Inf. thanks. _ Thanks a bunch for your help. _ He said “thanks a bunch” and walked out.
examples: Thanks a bunch for your help.

thaw out.monolingual: to warm up from being frozen. _How long will it take for the chicken to thaw out? _I can’t wait for the cake to thaw out. I want some now!
examples: I can’t wait for the cake to thaw out.

then and there.monolingual: Cliché right at that time and place. _ I asked him right then and there exactly what he meant. _ I decided to settle the matter then and there and not wait until Monday.
examples: I asked him right then and there exactly what he meant.

thin down.monolingual: to become thinner or slimmer. _ He stopped eating desserts and fatty foods so he could thin down. _ I have to thin down so I can get into my winter coat.
examples: He stopped eating desserts and fatty foods so he could thin down.

thin out.monolingual: to spread out; to become less dense. _ The trees began to thin out as we got higher up the mountain. _ The crowd began to thin out as we got a little farther from the theater.
examples: The trees began to thin out as we got higher up the mountain.

think for oneself.monolingual: to do one’s own thinking; to think independently. _ I think for myself. I don’t need anyone to tell me what to do, do I? _ Sam has to learn to think for himself. He can’t let other people make his decisions for him all his life.
examples: I think for myself.

think out loud.monolingual: Fig. to say one’s thoughts aloud. _Excuse me. I didn’t really mean to say that. I was just thinking out loud. _ Mr. Johnson didn’t prepare a speech. He just stood there and thought out loud. It was a terrible presentation.
examples: Excuse me. I didn’t really mean to say that.

through thick and thin.monolingual: Cliché through good times and bad times. _ We’ve been together through thick and thin, and we won’t desert each other now. _ Over the years, we went through thick and thin and enjoyed every minute of it.
examples: We’ve been together through thick and thin, and we won’t desert each other now.

throw a tantrum.monolingual: to have a temper tantrum; to put on an active display of childish temper. _ I never dreamed that Bob would throw a tantrum right there in the department store. You must be so embarrassed!
examples: I never dreamed that Bob would throw a tantrum right there in the department store.

throw caution to the wind.monolingual: Cliché to become very careless. _ Jane, who is usually cautious, threw caution to the wind and went swimming in the ocean. _I don’t mind taking a little chance now and then, but I’m not the type of person who throws caution to the wind.
examples: Jane, who is usually cautious, threw caution to the wind and went swimming in the ocean.

throw down the gauntlet.monolingual: Fig. to challenge someone to an argument or to (figurative) combat. _When Bob chal- lenged my conclusions, he threw down the gauntlet. I was ready for an argument. _ Frowning at Bob is the same as throwing down the gauntlet. He loves to get into a fi
examples: When Bob chal- lenged my conclusions, he threw down the gauntlet.

throw good money after bad.monolingual: Fig. to waste additional money after wasting money once. _ I bought a used car and then had to spend $300 on repairs. That was throwing good money after bad. _ The Browns are always throwing good money after bad. They bought an acre of land that turn
examples: I bought a used car and then had to spend $300 on repairs.

throw up.monolingual: to vomit. _ I was afraid I would throw up, the food was so horrible. _This food is bad enough to make you throw up.
examples: I was afraid I would throw up, the food was so horrible.

thrust out.monolingual: to stick out; to stab outward; to protrude outward. _A deck thrust out from the back of the house, offering a lovely view of the stream far below. _ As he grew angrier, his chin thrust out farther and farther.
examples: A deck thrust out from the back of the house, offering a lovely view of the stream far below.

tick away.monolingual: [for seconds or minutes] to go by as the clock ticks. _ The seconds ticked away as the fateful time got closer. _ As time ticked away, the surgeons worked feverishly to repair the walls of Roger’s heart.
examples: The seconds ticked away as the fateful time got closer.

tickled pink.monolingual: Fig. very much pleased or entertained. _ I was tickled pink to have you visit us. _We were tickled pink when your f lowers arrived.
examples: I was tickled pink to have you visit us.

tidy up.monolingual: to clean up [oneself or a place]. _ Please tidy up. This place is a mess. _ Please tidy up. You are a mess.
examples: Please tidy up.

tie the knot.monolingual: 1. Fig. to marry a mate. _ We tied the knot in a little chapel on the Arkansas border. _They finally tied the knot.
examples: We tied the knot in a little chapel on the Arkansas border.

tighten up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to get tighter. _ The door hinges began to tighten up, making the door hard to open and close. _ His grip around the handle tightened up and he refused to let go.
examples: The door hinges began to tighten up, making the door hard to open and close.

tilt at windmills.monolingual: Fig. to fight battles with imaginary enemies; to fight against unimportant enemies or issues. (As with the fictional character, Don Quixote, who attacked windmills.) _ Aren’t you too smart to go around tilting at windmills? _ I’m not going to fight t
examples: I’m not going to fight this issue.

time in.monolingual: to record one’s arrival time. _ Did you remember to time in this morning? _ When did she time in?

time out.monolingual: 1. to record one’s departure time. _ Did you remember to time out when you left work? _I timed out at the regular time.
examples: I timed out at the regular time.

tip over.monolingual: to topple over and fall. _ Roger shook the table slightly, and the vase tipped over. _ The truck was overloaded and looked so heavy that I thought it would tip over.
examples: Roger shook the table slightly, and the vase tipped over.

tire out.monolingual: to become exhausted. _ I tire out easily. _ When I had the f lu, I found that I tired out easily.
examples: I tire out easily.

to and fro.monolingual: [of movement] toward and away from something. _The puppy was very active—running to and fro— wagging its tail. _ The lion in the cage moved to and fro, watching the people in front of the cage.
examples: The puppy was very active—running to and fro— wagging its tail.

to beat the band.monolingual: very briskly; very fast. _ He’s selling computers to beat the band since he started advertising. _ She worked to beat the band to get ready for this.
examples: He’s selling computers to beat the band since he started advertising.

to boot.monolingual: in addition. _For graduation, I got a new suit and a coat to boot. _She got an F on her term paper and flunked the final to boot.
examples: For graduation, I got a new suit and a coat to boot.

to date.monolingual: up to the present time. _ How much have you accomplished to date? _ I’ve done everything I’m supposed to have done to date.
examples: I’ve done everything I’m supposed to have done to date.

to die for.monolingual: Sl. important or desirable enough to die for; worth dying for. _ This chocolate cake is to die for! _ We had a beautiful room at the hotel and the service was to die for.
examples: We had a beautiful room at the hotel and the service was to die for.

to say the least.monolingual: at the very least; without overemphasizing the subject; to put it mildly. _ We were not at all pleased with her work—to say the least. _ When they had an accident, they were upset to say the least.
examples: We were not at all pleased with her work—to say the least.

to the letter.monolingual: exactly as instructed; exactly as written. _ I didn’t make an error. I followed your instruction to the letter. _We didn’t prepare the recipe to the letter, but the cake still turned out very well.
examples: I didn’t make an error.

to the max.monolingual: Sl. as much as possible, maximally. _ She is happy to the max. _ They worked to the max their whole shift.
examples: She is happy to the max.

to the nth degree.monolingual: to the maximum amount. _ Jane is a perfectionist and tries to be careful to the nth degree. _This scientific instrument is accurate to the nth degree.
examples: Jane is a perfectionist and tries to be careful to the nth degree.

too little, too late.monolingual: Prov. Not enough help to save the situation, and arriving too late. _After a lifetime of bad diet and no exercise, Lorna tried to save her health by improving her habits, but it was too little, too late. _ Fred: I know how to keep my business from go
examples: After a lifetime of bad diet and no exercise, Lorna tried to save her health by improving her habits, but it was too little, too late.

tool up.monolingual: to become equipped with tools. _ I need some money so I can tool up to do the job. _ The factory tooled up to make the new cars in only two weeks.
examples: I need some money so I can tool up to do the job.

top notch.monolingual: the absolute best. (Hyphenated before a nominal.) _Julie’s singing in the musical is top notch. _He prepared a top-notch meal before the movie and dessert for afterward.
examples: Julie’s singing in the musical is top notch.

topple over.monolingual: [for something very tall] to fall over. _I was afraid that Jimmy’s stack of blocks would topple over. _The stack of books toppled over and ended up as a jumbled mess on the f loor.
examples: I was afraid that Jimmy’s stack of blocks would topple over.

touch down.monolingual: [for an airplane] to come in contact with the ground; to land. _ Flight twelve is due to touch down at midnight. _ When will this plane touch down?
examples: Flight twelve is due to touch down at midnight.

tough going.monolingual: progress that is difficult. _It was tough going for the first few miles, but the trail became much easier as we got farther into the forest.
examples: It was tough going for the first few miles, but the trail became much easier as we got farther into the forest.

toughen up.monolingual: to become tougher, stronger, or more severe. _ She will toughen up after a while. You have to be tough around here to survive. _ You are going to have to toughen up if you want to play on the team.
examples: She will toughen up after a while.

trial balloon.monolingual: a test of someone’s or the public’s reaction. _It was just a trial balloon, and it didn’t work. _The trial balloon was a great success.
examples: It was just a trial balloon, and it didn’t work.

trials and tribulations.monolingual: Cliché problems and tests of one’s courage or perseverance. _I suppose I have the normal trials and tribulations for a person of my background, but some days are just a little too much for me. _ I promise not to tell you of the trials and tribulation
examples: I suppose I have the normal trials and tribulations for a person of my background, but some days are just a little too much for me.

true to form.monolingual: exactly as expected; following the usual pattern. (Often with running, as in the example.) _As usual, John is late. At least he’s running true to form. _ And true to form, Mary left before the meeting was adjourned.
examples: As usual, John is late.

tumble down.monolingual: to fall down; to topple. _The old barn was so rickety that it almost tumbled down on its own. _ The pile of books tumbled down all over the f loor.
examples: The old barn was so rickety that it almost tumbled down on its own.

tune out.monolingual: Fig. to cease paying attention to anything at all. _I wasn’t interested, so I just tuned out. _I think that most of the audience tuned out during the last part of the lecture.
examples: I wasn’t interested, so I just tuned out.

tune up.monolingual: [for one or more musicians] to bring their instruments into tune. _ You could hear the orchestra behind the curtain, tuning up. _We have to tune up before the concert.
examples: You could hear the orchestra behind the curtain, tuning up.

tuned in.monolingual: aware; up-to-date. _ Jan is tuned in and alert to what is going on around her. _ Hey, Jill! Get tuned in, why don’t you?
examples: Jan is tuned in and alert to what is going on around her.

turn a profit.monolingual: to earn a profit. _The company plans to turn a profit two years from now.
examples: The company plans to turn a profit two years from now.

turn a trick.monolingual: Sl. to perform an act of prostitution. (Use caution with the topic.) _ She can turn a trick and be on the streets again in six minutes f lat. _She’s upstairs, turning a trick.
examples: She can turn a trick and be on the streets again in six minutes f lat.

turn in.monolingual: 1. [for something] to fold or point inward. _ Do my toes turn in too much? _ The legs of the table turned in at the bottom, giving a quaint appearance to the piece of furniture.
examples: The legs of the table turned in at the bottom, giving a quaint appearance to the piece of furniture.

turn off.monolingual: [for something] to go off; to switch off. _ All the lights turn off automatically.
examples: All the lights turn off automatically.

turn on.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to switch on and start running. _The lights turned on right at dusk. _At what time do the street lights turn on?
examples: The lights turned on right at dusk.

turn out.monolingual: [for something] to aim outward. _ Her toes turned out just right for a ballet dancer. _ The legs of the chair turned out just a little, adding a bit of stability.
examples: Her toes turned out just right for a ballet dancer.

turn over a new leaf.monolingual: Fig. to begin again, fresh; to reform and begin again. (Fig. on turning to a fresh page. The leaf is a page—a fresh, clean page.) _ I have made a mess of my life. I’ll turn over a new leaf and hope to do better. _ Why don’t you turn over a new leaf a
examples: I have made a mess of my life.

turn the corner.monolingual: Fig. to pass a critical point in a process. _The patient turned the corner last night. She should begin to show improvement now. _ The project has turned the corner. The rest should be easy.
examples: The patient turned the corner last night.

turn the other cheek.monolingual: Fig. to ignore abuse or an insult. _ When Bob got mad at Mary and yelled at her, she just turned the other cheek. _ Usually I turn the other cheek when someone is rude to me.
examples: When Bob got mad at Mary and yelled at her, she just turned the other cheek.

turn the tide.monolingual: Fig. to cause a reversal in the direction of events; to cause a reversal in public opinion. _ It looked as if the team were going to lose, but near the end of the game, our star player turned the tide. _At first, people were opposed to our plan. Afte
examples: It looked as if the team were going to lose, but near the end of the game, our star player turned the tide.

turn to.monolingual: Fig. to begin to get busy. _Come on, you guys! Turn to! Let’s get to work. _If you people will turn to, we can finish this work in no time at all.
examples: Come on, you guys! Turn to! Let’s get to work.

turn turtle.monolingual: Fig. to turn upside down. _ The sailboat turned turtle, but the sailors only got wet. _ The car ran off the road and turned turtle in the ditch.
examples: The sailboat turned turtle, but the sailors only got wet.

turn up.monolingual: 1. [for part of something] to point upward. _The ends of the elf ’s funny little shoes turned up.
examples: The ends of the elf ’s funny little shoes turned up.

twilight years.monolingual: Fig. the last years before death. _ In his twilight years, he became more mellow and stopped yelling at people.
examples: In his twilight years, he became more mellow and stopped yelling at people.

twist up.monolingual: 1. to move upward in a twisting path. _ The smoke twisted up into the sky. _ As the car twisted up the narrow path, we got a good view of the valley.
examples: The smoke twisted up into the sky.

under the sun.monolingual: Fig. anywhere on earth at all. _ This is the largest cattle ranch under the sun. _ Isn’t there anyone under the sun who can help me with this problem?
examples: This is the largest cattle ranch under the sun.

under the weather.monolingual: 1. ill. _ I feel sort of under the weather today. _Whatever I ate for lunch is making me feel a bit under the weather.
examples: I feel sort of under the weather today.

under the wire.monolingual: Fig. just barely in time or on time. _ I turned in my report just under the wire. _ Bill was the last person to get in the door. He got in under the wire.
examples: I turned in my report just under the wire.

unsung hero.monolingual: Fig. a hero who has gotten no praise or recognition. _ The time has come to recognize all the unsung heroes of the battle for low-cost housing.
examples: The time has come to recognize all the unsung heroes of the battle for low-cost housing.

up a tree.monolingual: 1. confused; without an answer to a problem; in difficulty. _This whole business has me up a tree. _I’m up a tree, and I need some help.
examples: This whole business has me up a tree.

up and away.monolingual: Fig. [of a bird or an airplane] up into the air and into flight. _After a few seconds of speeding down the runway, our f light to Tucson was up and away. _ Just before the cat pounced on the sparrows, they were up and away and the cat was left with e
examples: After a few seconds of speeding down the runway, our f light to Tucson was up and away.

up and running.monolingual: Fig. [of a machine] functioning. _ As soon as we can get the tractor up and running, we will plant the corn crop.
examples: As soon as we can get the tractor up and running, we will plant the corn crop.

up for grabs.monolingual: 1. Fig. available for anyone; not yet claimed. _The election is up for grabs. Everything is still very chancy. _I don’t know who will get the promotion. It’s up for grabs.
examples: The election is up for grabs.

up front.monolingual: 1. in the forefront; under fire (at the front). _ You guys who are up front are gonna get the most fire. _ You two go up front and see if you can help.
examples: You guys who are up front are gonna get the most fire.

up the river.monolingual: Sl. in prison. (Underworld.) _ Gary was up the river for a couple of years, but that doesn’t make him an outcast, does it? _The judge who sent him up the river was indicted for accepting bribery. If Gary had only known sooner!
examples: The judge who sent him up the river was indicted for accepting bribery.

up the wall.monolingual: Fig. in a very bad situation; very upset or anxious. _ He’s really up the wall about Mary’s illness. _ We were all up the wall until the matter was resolved.
examples: He’s really up the wall about Mary’s illness.

up to no good.monolingual: Fig. doing something bad. _ I could tell from the look on Tom’s face that he was up to no good. _ There are three boys in the front yard. I don’t know what they are doing, but I think they are up to no good.
examples: I could tell from the look on Tom’s face that he was up to no good.

upper crust.monolingual: Fig. the higher levels of society; the upper class. (From the top, as opposed to the bottom, crust of a pie.) _Jane speaks like that because she pretends to be from the upper crust, but her father was a miner. _James is from the upper crust, but he i
examples: Jane speaks like that because she pretends to be from the upper crust, but her father was a miner.

veg out.monolingual: to cease working and take it easy; to vegetate. _ Someday, I just want to veg out and enjoy life. _I think I’ll just veg this weekend.
examples: Someday, I just want to veg out and enjoy life.

vim and vigor.monolingual: Cliché energy; enthusiasm. _ Show more vim and vigor! Let us know you’re alive. _ She’s sure got a lot of vim and vigor.
examples: Show more vim and vigor! Let us know you’re alive.

wake the dead.monolingual: Fig. to be so loud as to wake those who are “sleeping” the most soundly: the dead. _You are making enough noise to wake the dead. _ Stop hollering! You’ll wake the dead!
examples: You are making enough noise to wake the dead.

wake up.monolingual: to awaken; to become alert. _Wake up! We have to get on the road. _ It’s time to wake up!
examples: Wake up! We have to get on the road.

walk around.monolingual: to move around walking; to pace around. _ I need to walk around and get some fresh air. _ Why don’t we walk around for a while before we go in?
examples: I need to walk around and get some fresh air.

walk off.monolingual: to walk away; to leave on foot abruptly. _ She didn’t even say good-bye. She just walked off. _ He walked off and never looked back.
examples: She didn’t even say good-bye.

walk on.monolingual: to continue walking. _ Walk on. Go all the way to the end. _ I knew I wasn’t there yet, so I just walked on.
examples: Walk on. Go all the way to the end.

walk on eggshells.monolingual: 1. Fig. to walk very carefully; to take steps gingerly. _ Since he stumbled and fell against the china cabinet, Bill has been walking on eggshells.
examples: Since he stumbled and fell against the china cabinet, Bill has been walking on eggshells.

walk the floor.monolingual: Fig. to pace nervously while waiting. _ While Bill waited for news of the operation, he walked the f loor for hours on end. _Walking the f loor won’t help. You might as well sit down and relax.
examples: While Bill waited for news of the operation, he walked the f loor for hours on end.

walk the plank.monolingual: Fig. to suffer punishment at the hand of someone. (Fig. on the image of pirates making their blindfolded captives die by walking off the end of a plank jutting out over the open sea.) _Fred may think he can make the members of my department walk the
examples: Fred may think he can make the members of my department walk the plank, but we will fight back.

want for nothing.monolingual: Fig. not to lack anything; to have everything one needs or desires. _The Smiths don’t have much money, but their children seem to want for nothing. _Lisa’s husband spoils her. She wants for nothing.
examples: The Smiths don’t have much money, but their children seem to want for nothing.

warm body.monolingual: a person; just any person (who can be counted on to be present). _ See if you can get a couple of warm bodies to stand at the door and hand out programs. _ You mean among all these warm bodies nobody knows calculus?
examples: See if you can get a couple of warm bodies to stand at the door and hand out programs.

warts and all.monolingual: Cliché even with the flaws. _ It’s a great performance—warts and all. _ Yes, we admire each other very much, warts and all.
examples: It’s a great performance—warts and all.

wash away.monolingual: to be carried away by water or some other liquid. _ The bridge washed away in the f lood. _ All the soil washed away and left the rocks exposed.
examples: The bridge washed away in the f lood.

wash out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to fail and be removed from something, such as school. _ I studied all I could, but I still washed out. _I don’t want to wash out. It’s my whole future.
examples: I studied all I could, but I still washed out.

washed out.monolingual: Inf. exhausted; tired. _ I feel too washed out to go to work today. _ Poor Ted really looks washed out.
examples: I feel too washed out to go to work today.

waste away.monolingual: to wither or dwindle away. _Our money just seemed to waste away. _ As she grew older, she just sort of wasted away.
examples: Our money just seemed to waste away.

watering hole.monolingual: 1. Lit. a place where there is water for animals (and people) to drink. _ The elephants came down to the watering hole and chased away the lions so they could drink in peace.
examples: The elephants came down to the watering hole and chased away the lions so they could drink in peace.

weak sister.monolingual: a timid person, usually a male. _It looks like Dave is the weak sister on the team. _ We’ve got to pull together and stop playing like a bunch of weak sisters.
examples: It looks like Dave is the weak sister on the team.

wear down.monolingual: Fig. to break down with wear; to erode. _The steps had worn down so much that each one was curved and slanted dangerously.
examples: The steps had worn down so much that each one was curved and slanted dangerously.

wear off.monolingual: [for the effects of something] to become less; to stop gradually. _ The effects of the painkiller wore off and my tooth began to hurt. _ I was annoyed at first, but my anger wore off.
examples: The effects of the painkiller wore off and my tooth began to hurt.

wear out.monolingual: to become worn from use; to become diminished or useless from use. _My car engine is about to wear out. _ It takes a lot of driving to wear out an engine.
examples: My car engine is about to wear out.

weather the storm.monolingual: 1. Fig. to experience and survive a storm. _ We decided to stay in the building and weather the storm there with the other visitors.
examples: We decided to stay in the building and weather the storm there with the other visitors.

week in, week out.monolingual: Fig. every week, week after week. _ We have the same old food, week in, week out. _ I’m tired of this job. I’ve done the same thing—week in, week out— for three years.
examples: We have the same old food, week in, week out.

weird out.monolingual: Sl. to become emotionally disturbed or unnerved; to flip out. _ The day was just gross. I thought I would weird out at noon. _ I weirded out at the news of Frankie’s death.
examples: The day was just gross.

wheel around.monolingual: to turn around quickly; to change direction quickly. _ She wheeled around quickly to face him. _ Suddenly, Roger wheeled around and started chasing Wally.
examples: She wheeled around quickly to face him.

when the chips are down.monolingual: Fig. at the final, critical moment; when things really get difficult. _ When the chips are down, I know that I can depend on Jean to help out. _I knew you would come and help when the chips were down.
examples: When the chips are down, I know that I can depend on Jean to help out.

whistle in the dark.monolingual: Fig. to guess aimlessly; to speculate as to a fact. _Am I close, or am I just whistling in the dark? _ She was whistling in the dark. She has no idea of what’s going on.
examples: She was whistling in the dark.

whoop it up.monolingual: to celebrate, especially with cheers and whoops. _It was a very noisy party. Everyone was whooping it up well past midnight. _ The campaign workers whooped it up for their candidate. _ I can’t get out there and whoop it up for something I don’t belie
examples: It was a very noisy party.

wide open.monolingual: 1. as fast as possible; at full throttle. _ I was driving along wide open when I became aware of a f lashing red light. _ It was wide open and still wouldn’t do better than eighty.
examples: I was driving along wide open when I became aware of a f lashing red light.

wig out.monolingual: Sl. to become intoxicated. _ One more drink and Wally will wig out. _This guy has wigged out. Get him out of here.
examples: One more drink and Wally will wig out.

win by a nose.monolingual: Fig. to win by the slightest amount of difference. (Can be literal in horses races.) _I ran the fastest race I could, but I only won by a nose. _Sally won the race, but she only won by a nose.
examples: I ran the fastest race I could, but I only won by a nose.

wind back.monolingual: [for something, such as a road] to turn so that it heads in the direction from whence it came. _The road we got lost on wound back and we were not able to reach the lake on time. _ When we were lost, we found a stream in the woods, but it wound back
examples: The road we got lost on wound back and we were not able to reach the lake on time.

wind down.monolingual: to start running or operating slower. _Things will begin to wind down at the end of the summer. _ As things wind down, life will be a lot easier. _ The clock wound down and finally stopped.
examples: Things will begin to wind down at the end of the summer.

wipe out.monolingual: 1. Inf. to crash. _ I wiped out on the curve. _ The car wiped out on the curve.
examples: I wiped out on the curve.

wishful thinking.monolingual: believing that something is true or that something will happen just because one wishes that it were true or would happen. _ Hoping for a car as a birthday present is just wishful thinking. Your parents can’t afford it. _Mary thinks that she is going
examples: Hoping for a car as a birthday present is just wishful thinking.

with a vengeance.monolingual: Cliché with determination and eagerness. _ The angry soldier attacked the enemy with a vengeance. _ Bill ate all his dinner and gobbled up his dessert with a vengeance.
examples: The angry soldier attacked the enemy with a vengeance.

with a will.monolingual: with determination and enthusiasm. _ The children worked with a will to finish the project on time. _ The workers set about manufacturing the new products with a will.
examples: The children worked with a will to finish the project on time.

with bated breath.monolingual: Cliché while holding one’s breath. _ We stood there with bated breath while the man hung on the side of the bridge. _ They listened with bated breath for the announcement about the winner.
examples: We stood there with bated breath while the man hung on the side of the bridge.

with flying colors.monolingual: Cliché easily and excellently. _ John passed his geometry test with f lying colors. _ Sally qualified for the race with f lying colors.
examples: John passed his geometry test with f lying colors.

wither away.monolingual: to shrivel up; to shrink up. _Soon, the wart withered away. _ Many of our roses withered away in the hot sun.
examples: Soon, the wart withered away.

without a hitch.monolingual: Fig. with no problem(s). _ Everything went off without a hitch. _ We hoped the job would go off without a hitch.
examples: Everything went off without a hitch.

without batting an eye.monolingual: Lit. Fig. without showing alarm or response; without blinking an eye. _ I knew I had insulted her, and she turned to me and asked me to leave without batting an eye. _ Right in the middle of the speech—without batting an eye—the speaker walked off th
examples: I knew I had insulted her, and she turned to me and asked me to leave without batting an eye.

without fail.monolingual: for certain; absolutely. _I’ll be there at noon without fail. _ The plane leaves on time every day without fail.
examples: I’ll be there at noon without fail.

without further ado.monolingual: Cliché without further talk. (An overworked phrase usually heard in public announcements.) _ And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr. Bill Franklin! _ The time has come to leave, so without further ado, good evening and good-bye.
examples: And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr.

work of art.monolingual: 1. Lit. a piece of art. _She purchased a lovely work of art for her living room.
examples: She purchased a lovely work of art for her living room.

work out.monolingual: 1. [for something] to turn out all right in the end. _ Don’t worry. Everything will work out. _ This will work out. Don’t worry.
examples: Don’t worry. Everything will work out.

work together.monolingual: [for people or things] to cooperate or function together. _Come now! Let’s all work together and get this done on time! _ We will work together on this and enjoy it more.
examples: We will work together on this and enjoy it more.

wrack and ruin.monolingual: Cliché complete destruction or ruin. _ They went back after the fire and saw the wrack and ruin that used to be their house. _ Drinking brought him nothing but wrack and ruin.
examples: They went back after the fire and saw the wrack and ruin that used to be their house.

year in, year out.monolingual: year after year; for years. _ I seem to have hay fever year in, year out. I never get over it. _ John wears the same old suit, year in, year out.
examples: I seem to have hay fever year in, year out.

yell out.monolingual: to cry out; to shout loudly. _ The pain caused the child to yell out. _ I yelled out, but no one heard me.
examples: The pain caused the child to yell out.

yours truly.monolingual: 1. a closing phrase at the end of a letter, just before the signature. _ Yours truly, Tom Jones. _ Best wishes from yours truly, Bill Smith.
examples: Yours truly, Tom Jones.

zonk out.monolingual: Sl. to collapse from exhaustion; to go into a stupor from drugs or exhaustion. _ I’m gonna go home and zonk out. _ I went home after the trip and just zonked out.
examples: I’m gonna go home and zonk out.

zoom out.monolingual: to move back to a wider angle picture using a zoom lens. _ The camera zoomed out. _ Pan out at this point in the script and give a wider view of the scene.
examples: The camera zoomed out.

all over.monolingual: 1. finished. _ Dinner is all over. I’m sorry you didn’t get any. _ It’s all over. He’s dead now.
examples: Dinner is all over.

as long as.monolingual: 1. since; because. _ As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread. _ So long as you’re here, please stay for dinner.
examples: As long as you’re going to the bakery, please buy some fresh bread.

so long as.monolingual: if; only if. _ You may have dessert so long as you eat all your vegetables. _You can go out this evening as long as you promise to be home by midnight.
examples: You may have dessert so long as you eat all your vegetables.

balance the books.monolingual: to determine through bookkeeping that accounts are in balance, that all money is accounted for. _Jane was up all night balancing the accounts. _The cashier was not allowed to leave the bank until the manager balanced the books.
examples: Jane was up all night balancing the accounts.

blow a fuse.monolingual: 1. to burn out the fuse on an electrical circuit and lose power. _The microwave oven blew a fuse, so we had no power. _ You’ll blow a fuse if you use too many appliances at once.
examples: The microwave oven blew a fuse, so we had no power.

blow off.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to be carried off something by moving air. _ The leaves of the trees blew off in the strong wind. _My papers blew off the table.
examples: The leaves of the trees blew off in the strong wind.

boil down.monolingual: Lit. [for a liquid] to be condensed to something by boiling. _Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.
examples: Boil this mixture down to about half of what it was.

cut across.monolingual: Lit. to travel across a particular area; to take a shortcut across a particular area. _ Please don’t cut across the neighbor’s yard anymore.
examples: Please don’t cut across the neighbor’s yard anymore.

fall into a trap.monolingual: 1. Lit. to get caught in a trap. _The tiger fell into a trap and leapt out again immediately. _The boys tried to get a squirrel to fall into a trap, but squirrels are too clever.
examples: The tiger fell into a trap and leapt out again immediately.

flare up.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for something] to ignite and burn. _The firewood flared up at last—four matches having been used.
examples: The firewood flared up at last—four matches having been used.

fly in.monolingual: to go to something or some place by air; to arrive by air. _ When are you going to f ly into the airport? _We will f ly into Detroit tomorrow.
examples: We will f ly into Detroit tomorrow.

go to seed.monolingual: 1. Lit. [for a plant] to grow long enough to produce seed; [for a plant] to spend its energy going to seed. _ The lettuce went to seed and we couldn’t eat it. _ Plants like that ought not to be allowed to go to seed.
examples: The lettuce went to seed and we couldn’t eat it.

hold up.monolingual: 1. Lit. to endure; to last a long time. _ How long will this cloth hold up? _ I want my money back for this chair. It isn’t holding up well.
examples: I want my money back for this chair.

in the spotlight.monolingual: 1. Fig. in the beam of a spotlight, as on a stage. _ The singer was in the spotlight but the band was almost in the dark.
examples: The singer was in the spotlight but the band was almost in the dark.

in the limelight.monolingual: Fig. at the center of attention. (Limelight refers to an obsolete type of spotlight, and the word occurs only in this phrase.) _ John will do almost anything to get himself into the limelight. _ I love being in the spotlight. _ All elected officials
examples: John will do almost anything to get himself into the limelight.

keep on.monolingual: Lit. to work to remain mounted on something, such as a horse, bicycle, etc._It’s really hard for me to keep on a horse. _ It’s hard to keep on when it’s moving all over the place.
examples: It’s really hard for me to keep on a horse.

kick off.monolingual: 1. Lit. to start play in a football game by kicking the ball. _ Tom kicked off in the last game. Now it’s my turn. _ John tripped when he was kicking off.
examples: Tom kicked off in the last game.

kick the bucket.monolingual: Fig. to die. _ Don’t say that George Washington “kicked off.” Say that he “passed away.” _ My cat kicked off last night. She was tough as a lion. _When I kick the bucket, I want a huge funeral with lots of flowers and crying.
examples: Don’t say that George Washington “kicked off.

knock around.monolingual: 1. to waste time. _ Stop knocking around and get to work! _ I need a couple of days a week just for knocking around.
examples: I need a couple of days a week just for knocking around.

kick around.monolingual: to wander around; to bum around. _ I think I’ll knock around a few months before looking for another job. _We’re just knocking around and keeping out of trouble.
examples: I think I’ll knock around a few months before looking for another job.

lather up.monolingual: 1. [for a horse] to develop a foam of sweat from working very hard. _ The horses lathered up heavily during the race. _Don’t let your horse lather up!
examples: The horses lathered up heavily during the race.

out to lunch.monolingual: 1. Lit. eating lunch away from one’s place of work or activity. _I’m sorry, but Sally Jones is out to lunch. May I take a message? _ She’s been out to lunch for nearly two hours. When will she be back?
examples: I’m sorry, but Sally Jones is out to lunch.

pan out.monolingual: to move back to a wider angle picture using a zoom lens. _ The camera zoomed out. _ Pan out at this point in the script and give a wider view of the scene.
examples: The camera zoomed out.

play by ear.monolingual: to play a musical instrument well, without formal training. _ John can play the piano by ear. _ If I could play by ear, I wouldn’t have to take lessons—or practice!
examples: John can play the piano by ear.

poke around.monolingual: 1. to look or search around. _ I’ve been poking around in the library looking for some statistics. _ I don’t mind if you look in my drawer for a paper clip, but please don’t poke about.
examples: I’ve been poking around in the library looking for some statistics.

poke about.monolingual: to look or search around. _ I’ve been poking around in the library looking for some statistics. _ I don’t mind if you look in my drawer for a paper clip, but please don’t poke about.
examples: I’ve been poking around in the library looking for some statistics.

reach for the sky.monolingual: 1. Fig. to set one’s sights high. _ Reach for the sky! Go for it! _You should always reach for the sky, but be prepared for not attaining your goals every time.
examples: You should always reach for the sky, but be prepared for not attaining your goals every time.

run the gauntlet.monolingual: 1. Lit. to race, as a punishment, between parallel lines of men who thrash one as one runs. _ The knight was forced to doff his clothes and run the gauntlet.
examples: The knight was forced to doff his clothes and run the gauntlet.

slip away.monolingual: 1. to go away or escape quietly or in secret; to slip out. _ I slipped away when no one was looking. _Let’s slip off somewhere and have a little talk. _ I’ll try to slip out for an hour or two when Tom is asleep.
examples: I slipped away when no one was looking.

slip off.monolingual: to go away or escape quietly or in secret; to slip out. _ I slipped away when no one was looking. _Let’s slip off somewhere and have a little talk. _ I’ll try to slip out for an hour or two when Tom is asleep.
examples: I slipped away when no one was looking.

slip by.monolingual: 1. to move by someone or something quickly or unnoticed; to move through a tight area or past someone or something in a tight area. _The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.
examples: The hall was narrow, and I could hardly have slipped by.

slow on the uptake.monolingual: Fig. slow to figure something out; slow-thinking. _ Sally didn’t get the joke because she’s sort of slow on the draw. _ Bill—who’s slow on the uptake—didn’t get the joke until it was explained to him.
examples: Sally didn’t get the joke because she’s sort of slow on the draw.

turn over.monolingual: 1. Lit. to rotate so that the side that was on the bottom is now on top. _ The turtle turned over and crawled away. _ She turned over to get some sun on her back.
examples: The turtle turned over and crawled away.

kick over.monolingual: Fig. [for an engine] to start or to rotate. _ My car engine was so cold that it wouldn’t even turn over. _ The engine kicked over a few times and then stopped for good.
examples: My car engine was so cold that it wouldn’t even turn over.

warm up.monolingual: 1. [for the weather or a person] to become warmer or hotter. _ I think it is going to warm up next week.
examples: I think it is going to warm up next week.
